bio_edx.0.0.summary: All living things are made of cells, and every cell contains smaller parts called **sub-cellular structures**, each with a job that keeps the cell alive. **Eukaryotic cells** (animal and plant cells) keep their genetic material inside a **nucleus**, while **prokaryotic cells** (bacteria) are much smaller and have no nucleus, so their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm. For Edexcel you must be able to name each structure, state its function and explain how the structure is related to that function.

core.h: The big picture: cells and sub-cellular structures
core.p: A cell is the basic unit of all living organisms. Inside a cell are sub-cellular structures. Each one carries out a particular function, and the cell only survives because all of them work together. Edexcel asks you to explain how the structures are **related to their functions**, so a list of names is never enough: you must link each part to what it does.
bullets: Animal cells: you must know the **nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes**.
Plant cells: you must know the **nucleus, cell membrane, cell wall, chloroplasts, mitochondria, vacuole and ribosomes**.
Bacteria: you must know **chromosomal DNA, plasmid DNA, cell membrane, ribosomes and flagella**.
The **cytoplasm** is the jelly-like substance that fills every cell and is where most chemical reactions take place.
Singular and plural matter: one mitochondrion, many mitochondria; one flagellum, many flagella; one nucleus, many nuclei.

callouts.p: A part of a cell that has a particular function, for example the nucleus, a mitochondrion or a ribosome.
When a question says 'describe the function', say what the structure does. When it says 'explain', add why that matters to the cell.

core.p: Cells are divided into two groups according to how their genetic material is stored. In **eukaryotic cells** the DNA is enclosed in a nucleus. In **prokaryotic cells** there is no nucleus, so the DNA is found free in the cytoplasm.
bullets: **Eukaryotic cells** include animal cells and plant cells. Organisms made of eukaryotic cells are called eukaryotes.
**Prokaryotic cells** are bacteria. A bacterium is a single-celled organism, so the one cell is the whole organism.
Prokaryotic cells are **much smaller** than eukaryotic cells.
Eukaryotic cells contain mitochondria (and chloroplasts in plants). Prokaryotic cells have **no mitochondria and no chloroplasts**.
Both types have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes.

head: Feature
Eukaryotic cell
Prokaryotic cell
rows: Free in the cytoplasm as chromosomal DNA, plus plasmids

callouts.p: A cell that has its genetic material enclosed in a nucleus.
A cell that does not have a nucleus; its genetic material is free in the cytoplasm.

core.p: The nucleus is found in animal and plant cells. It contains the cell's **genetic material (DNA)**, arranged as chromosomes. The DNA carries the genes, which are the instructions for making proteins, so the nucleus **controls the activities of the cell**.
bullets: Function: contains genetic material (DNA) that controls the activities of the cell.
WHY it controls the cell: genes are instructions for making proteins, and proteins (such as enzymes) control the reactions that happen in the cell.
The nucleus is usually the largest structure you can see in an animal cell with a light microscope.
Bacteria do NOT have a nucleus. Never label a nucleus on a bacterial cell.

callouts.p: Nucleus: contains DNA / genetic material and controls the activities of the cell. 'The brain of the cell' does not score.

core.p: Every cell, eukaryotic or prokaryotic, is surrounded by a cell membrane. It forms the boundary between the cytoplasm and the outside, and it **controls which substances enter and leave the cell**.
bullets: Function: controls what enters and leaves the cell.
It lets some substances pass through but not others.
WHY it matters: the cell must take in useful substances such as glucose and oxygen and get rid of waste such as carbon dioxide, while holding the contents of the cell together.
In plant cells and bacteria the cell membrane lies just **inside** the cell wall. It is still there even though it is hard to see.
Animal cells have a cell membrane but no cell wall, so the membrane is the outer boundary of an animal cell.

callouts.p: The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves. The cell wall supports and strengthens. Do not swap these two functions.

core.p: Mitochondria are found in the cytoplasm of animal and plant cells. They are where **aerobic respiration** takes place. Respiration **releases energy** from glucose, and the cell uses that energy for all its other processes.
bullets: Function: site of (aerobic) respiration, which releases energy for the cell.
Say energy is **released** or **transferred**. Energy is never 'made', 'produced' or 'created'.
WHY cells differ: a cell that needs a lot of energy has **many mitochondria**. Examples are muscle cells and sperm cells.
Plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts, because plant cells respire all the time.
Bacteria have no mitochondria.

callouts.p: More mitochondria means more respiration, so more energy is released. Use this chain whenever a question shows a cell packed with mitochondria.

core.p: Ribosomes are very small structures found in the cytoplasm of ALL cells: animal, plant and bacterial. They are the site of **protein synthesis**, which means they are where proteins are made.
bullets: Function: where proteins are made (protein synthesis).
WHY they matter: proteins include enzymes, so a cell cannot carry out its reactions or grow without ribosomes.
Cells that make a lot of protein have a large number of ribosomes.
Ribosomes are too small to be seen with a light microscope. They appear as tiny dots in electron microscope images.

callouts.p: Write 'protein synthesis' or 'proteins are made here'. Ribosomes do not release energy and do not 'store' protein.

core.h: Plant cell extras: cell wall, chloroplasts and vacuole
core.p: Plant cells have every structure listed for animal cells plus three more. Each extra structure is linked to how a plant lives: it stays in one place, makes its own food by photosynthesis and has no skeleton to hold it up.
bullets: **Cell wall**: made of **cellulose**. It **supports and strengthens** the cell and helps it keep its shape.
**Chloroplasts**: contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which absorbs light. They are where **photosynthesis** takes place, making glucose for the plant.
**Vacuole**: a large permanent space filled with **cell sap**. It helps to **support** the cell by keeping it firm (turgid).
Chloroplasts are only found in the green parts of a plant that receive light. **Root cells have no chloroplasts** because they are underground in the dark, where photosynthesis cannot happen.
The cell wall lets water and dissolved substances pass through freely; it is the cell membrane, not the wall, that controls what enters and leaves.

head: Structure
What it is like
Function
rows: Rigid layer of cellulose outside the cell membrane
Absorbs light for photosynthesis, which makes glucose
Stores cell sap and helps keep the cell firm for support

callouts.p: The chloroplast is the structure. Chlorophyll is the green substance inside it that absorbs light. Check which one the question asks for.

core.h: Comparing animal cells and plant cells
core.p: Animal and plant cells are both eukaryotic, so they share four of the named structures. A plant cell has three more. Comparison questions want both the similarities and the differences.
bullets: Both have: nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes (and cytoplasm).
Only plant cells have: a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole.
Plant cells usually have a regular, fixed shape because of the cell wall. Animal cells have a less regular shape.
When you compare, make a statement about BOTH cells, for example 'plant cells have a cell wall but animal cells do not'.

core.h: Bacterial cells: chromosomal DNA and plasmid DNA
core.p: A bacterium has no nucleus, so its genetic material is arranged differently. It has two kinds of DNA, and you must be able to tell them apart.
bullets: **Chromosomal DNA**: one large loop of DNA that lies **free in the cytoplasm**. It carries most of the cell's genes and controls the activities of the cell.
**Plasmid DNA**: **small loops (rings) of extra DNA**, separate from the chromosomal DNA. A bacterium can have several plasmids.
Plasmids carry a small number of extra genes. A common example is genes for **antibiotic resistance**.
Chromosomal DNA does the job that the DNA in a nucleus does in a eukaryotic cell. The difference is that it is not enclosed in a nucleus.

head: Chromosomal DNA
Plasmid DNA
rows: A few extra genes, for example antibiotic resistance

callouts.p: A small loop of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the chromosomal DNA.
Never write that bacterial DNA is 'in the nucleus'. Write that it is free in the cytoplasm.

core.h: Bacterial cells: cell membrane, ribosomes and flagella
core.p: Bacteria share some structures with eukaryotic cells, and some bacteria have flagella so that they can move.
bullets: **Cell membrane**: controls what enters and leaves the cell, exactly as in animal and plant cells.
**Ribosomes**: where proteins are made. Bacterial ribosomes are smaller than those of eukaryotic cells.
**Flagella** (singular: flagellum): long tail-like structures on the outside of the cell. A flagellum **rotates** to **move the bacterium** along.
WHY movement helps: the bacterium can move towards useful substances such as food and away from harmful substances.
Not all bacteria have flagella. Some have one and some have several.
Bacteria also have a cell wall outside the membrane, but it is **not made of cellulose**, so it is different from a plant cell wall.

callouts.p: For bacteria the spec lists chromosomal DNA, plasmid DNA, cell membrane, ribosomes and flagella. Learn a function for each.

core.h: Comparing bacteria with animal and plant cells
core.p: The most common exam question on this point asks for differences between a bacterial cell and an animal or plant cell. Give paired statements and use the words eukaryotic and prokaryotic correctly.
bullets: A bacterial cell has no nucleus; animal and plant cells have a nucleus.
A bacterial cell has chromosomal DNA free in the cytoplasm and plasmids; animal and plant cells have neither plasmids nor free chromosomal DNA.
A bacterial cell has no mitochondria and no chloroplasts.
Some bacterial cells have flagella for movement.
Similarities: all three have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes.
Bacterial cells are much smaller than animal and plant cells.

callouts.p: If a cell diagram shows loops of DNA and no nucleus, it is prokaryotic. If it shows a nucleus, it is eukaryotic. State the evidence you used.

core.h: Linking structures to what a cell does
core.p: Grade 9 answers explain why a particular cell has more or less of a structure. The amount of each structure matches the job of the cell.
bullets: A cell that needs lots of energy has many **mitochondria**, because more respiration releases more energy.
A cell that makes lots of protein (for example enzymes) has many **ribosomes**, because proteins are made at ribosomes.
A leaf cell near the top of a leaf has many **chloroplasts**, because it receives most light, so more light is absorbed for photosynthesis.
A root cell has **no chloroplasts**, because it receives no light.
Build a three-step chain: name the structure, state its function, link it to the job of that cell.

callouts.p: Structure, then function, then benefit to this cell. Example: many mitochondria; respiration takes place there; so more energy is released for movement.

analogy.t: A cell is like a factory
analogy.p: Think of a eukaryotic cell as a factory. The **nucleus** is the manager's office where the instruction manuals (DNA) are kept. The **cell membrane** is the security gate that controls what comes in and goes out. **Mitochondria** are the generators that release the energy the factory runs on. **Ribosomes** are the workbenches where the products (proteins) are assembled. A plant cell adds strong outer walls (the **cell wall**), solar panels (**chloroplasts**) and a big water tank that keeps the building firm (the **vacuole**). A bacterium is a one-room workshop: the instructions lie loose on the floor (**chromosomal DNA**) with a few extra instruction cards (**plasmids**), and there is an outboard motor on the outside (the **flagellum**). Where it breaks down: a factory is built by outside builders, but a cell makes all its own parts and can copy itself, and a generator burns fuel whereas mitochondria release energy by respiration, which is a series of enzyme-controlled reactions.

terms.d: A part of a cell that has a particular function.
A cell with its genetic material enclosed in a nucleus, such as an animal or plant cell.
A cell with no nucleus, such as a bacterium; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm.
Structure in eukaryotic cells that contains the genetic material (DNA) and controls the activities of the cell.
The boundary of the cell that controls which substances enter and leave.
The jelly-like substance inside a cell where most chemical reactions take place.
Structures where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy for the cell.
Very small structures where proteins are made (protein synthesis).
In plants, a layer of cellulose outside the cell membrane that supports and strengthens the cell.
The substance that plant cell walls are made of.
Structure in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place; it contains chlorophyll.
The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light for photosynthesis.
A large permanent space in a plant cell filled with cell sap; it helps to keep the cell firm.
The watery liquid stored in the vacuole of a plant cell.
The large loop of DNA in a bacterium that lies free in the cytoplasm and carries most of its genes.
Small loops of extra DNA in a bacterium, separate from the chromosomal DNA.
A long tail-like structure that rotates to move a bacterium; the plural is flagella.

mistakes.w: Mitochondria make energy for the cell.
mistakes.r: Energy cannot be made. Mitochondria are where respiration takes place, which RELEASES energy.

mistakes.w: The nucleus is the brain of the cell.
mistakes.r: The nucleus contains the genetic material (DNA) and controls the activities of the cell.

mistakes.w: The cell wall controls what enters and leaves the cell.
mistakes.r: The cell MEMBRANE controls what enters and leaves. The cell wall supports and strengthens the cell.

mistakes.w: The DNA of a bacterium is found in its nucleus.
mistakes.r: Bacteria have no nucleus. Their chromosomal DNA is free in the cytoplasm, and they also have plasmids.

mistakes.w: Plant cells have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria.
mistakes.r: Plant cells have BOTH. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis and mitochondria carry out respiration.

mistakes.w: Chloroplasts absorb light.
mistakes.r: Better: chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis.

mistakes.w: Ribosomes make energy / ribosomes make DNA.
mistakes.r: Ribosomes are where PROTEINS are made (protein synthesis).

mistakes.w: All plant cells contain chloroplasts.
mistakes.r: Only cells in the green parts that receive light do. Root cells have no chloroplasts.

mistakes.w: Animal cells have a cell wall.
mistakes.r: Animal cells have a cell membrane only. Plant cells and bacteria have a cell wall.

mistakes.w: The flagellum is used for protection or for feeding.
mistakes.r: A flagellum is used for movement; it rotates to move the bacterium.

exam.q: State the function of ribosomes.
model: (Site of) protein synthesis / where proteins are made.
exam.tip: One mark, one fact. 'Make proteins' is enough.

exam.q: Name the sub-cellular structure where aerobic respiration takes place.
model: Mitochondria / mitochondrion.
exam.tip: Spell it clearly; 'mitocondria' is usually accepted but 'chloroplast' never is.

exam.q: State two structures found in a plant cell that are not found in an animal cell.
model: Any two from: cell wall; chloroplast(s); (large permanent) vacuole.
exam.tip: Do not write 'cell membrane' or 'nucleus': both cells have those.

exam.q: Describe the function of the cell membrane.
model: Controls what / which substances enter and leave the cell.
exam.tip: Include both directions: enter AND leave.

exam.q: Give two differences between a bacterial cell and an animal cell.
model: Bacterial cell has no nucleus / has chromosomal DNA free in the cytoplasm, but an animal cell has a nucleus.
Bacterial cell has plasmids / flagella / a cell wall, but an animal cell does not. (Or: bacterial cell has no mitochondria but an animal cell has.)
exam.tip: Each difference needs a statement about both cells.

exam.q: Describe the function of the nucleus.
model: Contains genetic material / DNA / chromosomes / genes.
Controls the activities of the cell.
exam.tip: Two marks, so give two separate points.

exam.q: Muscle cells contain many mitochondria. Explain why.
model: Mitochondria are where (aerobic) respiration takes place.
So more energy is released for muscle contraction / movement.
exam.tip: Say energy is released, not produced.

exam.q: Explain why cells in the root of a plant do not contain chloroplasts.
model: Root cells are underground so they receive no light.
Chloroplasts are needed for photosynthesis, which cannot take place without light, so they would have no function.
exam.tip: Link the absence of the structure to the absence of light.

exam.q: Describe the roles of the cell wall and the vacuole in a plant cell.
model: Cell wall is made of cellulose.
Cell wall supports / strengthens the cell.
Vacuole contains cell sap and helps keep the cell firm / rigid / supported.
exam.tip: Mention cellulose: it is an easy mark that many students miss.

exam.q: A bacterium contains chromosomal DNA and plasmid DNA. Compare these two types of DNA.
model: Both are found free in the cytoplasm / neither is in a nucleus.
Chromosomal DNA is one large loop, whereas plasmids are small loops.
Chromosomal DNA carries most of the genes, whereas plasmids carry a few extra genes, for example for antibiotic resistance.
exam.tip: 'Compare' needs a similarity as well as differences.

exam.q: Explain how the sub-cellular structures of a bacterial cell are related to their functions.
model: Chromosomal DNA carries the genes that control the activities of the cell.
Plasmids are small loops of DNA carrying extra genes, such as antibiotic resistance.
Ribosomes are where proteins are made.
Flagella rotate to move the bacterium / cell membrane controls what enters and leaves.
exam.tip: Name a structure and give its function in the same sentence, four times.

exam.q: Compare the structure of a plant cell with the structure of a bacterial cell.
model: Similarities: both have a cell membrane, which controls what enters and leaves.
Both have ribosomes, where proteins are made, and both have cytoplasm.
Both have a cell wall, but the plant cell wall is made of cellulose and the bacterial cell wall is not.
The plant cell is eukaryotic: its DNA is in a nucleus. The bacterial cell is prokaryotic: it has no nucleus and its chromosomal DNA is free in the cytoplasm.
The bacterial cell has plasmids (small loops of DNA); the plant cell does not.
The plant cell has mitochondria, chloroplasts and a large vacuole; the bacterial cell has none of these.
Some bacterial cells have flagella for movement; plant cells do not. The bacterial cell is much smaller.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers are marked on levels. Give similarities AND differences, use the words eukaryotic and prokaryotic, and organise the answer in a logical order.

worked.q: A student is given a diagram of an unknown cell. It shows a cell wall, a cell membrane, ribosomes, one large loop of DNA in the cytoplasm, two small rings of DNA and a long tail-like structure. Identify the type of cell and justify your answer.
steps: Look for a nucleus. There is none: the DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm, so the cell is prokaryotic.
The large loop is chromosomal DNA and the two small rings are plasmids. Only bacteria have plasmids.
The long tail-like structure is a flagellum, used for movement.
There are no mitochondria or chloroplasts, which also fits a prokaryotic cell.
A cell wall alone does not decide it, because plant cells also have one.
worked.ans: It is a bacterial (prokaryotic) cell, because it has no nucleus, its chromosomal DNA is free in the cytoplasm, and it has plasmids and a flagellum.

worked.q: Cells in the pancreas make large amounts of enzymes, which are proteins. Predict and explain which two sub-cellular structures these cells will contain in large numbers.
steps: Enzymes are proteins, and proteins are made at ribosomes.
So the cells need many ribosomes to carry out a lot of protein synthesis.
Making proteins needs energy.
Energy is released by respiration in mitochondria, so the cells also need many mitochondria.
worked.ans: Many ribosomes, because these are where the protein (enzyme) is made, and many mitochondria, because respiration there releases the energy needed for protein synthesis.

worked.q: Explain why a plant cell from a leaf has both chloroplasts and mitochondria.
steps: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light.
Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts and makes glucose.
The cell still needs energy for its processes, and energy is released from glucose by respiration.
Respiration takes place in mitochondria, in the light and in the dark.
worked.ans: Chloroplasts are needed for photosynthesis, which makes glucose; mitochondria are needed for respiration, which releases the energy from glucose. The two structures do different jobs, so the cell needs both.

bio_edx.0.1.summary: A **specialised cell** has a structure that is adapted to carry out one particular function. Edexcel names three that you must know in detail: the **sperm cell** (acrosome, haploid nucleus, mitochondria and tail), the **egg cell** (nutrients in the cytoplasm, haploid nucleus and changes in the cell membrane after fertilisation) and the **ciliated epithelial cell** (cilia that move substances along a surface). For every adaptation you must name the feature and explain how it helps the cell do its job.

core.p: Most cells in a multicellular organism are not general-purpose cells. Each type has a particular shape and particular sub-cellular structures that suit one function. A feature that helps a cell carry out its function is called an **adaptation**.
bullets: Specialised cells have a specific function, and their structure is related to that function.
The three cells named by the specification are the **sperm cell**, the **egg cell** and the **ciliated epithelial cell**.
Sperm cells and egg cells are **gametes** (sex cells). Their function is sexual reproduction.
Ciliated epithelial cells line some tubes in the body. Their function is to move substances along the surface of the tube.
Exam answers follow one pattern: **name the feature, then say how it helps**.

callouts.p: A cell that has a structure adapted to carry out a particular function.
'It has a tail' scores nothing by itself in an explain question. 'It has a tail so that it can swim to the egg' scores.

core.h: Haploid and diploid: the idea behind both gametes
core.p: Most cells in the body are **diploid**: their nucleus contains two sets of chromosomes. Gametes are **haploid**: their nucleus contains only one set, which is half the number found in a body cell. In humans a body cell has 46 chromosomes and a gamete has 23.
bullets: Sperm cell: haploid nucleus with 23 chromosomes (in humans).
Egg cell: haploid nucleus with 23 chromosomes (in humans).
At **fertilisation** the two haploid nuclei fuse (join), so the fertilised egg cell has 23 + 23 = 46 chromosomes. It is diploid.
WHY gametes must be haploid: if they were diploid, the number of chromosomes would double every generation (46 + 46 = 92).
The fertilised egg cell is called a **zygote**. It divides by mitosis to form an embryo.

head: Cell
Haploid or diploid
Chromosomes in humans
rows: Body cell, for example a skin cell

callouts.p: Having one set of chromosomes; half the number of chromosomes found in a normal body cell.
Having two sets of chromosomes.

core.h: The function of a sperm cell
core.p: The sperm cell is the male gamete. Its function is to **carry the male DNA to the egg cell** and fertilise it. To do that it has to swim a long way compared with its own size, reach the egg and then get through the layers around the egg. Each of its four named adaptations solves one of those problems.
bullets: Problem 1: getting to the egg. Solved by the **tail**.
Problem 2: energy for swimming. Solved by many **mitochondria**.
Problem 3: getting into the egg. Solved by the **acrosome**.
Problem 4: giving the correct number of chromosomes. Solved by the **haploid nucleus**.
Sperm cells are also small with a streamlined shape, which helps them swim.

callouts.p: Acrosome, haploid nucleus, mitochondria, tail. These are the four the spec lists, so these are the four to learn.

core.h: Sperm cell: the tail and the mitochondria
core.p: The tail and the mitochondria work together, so learn them as a pair. The tail gives movement, and the mitochondria release the energy that the movement needs.
bullets: The **tail** moves from side to side so that the sperm cell can **swim** towards the egg cell.
The middle section of the sperm cell, between the head and the tail, is packed with **mitochondria**.
Mitochondria are where **respiration** takes place. Respiration **releases energy**.
That energy is needed for the tail to move.
WHY so many: swimming needs a lot of energy, and more mitochondria means more respiration, so more energy is released.
WHY they sit next to the tail: the energy is released close to where it is needed.

callouts.p: Mitochondria release energy by respiration. Writing that they make, produce or create energy loses the mark.

core.h: Sperm cell: the acrosome and the haploid nucleus
core.p: Both of these structures are in the head of the sperm cell. The acrosome is at the very front tip and the nucleus fills most of the rest of the head.
bullets: The **acrosome** contains **enzymes**.
When the sperm cell reaches the egg cell, the enzymes are released and **digest (break down) the outer layers of the egg cell**, including the jelly coat.
This lets the sperm cell get through to the egg's cell membrane so that the sperm nucleus can enter the egg.
The **haploid nucleus** contains one set of chromosomes: the male parent's genetic material.
It fuses with the haploid nucleus of the egg cell at fertilisation, giving a diploid fertilised egg cell.
The head contains very little cytoplasm, which helps keep the cell small and streamlined.

head: Sperm feature
What it is
How it helps
rows: Store of enzymes at the tip of the head
Enzymes digest the outer layers of the egg cell so the sperm can get in
Nucleus with one set of chromosomes
Fertilisation gives a diploid cell with the correct number of chromosomes
Respiration releases energy for the tail to move
Lets the sperm cell swim to the egg cell

callouts.p: 'The acrosome contains enzymes' is one mark. 'To digest / break down the outer layer of the egg cell' is the second.

core.h: The function of an egg cell
core.p: The egg cell is the female gamete. Its function is to **carry the female DNA** and, once fertilised, to **provide for the embryo in its early stages**. It does not need to move by itself, so it has no tail. Instead it is large, because it has to hold a store of nutrients.
bullets: The egg cell is much larger than the sperm cell.
It has a haploid nucleus, a cytoplasm packed with nutrients and a cell membrane that changes after fertilisation.
It is surrounded by a layer called the **jelly coat**, outside the cell membrane.
The three adaptations listed in the spec are: **nutrients in the cytoplasm, haploid nucleus, changes in the cell membrane after fertilisation**.

callouts.p: Nutrients in the cytoplasm, haploid nucleus, cell membrane changes after fertilisation.

core.h: Egg cell: nutrients in the cytoplasm
core.p: The cytoplasm of the egg cell contains a store of **nutrients**. After fertilisation, the fertilised egg cell divides again and again by mitosis to form an embryo. The stored nutrients supply the embryo during this early growth.
bullets: Feature: the cytoplasm contains lots of nutrients.
Function: the nutrients **supply the developing embryo** with what it needs for growth.
WHY the sperm cannot do this: the sperm cell has almost no cytoplasm, so nearly all of the cytoplasm of the fertilised egg cell comes from the egg.
WHY the egg cell is large: it needs room to store the nutrients.

callouts.p: The nutrients are for the embryo after fertilisation. They are not food for the sperm cell.

core.h: Egg cell: haploid nucleus and the changing cell membrane
core.p: The egg cell's nucleus is haploid for the same reason as the sperm cell's. The clever adaptation is what happens to the egg's cell membrane straight after one sperm cell has entered.
bullets: The **haploid nucleus** contains one set of chromosomes: the female parent's genetic material.
At fertilisation it fuses with the haploid sperm nucleus to give a diploid nucleus.
**Immediately after fertilisation, the cell membrane of the egg cell changes** so that **no more sperm cells can enter**.
WHY this matters: if a second sperm cell got in, the fertilised egg cell would have too many chromosomes (three sets instead of two).
So the change in the cell membrane makes sure that the fertilised egg cell has exactly the diploid number of chromosomes.

head: Egg feature
How it helps
rows: Supply the embryo with what it needs for growth after fertilisation
Fuses with the haploid sperm nucleus so the fertilised egg cell is diploid
Stops any more sperm cells entering, so the chromosome number stays correct

callouts.p: The cell membrane changes AFTER one sperm cell has fertilised the egg. Before fertilisation a sperm cell must be able to get in.

core.h: Comparing the sperm cell and the egg cell
core.p: Compare questions are common. The two gametes share one adaptation (the haploid nucleus) and differ in almost everything else, because one has to travel and the other has to provide.
bullets: Both have a haploid nucleus, and both have a cell membrane and cytoplasm.
The sperm cell is small and has a tail for swimming; the egg cell is large and has no tail.
The sperm cell has very little cytoplasm; the egg cell has a lot of cytoplasm containing nutrients.
The sperm cell has an acrosome containing enzymes; the egg cell has no acrosome.
The egg cell's membrane changes after fertilisation; the sperm cell's does not.

core.p: Epithelial cells line the surfaces of tubes and organs. A **ciliated** epithelial cell has **cilia** on its surface. Cilia are tiny hair-like structures that stick out from the top of the cell into the space inside the tube.
bullets: **Cilia** (singular: cilium) are hair-like structures on the surface of the cell.
The cilia **beat (wave) from side to side** in a co-ordinated way.
This beating **moves substances along the surface** of the cells, in **one direction**.
The cell itself stays where it is. It is the substance on top that is moved.
Moving the cilia needs energy, so these cells contain many mitochondria to release energy by respiration.

callouts.p: Tiny hair-like structures on the surface of a cell that beat to move substances along the surface.
Cilia do not trap or filter anything themselves. They MOVE substances. In the airways it is the mucus that traps dust and pathogens.

core.h: Ciliated epithelial cells: where they work
core.p: You should be able to apply the idea to two places in the body. In each case, say what is being moved and in which direction.
bullets: **Oviducts**: ciliated epithelial cells line the oviducts. The cilia beat to **move the egg cell along the oviduct towards the uterus**. The egg cell cannot move by itself, so it relies on the cilia.
**Airways** (trachea and bronchi): the cilia beat to **move mucus up towards the throat**, away from the lungs. The mucus has trapped dust and pathogens, so moving it away helps protect the lungs.
In both places the cilia move the substance in one direction only.

head: Location
What is moved
Direction and reason
rows: Towards the uterus, because the egg cell cannot swim
Mucus with trapped dust and pathogens
Up to the throat, away from the lungs

callouts.p: Do not just write 'cilia move things'. Write 'cilia move the egg cell towards the uterus' or 'cilia move mucus away from the lungs'.

core.h: How to write a top-mark adaptation answer
core.p: Questions on this point are marked for linked ideas. A feature and its explanation normally earn one mark each, so pair them every time.
bullets: Step 1: name the feature exactly (acrosome, not 'the pointy bit').
Step 2: say what the feature contains or does (contains enzymes).
Step 3: link to the function of the cell (to digest the outer layers of the egg cell so the sperm can enter).
For 'describe' questions give the features and what they do. For 'explain' questions add the reason why that helps.
If a question shows an unfamiliar specialised cell, use the same method: look for many mitochondria, a tail, cilia or a large store of nutrients and link each to the function given in the question.

callouts.p: A 4-mark question on a sperm cell usually wants two features, each with its explanation.

analogy.t: A delivery rider and a stocked safe house
analogy.p: The sperm cell is like a delivery rider on a motorbike. The **tail** is the wheels that get it there, the **mitochondria** are the engine that releases the energy for the journey, the **acrosome** is a set of bolt cutters to get through the gate, and the **haploid nucleus** is the small parcel being delivered: exactly half of a set of instructions. The egg cell is like a safe house waiting for the delivery. It holds the other half of the instructions (its own **haploid nucleus**), has a larder full of food for the days ahead (**nutrients in the cytoplasm**) and, the moment one rider gets in, it changes the locks so nobody else can enter (the **cell membrane changes after fertilisation**). Ciliated epithelial cells are like a crowd passing a ball overhead in one direction: the people (cells) stay still while their hands (**cilia**) move the ball along. Where it breaks down: a rider chooses a route, but a sperm cell does not think or decide, and bolt cutters cut by force whereas the acrosome uses enzymes to digest the outer layers chemically.

terms.d: A cell with a structure adapted to carry out a particular function.
A feature of a cell that helps it to carry out its function.
A sex cell (sperm cell or egg cell); it has a haploid nucleus.
The male gamete, adapted to swim to the egg cell and fertilise it.
The female gamete, adapted to be fertilised and to supply nutrients to the early embryo.
Having one set of chromosomes; half the number found in a normal body cell (23 in humans).
Having two sets of chromosomes (46 in humans).
The fusing of the haploid nucleus of a sperm cell with the haploid nucleus of an egg cell.
A fertilised egg cell; it is diploid.
A structure at the tip of the sperm head containing enzymes that digest the outer layers of the egg cell.
Sub-cellular structures where respiration takes place, releasing energy; sperm cells have many to power the tail.
The long structure that moves to let the sperm cell swim to the egg cell.
The protective layer surrounding the cell membrane of an egg cell.
The ball of cells formed when a fertilised egg cell divides by mitosis.
A cell that lines the surface of a tube or organ.
Tiny hair-like structures on the surface of a cell that beat to move substances along.
The tube that carries the egg cell from the ovary to the uterus; it is lined with ciliated epithelial cells.

mistakes.w: The mitochondria make energy so the sperm can swim.
mistakes.r: Mitochondria RELEASE energy (by respiration), which is needed for the tail to move.

mistakes.w: The acrosome helps the sperm get into the egg.
mistakes.r: Too vague. The acrosome contains ENZYMES that digest / break down the outer layers of the egg cell.

mistakes.w: The sperm has a haploid nucleus so it is lighter and swims faster.
mistakes.r: The nucleus is haploid so that when it fuses with the haploid egg nucleus, the fertilised egg cell has the correct (diploid) number of chromosomes.

mistakes.w: The nutrients in the egg cytoplasm feed the sperm.
mistakes.r: The nutrients supply the developing EMBRYO with what it needs for growth after fertilisation.

mistakes.w: The egg cell membrane changes to let the sperm in.
mistakes.r: It changes AFTER fertilisation to STOP any more sperm cells entering.

mistakes.w: Cilia trap dust and bacteria.
mistakes.r: Mucus traps dust and pathogens. Cilia beat to MOVE the mucus away from the lungs.

mistakes.w: Cilia help the cell to move.
mistakes.r: The cell stays in place. Cilia move substances (such as an egg cell or mucus) across the surface of the cell.

mistakes.w: The sperm has 46 chromosomes / half a chromosome.
mistakes.r: A human sperm cell has 23 chromosomes: half the NUMBER of chromosomes of a body cell, that is one set.

mistakes.w: The sperm has a tail. (as a complete answer to an 'explain' question)
mistakes.r: Add the function: the tail allows the sperm cell to swim to the egg cell.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term haploid.
model: Having one set of chromosomes / half the number of chromosomes (of a body cell).
exam.tip: Do not write 'half a chromosome'. It is half the number.

exam.q: Name the part of a sperm cell that contains enzymes.
model: Acrosome.
exam.tip: A one-word answer is all that is needed for 'name'.

exam.q: Describe the function of the acrosome in a sperm cell.
model: Contains / releases enzymes.
To digest / break down the outer layers / jelly coat of the egg cell (so the sperm can enter).
exam.tip: Two marks: what it contains, and what that does.

exam.q: Explain why a sperm cell contains many mitochondria.
model: Mitochondria are where respiration takes place / mitochondria release energy.
Energy is needed for the tail to move / for the sperm cell to swim to the egg cell.
exam.tip: Link respiration, energy and the tail in one chain.

exam.q: Explain why the nucleus of a sperm cell is haploid.
model: So that at fertilisation it fuses with the haploid nucleus of the egg cell.
To give a diploid cell / the full (correct) number of chromosomes / so the chromosome number does not double.
exam.tip: Use both words: haploid and diploid.

exam.q: Describe how the cytoplasm of an egg cell is adapted to its function.
model: The cytoplasm contains (a store of) nutrients.
To supply the embryo with what it needs for growth / development after fertilisation.
exam.tip: Say who the nutrients are for: the embryo.

exam.q: Explain why the cell membrane of an egg cell changes immediately after fertilisation.
model: To stop / prevent any more sperm cells entering the egg cell.
So that the fertilised egg cell has the correct / diploid number of chromosomes (not too many).
exam.tip: The second mark is for the consequence for chromosome number.

exam.q: Ciliated epithelial cells line the oviducts. Describe the function of these cells.
model: The cilia beat / wave / move.
To move the egg cell along the oviduct towards the uterus.
exam.tip: Name what is moved and where it is moved to.

exam.q: Ciliated epithelial cells line the airways. Explain how these cells help to protect the lungs.
model: Mucus traps dust / pathogens / bacteria.
Cilia beat / wave.
Moving the mucus up to the throat / away from the lungs.
exam.tip: Mucus traps, cilia move. Keep those two jobs separate.

exam.q: Explain how two features of a sperm cell adapt it to its function.
model: Tail.
So it can swim to the egg cell.
Acrosome containing enzymes.
To digest the outer layers of the egg cell. (Alternatives: many mitochondria / to release energy for the tail; haploid nucleus / so fertilisation gives a diploid cell.)
exam.tip: Two features, each with its own explanation: feature, reason, feature, reason.

exam.q: Give two differences between the structure of a sperm cell and the structure of an egg cell.
model: Sperm cell has a tail, egg cell does not.
Sperm cell has an acrosome, egg cell does not / egg cell has a large amount of cytoplasm with nutrients, sperm cell has very little / egg cell is much larger.
exam.tip: Do not give 'haploid nucleus': that is a similarity.

exam.q: Sperm cells and egg cells are specialised cells. Explain how sperm cells and egg cells are adapted to their functions.
model: Sperm: tail allows it to swim to the egg cell.
Sperm: many mitochondria, where respiration releases the energy needed for the tail to move.
Sperm: acrosome contains enzymes that digest the outer layers of the egg cell so the sperm can enter.
Both: haploid nucleus, so that fertilisation produces a diploid cell with the correct number of chromosomes.
Egg: cytoplasm contains nutrients to supply the embryo with what it needs for growth after fertilisation.
Egg: cell membrane changes immediately after fertilisation so that no more sperm cells can enter, keeping the chromosome number correct.
exam.tip: Levels-marked. Cover BOTH cells, link every feature to its function and write in a logical order: sperm first, then egg.

worked.q: A horse body cell contains 64 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in a horse sperm cell and in a fertilised horse egg cell. Explain your answers.
steps: A body cell is diploid, so 64 is the diploid number.
A sperm cell is a gamete, so it is haploid: it has half the number. 64 / 2 = 32.
The egg cell is also haploid, so it has 32 chromosomes.
At fertilisation the two haploid nuclei fuse: 32 + 32 = 64.
worked.ans: Sperm cell: 32 chromosomes (haploid). Fertilised egg cell: 64 chromosomes (diploid), because fertilisation joins two haploid nuclei.

worked.q: A man produces sperm cells that have very few mitochondria. Explain why he may be unable to father children.
steps: Mitochondria are where respiration takes place.
Fewer mitochondria means less respiration, so less energy is released.
The tail needs energy to move, so the sperm cells swim slowly or not at all.
The sperm cells may not reach the egg cell, so fertilisation does not happen.
worked.ans: With few mitochondria, less energy is released by respiration, so the tail cannot move enough for the sperm cell to swim to the egg cell and fertilise it.

worked.q: Chemicals in cigarette smoke stop cilia in the airways from beating. Explain why smokers are more likely to get lung infections.
steps: Mucus in the airways traps dust and pathogens.
Normally the cilia on ciliated epithelial cells beat to move this mucus up to the throat, away from the lungs.
If the cilia stop beating, the mucus is not moved.
Mucus containing pathogens builds up in the airways and lungs, so pathogens stay there and can cause infection.
worked.ans: The cilia can no longer move mucus away from the lungs, so mucus containing trapped pathogens builds up and the pathogens can cause infections.

The cilia on the top surface beat together to move substances in one direction: mucus (with trapped dust and pathogens) away from the lungs, or an egg cell along the oviduct towards the uterus. Many mitochondria release the energy needed.

bio_edx.0.12.summary: Cells must take in useful substances (oxygen, glucose, water, mineral ions) and get rid of waste (carbon dioxide, urea), and everything has to cross the cell membrane. Three processes do this: **diffusion** and **osmosis** are passive and move substances down a concentration gradient, while **active transport** uses energy from respiration to move substances against a concentration gradient. For a grade 9 you must define each process precisely, say which direction substances move and why, and apply the ideas to unfamiliar examples.

core.p: Every living cell is surrounded by a cell membrane that controls what enters and leaves. The chemical reactions inside a cell (such as respiration) constantly use up some substances and make others, so a cell would quickly stop working if it could not exchange substances with its surroundings.
bullets: Substances that must enter cells include **oxygen** and **glucose** (for aerobic respiration), **water**, **amino acids** and **mineral ions**.
Substances that must leave cells include **carbon dioxide** (from respiration) and other waste products such as **urea**.
The cell membrane lets some substances through but not others, so it is described as **partially permeable**.
There are three ways substances cross: **diffusion**, **osmosis** and **active transport**.
The key questions for any example are: what is moving, in which direction compared with the concentration gradient, and is energy needed?

callouts.p: Diffusion and osmosis are passive (no energy from respiration needed). Active transport needs energy and moves substances against the concentration gradient.

core.p: Concentration is how many particles of a substance there are in a given volume. Where there is a difference in concentration between two places, we say there is a **concentration gradient**. All three transport processes are described in terms of this gradient.
bullets: Moving **down** a concentration gradient means moving from a higher concentration to a lower concentration.
Moving **against** a concentration gradient means moving from a lower concentration to a higher concentration.
The bigger the difference in concentration, the **steeper** the concentration gradient.
A steeper gradient gives a faster rate of diffusion, because there is a bigger difference between the number of particles moving one way and the number moving the other way.
When the concentration is the same everywhere there is no gradient: particles still move, but there is no **net** movement.

callouts.p: A difference in the concentration of a substance between two regions.

core.p: Particles in liquids and gases are always moving randomly. Because of this random movement they spread out, so overall more particles move away from a crowded region than move into it. This overall (net) movement is diffusion.
bullets: Diffusion happens in **gases** and in **solutions** (dissolved particles), because the particles are free to move.
The particles move in **both** directions; diffusion is the **net** movement, the overall result.
It is a **passive** process: it relies on the random movement of the particles themselves and does not need energy from respiration.
It continues until the particles are evenly spread out (equilibrium), when there is no further net movement.

Only particles that are small enough can diffuse through the cell membrane, for example oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, glucose and amino acids. Large molecules such as starch and proteins cannot pass through.

callouts.p: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration (down a concentration gradient).
Mark schemes reward **net movement**. Writing only that particles move from high to low suggests that none move the other way, which is not true.

core.p: You need to be able to apply the definition to real examples. In each case identify where the concentration is higher, where it is lower, and so which way the net movement goes.
bullets: **Oxygen into a respiring cell**: the cell uses oxygen in respiration, so the oxygen concentration inside the cell is lower than outside. Oxygen diffuses in, down its concentration gradient.
**Carbon dioxide out of a respiring cell**: respiration produces carbon dioxide, so its concentration is higher inside the cell than outside. Carbon dioxide diffuses out.
**Gas exchange in the lungs**: oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli (higher concentration) into the blood (lower concentration); carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.
**Digested food in the small intestine**: when the concentration of glucose or amino acids is higher in the gut than in the blood, they diffuse into the blood.
**Gas exchange in a leaf**: carbon dioxide diffuses into a photosynthesising leaf through the stomata because the cells are using it up.
Because cells keep using up or producing these substances, the concentration gradient is **maintained**, so diffusion keeps going.

head: Substance
Moves from
Moves to
Why the gradient exists
rows: Cell uses oxygen in aerobic respiration
Out of the cell / into blood
Cell produces carbon dioxide in respiration
Digestion makes glucose concentration high in the gut

core.h: What affects the rate of diffusion
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to explain why diffusion is faster in one situation than another. Link each factor to the movement of particles.
bullets: **Concentration gradient**: a bigger difference in concentration gives a faster rate of diffusion.
**Temperature**: at a higher temperature the particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so diffusion is faster.
**Surface area**: a larger surface area of membrane lets more particles cross at the same time, so the rate is faster.
**Distance**: a shorter diffusion distance (for example a thin membrane or a wall one cell thick) gives a faster rate.
These ideas explain the adaptations of exchange surfaces that you study later in the course.

callouts.t: Say faster rate, not more diffusion
callouts.p: When comparing, write in terms of the **rate** of diffusion and always give the direction of the change, for example a steeper concentration gradient so a faster rate of diffusion.

core.p: Osmosis is a special case of diffusion that applies only to **water** molecules crossing a **partially permeable membrane**. Water molecules are small enough to pass through the membrane but larger solute molecules (such as sucrose) are not, so only the water can move to even out the concentrations.
bullets: A **dilute** solution has a low solute concentration, so it has a **high concentration of water molecules**.
A **concentrated** solution has a high solute concentration, so it has a **low concentration of water molecules**.
Water molecules move in both directions across the membrane, but more move from the dilute side to the concentrated side, so there is a **net** movement in that direction.
Osmosis is **passive**: it does not need energy from respiration.
The solute molecules do not cross the membrane, because they are too large to pass through it.
If the solutions on both sides have the same concentration there is no net movement of water.

callouts.p: The net movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration (a dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (a more concentrated solution).
A membrane that allows some molecules (such as water) to pass through but not others (such as larger solute molecules).

Never write just from high concentration to low concentration for osmosis without saying of what. Either say high **water** concentration to low water concentration, or low **solute** concentration to high solute concentration.

core.p: The cell membrane is partially permeable and the cytoplasm is a solution of sugars, salts and other solutes, so water moves into or out of cells by osmosis depending on the solution around them.
bullets: If the solution outside is **more dilute** than the cell contents, there is a net movement of water **into** the cell by osmosis. The cell gains mass and swells.
If the solution outside is **more concentrated** than the cell contents, there is a net movement of water **out of** the cell by osmosis. The cell loses mass and shrinks.
If the solution outside has the **same concentration** as the cell contents, there is no net movement of water and the cell stays the same size and mass.
An animal cell placed in pure water can take in so much water that it bursts, because it has no cell wall to support it.
A plant cell does not burst, because its strong **cell wall** resists the pressure. Plant tissue placed in a concentrated solution loses water and becomes soft.
**Root hair cells** take in water from the soil by osmosis, because soil water is more dilute than the cell contents.

head: Solution outside the cell
Net movement of water
Effect on the cell
rows: More dilute than cell contents (or pure water)

core.p: Sometimes a cell needs to take in a substance that is already at a higher concentration inside the cell than outside. Diffusion would move the substance the wrong way, out of the cell. Active transport lets the cell move the substance **against** its concentration gradient, but this costs energy.
bullets: Substances move from a **lower** concentration to a **higher** concentration.
It needs **energy**, which is released by **respiration** in the cell.
It happens across a cell membrane, using proteins in the membrane that carry the particles across.
Because it needs respiration, cells that carry out a lot of active transport contain many **mitochondria**.
Anything that stops respiration (for example a lack of oxygen, or a poison that stops respiration) also stops active transport, but does not stop diffusion.

callouts.p: The movement of particles across a membrane against a concentration gradient (from a lower concentration to a higher concentration), using energy released by respiration.
Do not write that respiration makes or produces energy. Energy is **released** (or transferred) by respiration.

core.p: The two examples you are most likely to meet are root hair cells in plants and the absorption of glucose in the small intestine.
bullets: **Root hair cells and mineral ions**: the concentration of mineral ions (such as nitrate ions) is usually lower in the soil water than inside the root hair cell. Diffusion cannot bring them in, so the cell absorbs them by active transport.
Plants need these mineral ions for healthy growth, for example nitrate ions to make proteins.
Root hair cells have many mitochondria to release the energy needed, and a large surface area for absorption.
Waterlogged soil contains little oxygen, so root cells respire less, release less energy and absorb fewer mineral ions by active transport.
**Glucose in the small intestine**: when the concentration of glucose in the gut is lower than in the blood, glucose is still absorbed into the blood by active transport, so that none is wasted.
The same root hair cell takes in **water by osmosis** and **mineral ions by active transport**: do not mix these up.

core.p: A very common exam question asks you to compare two of the processes. Give a similarity and a difference, and make each statement a true comparison (mention both processes).
bullets: Diffusion and osmosis are both **passive** and both go **down** a concentration gradient.
Osmosis involves **only water** molecules and always needs a **partially permeable membrane**; diffusion can involve any small particles and does not always need a membrane.
Active transport is the only one that goes **against** the concentration gradient and the only one that needs **energy from respiration**.
All three can move substances into or out of cells.

head: Feature
Diffusion
Osmosis
Active transport
rows: Particles such as mineral ions and glucose
Higher water concentration to lower water concentration

core.h: How to work out which process is happening
core.p: In an unfamiliar context, use the information in the question to decide which process is involved, then justify it using the concentrations given.
bullets: If the substance is **water** crossing a membrane, the process is **osmosis**.
If the substance moves from a **lower to a higher** concentration, or the question mentions energy, respiration, oxygen supply or mitochondria, it is **active transport**.
If any other substance moves from a **higher to a lower** concentration, it is **diffusion**.
Always quote the data: for example the concentration of nitrate ions is higher in the cell than in the soil, so the ions move against the concentration gradient.
Then add the consequence: this needs energy from respiration, so it is active transport.

callouts.p: Name the process, state the direction in terms of concentration, then say whether energy from respiration is needed. That pattern scores most of the marks on explain questions.

analogy.p: Think of the concentration gradient as a hill. Diffusion is a ball rolling **down** the hill: it happens by itself, with no push needed. Osmosis is the same hill, but only water is allowed through the gate (the partially permeable membrane) at the bottom of the fence, so only water rolls down. Active transport is carrying the ball back **up** the hill: it will never happen by itself, and you have to use energy (from respiration) to do it. Where it breaks down: a ball rolls only one way, but in real diffusion and osmosis particles move randomly in both directions and it is only the **net** movement that goes downhill. Also, there is no real force pulling particles down a concentration gradient; the net movement is simply the result of random motion.

terms.d: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
The net movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration.
The movement of particles across a membrane against a concentration gradient, using energy released by respiration.
A difference in concentration of a substance between two regions.
From a higher concentration to a lower concentration.
From a lower concentration to a higher concentration.
The overall movement of particles, after taking into account that particles move in both directions.
A membrane that lets some molecules (such as water) pass through but not others (such as larger solute molecules).
A process that does not need energy from respiration; diffusion and osmosis are passive.
A substance that is dissolved in a liquid, for example sucrose or salt dissolved in water.
A solution with a low solute concentration and therefore a high concentration of water molecules.
A solution with a high solute concentration and therefore a low concentration of water molecules.
The partially permeable boundary of a cell that controls which substances enter and leave.
The process in cells that releases energy; this energy is needed for active transport.
Sub-cellular structures where aerobic respiration takes place; plentiful in cells that carry out a lot of active transport.
A plant root cell with a large surface area that absorbs water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport.

mistakes.w: Osmosis is the movement of water from a high concentration to a low concentration.
mistakes.r: Say what the concentration is of, include net and the membrane: the net movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a lower water concentration (concentrated solution).

mistakes.w: Particles move from high to low concentration (no mention of net).
mistakes.r: Particles move randomly in both directions; diffusion is the **net** movement from higher to lower concentration.

mistakes.w: The sugar moves out of the cell by osmosis.
mistakes.r: Osmosis is only ever the movement of **water** molecules. The solute cannot pass through the partially permeable membrane.

mistakes.w: Active transport moves substances along the concentration gradient.
mistakes.r: Active transport moves substances **against** the concentration gradient, from a lower to a higher concentration.

mistakes.w: Respiration produces energy for active transport.
mistakes.r: Respiration **releases** energy; energy is not made or produced.

mistakes.w: Root hair cells take in mineral ions by osmosis.
mistakes.r: Mineral ions are absorbed by **active transport** (the concentration is higher inside the cell); only water enters by osmosis.

mistakes.w: Diffusion needs energy because the particles are moving.
mistakes.r: Diffusion is passive: it depends on the random movement of the particles and does not need energy from respiration.

mistakes.w: Water moves to the weaker solution.
mistakes.r: There is a net movement of water from the more dilute solution to the more **concentrated** solution. Use dilute and concentrated, not weak and strong.

mistakes.w: When concentrations are equal the particles stop moving.
mistakes.r: Particles keep moving, but equal numbers move in each direction, so there is no **net** movement.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term diffusion.
model: Net movement of particles / molecules
From an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration / down a concentration gradient
exam.tip: Two marks: one for net movement of particles, one for the direction.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by the term osmosis.
model: Net movement of water molecules
Across a partially permeable membrane
From a higher water concentration to a lower water concentration / from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution
exam.tip: Water, membrane, direction: check that all three are in your answer.

exam.q: Which process moves substances against a concentration gradient? A active transport, B diffusion, C osmosis, D evaporation.
model: A active transport
exam.tip: Against the gradient always means active transport.

exam.q: Explain how oxygen moves from the blood into a respiring muscle cell.
model: By diffusion
Because the concentration of oxygen is higher in the blood than in the cell / oxygen moves down its concentration gradient (as the cell uses oxygen in respiration)
exam.tip: Name the process and justify the direction using concentrations.

exam.q: The concentration of nitrate ions is higher inside a root hair cell than in the soil water. Explain how nitrate ions enter the root hair cell.
model: By active transport
The ions move against the concentration gradient / from a lower concentration to a higher concentration
This requires energy (released by respiration)
exam.tip: Use the data in the stem: quote where the concentration is higher.

exam.q: Root hair cells contain many mitochondria. Explain why.
model: Mitochondria are where respiration takes place, releasing energy
The energy is needed for active transport of mineral ions into the cell
exam.tip: Link structure (mitochondria) to process (respiration) to function (active transport).

exam.q: Give two differences between diffusion and active transport.
model: Diffusion is down a concentration gradient / high to low, whereas active transport is against the concentration gradient / low to high
Active transport needs energy (from respiration), whereas diffusion does not / is passive
exam.tip: A difference needs both sides: say what each process does.

exam.q: A red blood cell is placed in pure water. Explain what happens to the cell.
model: Water enters the cell by osmosis
Because the water concentration is higher outside the cell than inside / the cell contents are more concentrated than the water
The cell swells and bursts (as it has no cell wall)
exam.tip: State the process, the reason in terms of concentrations, then the effect.

exam.q: Explain why plants growing in waterlogged soil absorb fewer mineral ions.
model: Waterlogged soil contains little oxygen
So there is less (aerobic) respiration in the root cells and less energy is released
Mineral ions are absorbed by active transport, which needs energy, so fewer ions are absorbed
exam.tip: Build a chain: oxygen, respiration, energy, active transport.

exam.q: Compare the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport in moving substances into and out of cells.
model: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration
Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution
Diffusion and osmosis are both passive / do not need energy and both go down a concentration gradient
Osmosis only involves water, whereas diffusion can involve other particles such as oxygen and carbon dioxide
Active transport moves particles against a concentration gradient, from a lower to a higher concentration
Active transport needs energy released by respiration, unlike diffusion and osmosis
Examples: oxygen diffusing into cells, water entering root hair cells by osmosis, mineral ions entering root hair cells by active transport
exam.tip: For 6 marks cover all three processes, make direct comparisons (both, whereas) and give examples.

worked.q: A plant root cell has a nitrate ion concentration of 2.5 arbitrary units. The soil water around it has a nitrate ion concentration of 0.4 arbitrary units. The plant continues to absorb nitrate ions. Identify the process and explain your answer.
steps: Compare the concentrations: 2.5 inside the cell is higher than 0.4 in the soil.
The ions are moving from the soil (lower concentration) into the cell (higher concentration).
This is against the concentration gradient, so it cannot be diffusion.
Movement against a concentration gradient needs energy released by respiration.
worked.ans: Active transport, because nitrate ions move from a lower concentration (0.4) to a higher concentration (2.5), against the concentration gradient, using energy from respiration.

worked.q: A bag made of partially permeable tubing is filled with 10% sucrose solution and placed in a beaker of 2% sucrose solution. Predict and explain what happens to the mass of the bag.
steps: Decide which solution is more dilute: the 2% solution outside has a lower solute concentration, so a higher water concentration.
The 10% solution inside is more concentrated, so it has a lower water concentration.
Water moves by osmosis from higher water concentration to lower water concentration, so the net movement is into the bag.
Sucrose molecules are too large to pass through the partially permeable membrane, so they stay where they are.
worked.ans: The mass of the bag increases, because there is a net movement of water into the bag by osmosis, from the dilute solution (2%) to the more concentrated solution (10%) across the partially permeable membrane.

worked.q: In an experiment, cells are given a poison that stops respiration. The uptake of oxygen into the cells continues but the uptake of mineral ions stops. Explain these results.
steps: The poison stops respiration, so no energy is released in the cells.
Oxygen enters cells by diffusion, which is passive, so it does not need energy and continues.
Mineral ions enter by active transport, which needs energy from respiration.
With no energy released, active transport stops.
worked.ans: Oxygen uptake is by diffusion, which needs no energy from respiration, so it continues. Mineral ion uptake is by active transport, which needs energy released by respiration, so it stops when respiration is stopped.

svg.cap: Diffusion. Particles move randomly in all directions, but because there are more particles on the left, more move from left to right than from right to left. The result is a net movement from the higher concentration to the lower concentration, down the concentration gradient.

Water molecules can pass through the gaps in the partially permeable membrane but the larger solute molecules cannot, so there is a net movement of water from the dilute solution to the concentrated solution.
