bio_edx.0.13.summary: This core practical investigates osmosis by placing pieces of potato in sucrose solutions of different concentrations and measuring how their mass changes. Potato pieces gain mass in dilute solutions (water enters the cells by osmosis) and lose mass in concentrated solutions (water leaves by osmosis). Plotting percentage change in mass against concentration lets you find the concentration at which there is no change in mass, which is an estimate of the solute concentration of the potato cells. You must know the method, the variables, the sources of error and how to interpret the results.

core.h: The aim and the science behind it
core.p: The aim is to investigate how the concentration of a solution affects the movement of water into and out of potato tissue by osmosis. Potato cells have partially permeable cell membranes, and their contents are a solution, so water moves in or out depending on the solution surrounding them.
bullets: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules across a **partially permeable membrane** from a dilute solution (higher water concentration) to a more concentrated solution (lower water concentration).
If the surrounding solution is **more dilute** than the cell contents, there is a net movement of water **into** the potato cells and the potato **gains mass**.
If the surrounding solution is **more concentrated** than the cell contents, there is a net movement of water **out of** the potato cells and the potato **loses mass**.
If the surrounding solution has the **same concentration** as the cell contents, there is **no net movement** of water and the mass does not change.
The change in mass of the potato is therefore a way of measuring how much water has moved by osmosis.

callouts.p: You cannot see water molecules move, so the change in **mass** of the potato piece is used to show the net movement of water.

core.p: Examiners very often ask you to identify the variables or to explain why a particular variable must be controlled. Learn them in the three standard groups.
bullets: **Independent variable** (the one you change): the concentration of the sucrose solution.
**Dependent variable** (the one you measure): the change in mass of the potato piece, calculated as a percentage change.

**Control variables** (kept the same so the test is valid): the volume of solution, the size and surface area of the potato pieces, the type and age of potato (use the same potato), the temperature, and the time the pieces are left in the solution.
Surface area must be the same because a larger surface area would let more water move in a given time.
Temperature must be the same because water molecules move faster at higher temperatures, which changes the rate of osmosis.
Using the same potato matters because different potatoes can have different solute concentrations in their cells.

head: Variable
In this practical
How / why
rows: A range such as 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol dm-3
Mass measured before and after with a balance
Measure with a measuring cylinder; pieces must be fully covered
Same cork borer and same length, no skin
Use a stop clock; all pieces left for the same time
All tubes kept at the same room temperature

core.p: You should be able to name each piece of apparatus and say what it is for.
bullets: A **potato**, a **cork borer** (or knife), a **scalpel** and a **white tile** for cutting equal potato pieces safely.
A **ruler** to cut every piece to the same length.
**Boiling tubes** (or beakers) in a rack, each **labelled** with the concentration of its solution.
**Sucrose solutions** of a range of concentrations, including 0.0 mol dm-3 (distilled water).
A **measuring cylinder** to measure the same volume of solution for each tube.
A **balance** (reading to at least 0.01 g) to measure mass.
**Paper towels** to blot the pieces dry, **forceps** to handle them and a **stop clock** for timing.

core.p: This is the sequence you need to be able to describe in a 6 mark question. Give a reason for each step where you can.
bullets: 1. Use a cork borer to cut cylinders from the **same potato**; remove any skin and trim them all to the **same length** with a scalpel.
2. **Blot** each piece dry with a paper towel, then measure and record its **initial mass** using a balance.
3. Use a measuring cylinder to put the **same volume** of each sucrose solution into separate labelled boiling tubes. Include distilled water as the 0.0 mol dm-3 solution.
4. Put one potato piece into each tube (or several, for repeats), making sure it is fully covered by the solution, and start the stop clock.
5. Leave all the pieces for the **same length of time** (at least 15 to 20 minutes; longer gives bigger changes).
6. Remove each piece with forceps, **blot it dry** again in the same way, and measure and record its **final mass**.
7. Calculate the **change in mass** and then the **percentage change in mass** for each piece.
8. **Repeat** for each concentration and calculate a **mean** percentage change.
9. Plot a graph of percentage change in mass against sucrose concentration.

callouts.p: For a method question, write the steps in order and include the measurements (mass before and after), the control variables and repeats. Marks are lost for vague phrases such as measure the potato.

core.h: Why the potato is blotted dry
core.p: Blotting is the step most often tested. The balance measures everything on it, so any solution clinging to the outside of the potato piece would be included in the mass.
bullets: Blotting **removes excess surface liquid** so that only the mass of the potato tissue (and the water inside its cells) is measured.
If the piece is not blotted after soaking, the final mass is too high, so a gain in mass looks bigger and a loss in mass looks smaller than it really is.
Blot **gently** and in the **same way** each time: squeezing would force water out of the cells and make the final mass too low.
Blotting must be done both **before** the initial mass and **before** the final mass so that the two readings are comparable.

callouts.p: Saying the potato is blotted to dry it scores nothing. Say it removes excess water or solution **from the surface**, which would otherwise increase the mass reading.

core.p: The potato pieces never start with exactly the same mass, however carefully they are cut. A piece that starts heavier contains more cells and would be expected to gain or lose more grams of water.
bullets: Percentage change takes the **starting mass** into account, so results from pieces with different initial masses can be **compared fairly**.
Percentage change in mass = (final mass - initial mass) / initial mass x 100.
A **positive** value shows a gain in mass (net movement of water in); a **negative** value shows a loss in mass (net movement of water out).
The detailed calculations are covered in the next spec point; here you need to know **why** the percentage is used.

callouts.p: Percentage change in mass allows comparison because the potato pieces had different initial masses.

core.p: Results should go in a table drawn before you start, with the independent variable in the first column and units in the headings only.
bullets: Column headings need **units**, for example sucrose concentration in mol dm-3 and mass in g.
Record all masses to the **same number of decimal places** (the precision of the balance).
Include columns for initial mass, final mass, change in mass and percentage change in mass.
Show the sign (+ or -) of each change so gains and losses are clear.
Look for **anomalous results** (ones that do not fit the pattern); repeat them or leave them out when calculating the mean.

core.p: The graph turns the table into a pattern you can interpret, and it gives the most important result of the practical: the concentration at which the potato neither gains nor loses mass.
bullets: Put **sucrose concentration** (independent variable) on the x-axis and **percentage change in mass** (dependent variable) on the y-axis.
The y-axis must go **above and below zero**, because some changes are positive and some are negative. The x-axis is drawn across at zero.
Plot the points accurately and draw a **line of best fit** (a straight line or smooth curve, as the points suggest).
Points **above** the x-axis: the potato gained mass, so the solution was more dilute than the cell contents.
Points **below** the x-axis: the potato lost mass, so the solution was more concentrated than the cell contents.
Where the line **crosses the x-axis** the percentage change is zero: there is no net movement of water, so this concentration is equal to the concentration of the potato cell contents.

callouts.p: The point where the line of best fit crosses the x-axis gives an estimate of the solute concentration of the potato cells, because there is no net osmosis at this concentration.

core.p: Explain questions want the science of osmosis applied to the data. Use the same structure each time: compare concentrations, state the direction of net water movement by osmosis, then state the effect on mass.
bullets: **In distilled water or dilute sucrose solution**: the solution has a higher water concentration than the cell contents, so there is a net movement of water into the cells by osmosis and the mass increases.
**In concentrated sucrose solution**: the solution has a lower water concentration than the cell contents, so there is a net movement of water out of the cells by osmosis and the mass decreases.
**The trend**: as the sucrose concentration increases, the percentage change in mass decreases (it becomes less positive and then more negative).
Sucrose molecules do not enter the cells, because they are too large to pass through the partially permeable cell membrane; only water moves.
Potato pieces that have lost water feel soft and flexible; pieces that have gained water feel firm.

core.h: Sources of error and how to improve the practical
core.p: Evaluation questions ask what could make the results inaccurate and how the method could be improved. Always pair a problem with a specific improvement.
bullets: **Inconsistent blotting**: leaving different amounts of liquid on the surface changes the final mass. Improvement: blot every piece in the same way for the same time.
**Different surface areas**: pieces of different size or shape exchange water at different rates. Improvement: use the same cork borer and cut to the same length with a ruler.
**Skin left on the potato**: the skin slows the movement of water. Improvement: remove all the skin.
**Evaporation from the tubes**: this changes the concentration of the solutions. Improvement: cover the tubes or put bungs in them.
**Too short a time**: small changes in mass are hard to measure accurately. Improvement: leave the pieces for longer, and use a balance with a higher resolution.
**Only one piece per concentration**: one result may be anomalous. Improvement: repeat with several pieces at each concentration and calculate a mean.
**Estimate of the intercept is rough**: Improvement: use more concentrations at smaller intervals around the point where the line crosses the x-axis.

callouts.p: Repeats let you identify anomalous results and calculate a mean, which makes the results more **repeatable** and the conclusion more reliable. Say this rather than just more accurate.

core.p: The hazards are minor, but a risk assessment can still be asked for.
bullets: The scalpel and cork borer are **sharp**: cut downwards onto a white tile, away from your fingers, and never cut towards your hand.
Mop up any **spilled solution** straight away so nobody slips.
Do not eat the potato or taste the solutions: nothing in a laboratory should be eaten.

core.h: Linking the practical to the bigger picture
core.p: The same method can be used with other plant tissues or other solutes, and examiners like to set the practical in an unfamiliar context to test understanding rather than memory.
bullets: Different vegetables (for example carrot or sweet potato) can be compared; the one whose line crosses the x-axis at a higher concentration has cells with a more concentrated solution inside.
Salt (sodium chloride) solutions can be used instead of sucrose; the principles are identical.
Length of the potato piece can be measured instead of mass, but mass measured on a balance is more precise than length measured with a ruler.
Whatever the context, the logic is the same: gain in mass means water entered by osmosis, loss in mass means water left by osmosis, no change means the concentrations were equal.

analogy.t: A tug of war over water
analogy.p: Imagine the potato cells and the surrounding solution in a tug of war, where the rope is the water. The side with the more concentrated solution pulls harder. In distilled water the potato cells win and water moves into them, so the potato gets heavier. In strong sucrose solution the solution wins and water moves out of the potato, so it gets lighter. Where the two sides are exactly matched the rope does not move: this is the point where your graph line crosses the x-axis, and it tells you how strong the potato side is. Where it breaks down: nothing is really pulling the water. Water molecules move randomly in both directions across the membrane all the time, and the net movement is simply because more of them move from the dilute side to the concentrated side.

terms.d: The net movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.
A membrane, such as the cell membrane, that lets water molecules through but not larger solute molecules such as sucrose.
The variable that is deliberately changed; here, the concentration of the sucrose solution.
The variable that is measured; here, the (percentage) change in mass of the potato.
A variable kept the same so that it does not affect the results, such as volume of solution, time, temperature and size of potato piece.
A solution of the sugar sucrose in water; sucrose is the solute and water is the solvent.
The amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, here measured in mol dm-3.
The mass of the blotted potato piece before it is placed in the solution.
The mass of the blotted potato piece after it has been left in the solution.
The change in mass divided by the initial mass, multiplied by 100; it allows pieces with different initial masses to be compared.
Gently drying the surface of the potato with a paper towel to remove excess liquid before weighing.
A metal tube used to cut cylinders of potato with the same diameter.
A straight line or smooth curve drawn through the pattern of plotted points, with points evenly spread either side.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others; it should be repeated or left out of the mean.
The sum of the repeat values divided by the number of values, used to reduce the effect of random errors.
When water molecules move into and out of the cells at the same rate, so the mass of the potato does not change.

mistakes.w: The potato is blotted to make it dry.
mistakes.r: It is blotted to remove excess water / solution from the **surface**, which would otherwise be included in the mass reading.

mistakes.w: Use change in mass in grams to compare the potato pieces.
mistakes.r: Use **percentage** change in mass, because the pieces had different initial masses.

mistakes.w: The independent variable is the potato.
mistakes.r: The independent variable is the **concentration of the sucrose solution**; the dependent variable is the change in mass.

mistakes.w: In concentrated solution the sucrose moves into the potato, so it shrinks.
mistakes.r: Sucrose cannot cross the partially permeable membrane. **Water** moves out of the potato cells by osmosis, so the mass decreases.

mistakes.w: Where the line crosses the x-axis, osmosis has stopped and no water moves.
mistakes.r: There is no **net** movement of water: water moves in and out at the same rate because the solution has the same concentration as the cell contents.

mistakes.w: Repeat the experiment to make it more accurate (with no further detail).
mistakes.r: Repeat to identify **anomalous results** and calculate a **mean**, making the results more repeatable.

mistakes.w: Keep everything the same.
mistakes.r: Name specific control variables: same volume of solution, same size / surface area of potato, same time, same temperature, same potato.

mistakes.w: Plotting percentage change with a y-axis that starts at zero.
mistakes.r: The y-axis must include **negative** values, with the x-axis drawn at zero, because some pieces lose mass.

mistakes.w: The potato gained mass because it absorbed the solution.
mistakes.r: The potato gained mass because of a net movement of **water** into the cells **by osmosis**, from the more dilute solution outside.

exam.q: State the independent variable in an investigation into osmosis in potato pieces placed in different sucrose solutions.
model: Concentration of the sucrose solution
exam.tip: The independent variable is the one the student chooses to change.

exam.q: Explain why the potato pieces were blotted with a paper towel before their mass was measured.
model: To remove excess water / solution from the surface of the potato
Because this would increase the mass reading / so that only the mass of the potato is measured
exam.tip: Say what is removed and why it matters for the measurement.

exam.q: Give two variables that should be controlled in this investigation.
model: Any two from: volume of solution; size / length / surface area of potato piece; time left in solution; temperature; same potato / type of potato
exam.tip: Be specific. Amount of solution is weaker than volume of solution.

exam.q: Explain why percentage change in mass was calculated rather than change in mass.
model: The potato pieces had different initial masses
Percentage change allows the results to be compared (fairly)
exam.tip: Both ideas are needed: different starting masses, and valid comparison.

exam.q: A potato piece was placed in distilled water. Explain why its mass increased.
model: Water moved into the potato cells by osmosis
Because the water concentration was higher outside the cells than inside / the cell contents were more concentrated than the water
Across the partially permeable (cell) membrane
exam.tip: Osmosis, direction with reason, membrane.

exam.q: A potato piece was placed in 1.0 mol dm-3 sucrose solution. Explain why its mass decreased.
model: Water moved out of the potato cells by osmosis
Because the solution outside was more concentrated than the cell contents / lower water concentration outside
Through the partially permeable membrane, so the cells lost water and mass
exam.tip: Never say sucrose moved: only water moves by osmosis.

exam.q: A graph of percentage change in mass against sucrose concentration crosses the x-axis at 0.35 mol dm-3. State what this shows about the potato cells.
model: There is no net movement of water / no change in mass at this concentration
So the concentration of the solution inside the potato cells is (approximately) 0.35 mol dm-3
exam.tip: Read the intercept and link it to equal concentrations.

exam.q: Describe how the student could improve the investigation to obtain a more accurate estimate of the concentration of the potato cell contents.
model: Use more sucrose concentrations at smaller intervals around the point where the line crosses the x-axis
Repeat each concentration and calculate a mean / leave out anomalous results
exam.tip: Improvements must be specific to this practical.

exam.q: Explain why all the potato pieces should have the same surface area.
model: Surface area affects the rate of osmosis / a larger surface area allows more water to move in the same time
So keeping it the same makes the comparison valid / ensures only concentration affects the change in mass
exam.tip: Link the control variable to its effect on the dependent variable.

exam.q: Describe the trend shown when percentage change in mass is plotted against sucrose concentration.
model: As the sucrose concentration increases, the percentage change in mass decreases
The potato gains mass at low concentrations and loses mass at high concentrations / the line crosses zero
exam.tip: Describe means say what the data show; quote values from the graph if you can.

exam.q: Devise a method to investigate the effect of sucrose concentration on osmosis in potato tissue.
model: Cut potato pieces of the same size / length using a cork borer and scalpel, from the same potato
Blot the pieces dry and measure the initial mass of each using a balance
Place each piece in the same volume of a different concentration of sucrose solution, including distilled water
Leave for the same length of time at the same temperature
Remove, blot dry and measure the final mass
Calculate the percentage change in mass for each piece
Repeat at each concentration and calculate a mean
Plot a graph of percentage change in mass against concentration
exam.tip: Write the steps in a logical order and name the independent, dependent and control variables to reach the top level.

worked.q: A student obtained these mean percentage changes in mass: 0.0 mol dm-3: +12; 0.2 mol dm-3: +5; 0.4 mol dm-3: -2; 0.6 mol dm-3: -10. Estimate the concentration of the potato cell contents.
steps: The percentage change is zero where the solution has the same concentration as the cell contents.
The change goes from +5 at 0.2 mol dm-3 to -2 at 0.4 mol dm-3, so the line crosses zero between these two concentrations.
The total change over this interval is 7 (from +5 to -2) and zero is 5 below +5, so the crossing point is 5/7 of the way from 0.2 to 0.4.
5/7 x 0.2 = 0.14, so the estimate is 0.2 + 0.14 = 0.34 mol dm-3.
On a graph you would read this directly from where the line of best fit crosses the x-axis.
worked.ans: Approximately 0.34 mol dm-3 (accept a value read from the graph between 0.3 and 0.4 mol dm-3).

worked.q: A student forgot to blot the potato pieces after removing them from the solutions. Explain the effect on the calculated percentage changes in mass and on the estimate of the cell concentration.
steps: Liquid left on the surface adds to the final mass, so every final mass is too high.
Pieces that gained mass appear to have gained more than they really did.
Pieces that lost mass appear to have lost less than they really did.
The whole line on the graph is shifted upwards, so it crosses the x-axis at a higher concentration.
worked.ans: All percentage changes are too high (too positive), so the line crosses the x-axis further to the right and the concentration of the cell contents is overestimated.

worked.q: Three repeat pieces in 0.6 mol dm-3 sucrose gave percentage changes of -9.8, -10.4 and -2.1. Calculate a suitable mean.
steps: Look for anomalous results: -2.1 is very different from the other two values.
Leave out the anomalous result (ideally the test would be repeated).
Add the remaining values: -9.8 + -10.4 = -20.2.
Divide by the number of values used: -20.2 / 2 = -10.1.
worked.ans: Mean percentage change in mass = -10.1 (the anomalous result of -2.1 is not included).

bio_edx.0.14.summary: In osmosis investigations, tissue such as potato gains mass when water enters its cells and loses mass when water leaves. Because pieces of tissue never start with exactly the same mass, the results are compared using **percentage change in mass**: the change in mass divided by the initial mass, multiplied by 100. A positive answer is a percentage gain and a negative answer is a percentage loss. You must be able to calculate these values accurately, round them sensibly, keep the correct sign and explain what the answer shows about the movement of water.

core.h: What percentage change in mass tells you
core.p: When plant tissue is placed in a solution, water moves into or out of its cells by osmosis, and the tissue becomes heavier or lighter. The percentage change in mass tells you how big that change is compared with the mass the tissue started with.
bullets: A **percentage gain** in mass means there was a net movement of water **into** the cells by osmosis.
A **percentage loss** in mass means there was a net movement of water **out of** the cells by osmosis.
A percentage change of **zero** means there was no net movement of water.
The **larger** the percentage change, the greater the net movement of water compared with the size of the piece.
The calculation is used in the potato osmosis core practical, but it can be applied to any tissue or model cell, for example a bag of partially permeable tubing.

callouts.p: Positive = gain in mass (water entered). Negative = loss in mass (water left).

core.h: Why use a percentage, not just grams
core.p: Pieces of tissue cut by hand always differ slightly in initial mass. A bigger piece has more cells and a larger surface, so it will gain or lose more grams of water than a smaller piece in the same solution. Comparing the change in grams would therefore be unfair.
bullets: Percentage change expresses the change as a **proportion of the initial mass**.
This allows a **valid comparison** between pieces that had **different initial masses**.
Example: piece A goes from 2.00 g to 2.30 g and piece B goes from 3.00 g to 3.30 g. Both gain 0.30 g.
The same gain in grams is a bigger proportion of the smaller piece, so piece A has taken in relatively more water.

callouts.p: If asked why percentage change is calculated: the pieces had **different initial masses** (1), so percentage change allows the results to be **compared** (1).

core.p: There is one equation to learn. It is not given to you in the exam, so memorise it exactly, including which mass goes on the bottom.
bullets: percentage change in mass = (final mass - initial mass) / initial mass x 100
The top line, final mass - initial mass, is the **change in mass**.
The bottom line is always the **initial mass** (the starting mass), never the final mass.
Both masses must be in the **same units** (usually grams); the units then cancel, so the answer is a percentage with no mass unit.
The same equation works for any percentage change, for example percentage change in length of a potato cylinder.

callouts.p: percentage change in mass = (final mass - initial mass) / initial mass x 100
The most common error is dividing by the final mass. A percentage change is always a percentage **of the starting value**.

core.p: Set the calculation out the same way every time. Showing each step means you can still gain marks for your working even if you make a slip with the calculator.
bullets: **Step 1**: write down the initial mass and the final mass, with units.
**Step 2**: subtract to find the change in mass: final mass - initial mass. Keep the sign.
**Step 3**: divide the change in mass by the **initial** mass.
**Step 4**: multiply by 100 and write the answer with its sign and the % symbol.
Finally, round to the number of significant figures or decimal places asked for in the question.

core.p: When the final mass is bigger than the initial mass, the change is positive and the answer is a percentage gain.
bullets: Example: a potato piece has an initial mass of 2.50 g and a final mass of 2.80 g.
Change in mass = 2.80 - 2.50 = +0.30 g.
The piece gained 12% of its original mass, so there was a net movement of water into the cells: the solution was more dilute than the cell contents.

core.p: When the final mass is smaller than the initial mass, final mass - initial mass gives a negative number. Keep the minus sign all the way through: it tells you the tissue lost mass.
bullets: Example: a potato piece has an initial mass of 2.40 g and a final mass of 1.92 g.
Change in mass = 1.92 - 2.40 = -0.48 g.
The piece lost 20% of its original mass, so there was a net movement of water out of the cells: the solution was more concentrated than the cell contents.
If a question asks for the **percentage loss** in mass, you can write 20% (the word loss already shows the direction). If it asks for the **percentage change**, write -20%.

callouts.p: Always do final minus initial. If you subtract the smaller from the larger to avoid a negative number, you lose the information about whether mass was gained or lost.

core.h: Rounding, significant figures and decimal places
core.p: Calculator answers often have many digits. The question usually tells you how to round; if it does not, use the same number of significant figures as the data (commonly 2 or 3).
bullets: Example: initial mass 2.56 g, final mass 2.31 g. Change = -0.25 g. -0.25 / 2.56 x 100 = -9.765625.
To 3 significant figures this is **-9.77%**; to 2 significant figures it is **-9.8%**; to 1 decimal place it is **-9.8%**.
Only round at the **end**. Rounding part-way through (for example rounding 0.0977 to 0.1) gives a wrong final answer.
Look at the digit after the last one you are keeping: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less stays the same.
In a results table, give every percentage change to the **same number of decimal places**.

callouts.p: If the question says give your answer to 2 significant figures, one mark is for the rounding. An unrounded answer loses that mark even if the calculation is right.

core.p: Investigations usually use several pieces of tissue in each solution. You calculate the percentage change for each piece separately and then find the mean of the percentages.
bullets: Mean = sum of the values / number of values.
Example: three pieces in the same solution give +8.2%, +7.6% and +8.5%. Mean = (8.2 + 7.6 + 8.5) / 3 = 24.3 / 3 = +8.1%.
Check for **anomalous results** first. A value that is very different from the others should be left out of the mean (or the test repeated).
Take care with signs when adding negative values: -9.8 + -10.4 = -20.2.
Give the mean to the same number of decimal places as the values it was calculated from.

core.p: Harder questions give you the percentage change and one of the masses, and ask for the other mass. These need the equation to be rearranged, which is a mathematical skill expected at the top grades.
bullets: **Finding the change in mass**: change in mass = percentage change / 100 x initial mass.
**Finding the final mass**: final mass = initial mass + change in mass.
Example: initial mass 2.00 g, percentage change -12%. Change = -12 / 100 x 2.00 = -0.24 g. Final mass = 2.00 - 0.24 = 1.76 g.
**Finding the initial mass** from the final mass: initial mass = final mass / (1 + percentage change / 100).
Example: final mass 2.76 g after a +15% change. Initial mass = 2.76 / 1.15 = 2.40 g.
Check by putting your answer back into the original equation: (2.76 - 2.40) / 2.40 x 100 = +15%.

core.h: Using the percentages: tables and graphs
core.p: Once calculated, the percentage changes are recorded in a table and plotted against the concentration of the solution. You need to handle positive and negative values correctly on the graph.
bullets: In a table, show the sign of every value (+ or -) and put the % unit in the column heading, not in every cell.
On the graph, percentage change in mass goes on the **y-axis**, with a scale that runs above and below zero.
Positive values are plotted above the x-axis and negative values below it.
Where the line of best fit crosses the x-axis, the percentage change is 0%: at this concentration there is no net movement of water.
To estimate a percentage change for a concentration that was not tested, read it from the line of best fit.

core.h: Linking the number back to osmosis
core.p: Calculation questions are often followed by an explain question. Your number is evidence: use it to say which way water moved and why.
bullets: **Positive percentage change**: the tissue gained mass because water moved into the cells by osmosis, from the more dilute solution outside to the more concentrated cell contents, across the partially permeable cell membrane.
**Negative percentage change**: the tissue lost mass because water moved out of the cells by osmosis, from the cell contents to the more concentrated solution outside.
**Zero**: the solution has the same concentration as the cell contents, so there is no net movement of water.
A larger percentage change means a bigger difference in concentration between the solution and the cell contents.
It is only **water** that moves; the solute (for example sucrose) does not cross the membrane.

core.p: A quick sense check catches most calculator slips before they cost marks.
bullets: **Sign check**: if the final mass is smaller than the initial mass, the answer must be negative.
**Size check**: changes in these experiments are usually a few percent up to about 30%. An answer such as 1200% or 0.12% suggests you forgot to multiply by 100 or multiplied twice.
**Denominator check**: confirm you divided by the initial mass.

**Bracket check**: on a calculator, work out the subtraction first (or use brackets). Typing 2.80 - 2.50 / 2.50 x 100 without brackets gives the wrong answer, because the calculator divides before it subtracts.
**Rounding check**: has the answer been given to the number of significant figures or decimal places requested?

callouts.p: Write the substitution line, for example (2.80 - 2.50) / 2.50 x 100. If the final answer is wrong, a correct substitution can still earn a mark.

analogy.p: Suppose two people each get a rise of 3 pounds in their weekly pocket money. One was on 20 pounds and the other was on 30 pounds. The rise in pounds is identical, but it is a 15% rise for the first person and only a 10% rise for the second, so it matters more to the person who started with less. Percentage change in mass works the same way: the change in grams is like the rise in pounds, and the initial mass is like the starting pocket money. Dividing by the starting amount makes the comparison fair. Where it breaks down: pocket money is changed by a decision, but the mass of the tissue changes because of the net movement of water by osmosis, and it can go down as well as up, giving a negative percentage.

terms.d: The mass of the tissue at the start, before it is placed in the solution.
The mass of the tissue at the end, after it has been in the solution.
Final mass minus initial mass; positive for a gain and negative for a loss.
(final mass - initial mass) / initial mass x 100.
A positive percentage change; the tissue has taken in water and its mass has increased.
A negative percentage change; the tissue has lost water and its mass has decreased.
The net movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.
The overall movement of water after movement in both directions is taken into account.
The digits in a number that carry meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit.
The number of digits after the decimal point.
The sum of a set of values divided by the number of values.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others and is left out when calculating a mean.
A fair comparison, in which differences in starting mass have been taken into account by using percentages.
A straight line or smooth curve drawn through plotted points to show the trend.
Putting the numbers from the question into the equation in place of the words.

mistakes.w: Dividing the change in mass by the final mass.
mistakes.r: Always divide by the **initial** mass: (final - initial) / initial x 100.

mistakes.w: Writing 20% when asked for the percentage change of a piece that lost mass.
mistakes.r: A percentage change for a loss needs a minus sign: **-20%**. (20% is only correct if the question asks for the percentage loss.)

mistakes.w: Doing initial mass - final mass.
mistakes.r: The change is **final - initial**, so that gains are positive and losses are negative.

mistakes.w: Giving the answer as 0.12 instead of 12%.
mistakes.r: Remember to **multiply by 100** to turn the decimal into a percentage.

mistakes.w: Typing 2.80 - 2.50 / 2.50 x 100 into the calculator.
mistakes.r: Work out the subtraction first or use brackets: (2.80 - 2.50) / 2.50 x 100 = 12%.

mistakes.w: Rounding in the middle of the calculation.
mistakes.r: Keep all the digits on the calculator and round only the final answer.

mistakes.w: Ignoring the instruction to give the answer to 2 significant figures.
mistakes.r: Round as instructed: for example -9.765625 becomes -9.8 to 2 significant figures.

mistakes.w: Percentage change is used because it is more accurate.
mistakes.r: It is used because the pieces had **different initial masses**, and percentages allow a fair comparison.

mistakes.w: Writing the answer as 12 g.
mistakes.r: The answer is a percentage, **12%**; the grams cancel out when one mass is divided by another.

exam.q: A potato piece had an initial mass of 3.20 g. After 30 minutes in distilled water its mass was 3.52 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
exam.tip: One mark for the substitution, one for the answer. Show the working.

exam.q: A potato piece had a mass of 4.00 g before being placed in 1.0 mol dm-3 sucrose solution and 3.40 g afterwards. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
exam.tip: The minus sign is needed because the question asks for the change.

exam.q: A piece of carrot had an initial mass of 1.85 g and a final mass of 2.07 g. Calculate the percentage gain in mass. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
exam.tip: The third mark is for correct rounding to 3 significant figures.

exam.q: State the equation used to calculate percentage change in mass.
model: (final mass - initial mass) / initial mass x 100
exam.tip: Accept change in mass / initial mass x 100. The initial mass must be on the bottom.

exam.q: Explain why the student calculated percentage change in mass rather than using the change in mass in grams.
model: The potato pieces had different initial / starting masses
So percentage change allows a (fair / valid) comparison between them
exam.tip: A standard answer worth learning word for word.

exam.q: Three potato pieces in the same solution had percentage changes in mass of -11.5%, -12.5% and -12.0%. Calculate the mean percentage change in mass.
exam.tip: Keep the negative signs when adding.

exam.q: A potato piece with an initial mass of 2.00 g was placed in a sucrose solution. Its percentage change in mass was -12%. Calculate the final mass of the potato piece.
model: Change in mass = 12 / 100 x 2.00 = 0.24 (g)
Final mass = 2.00 - 0.24
exam.tip: Find the change in grams first, then subtract it because the change is a loss.

exam.q: A potato piece had a percentage change in mass of +8%. Explain this result.
model: Water moved into the potato cells by osmosis
Because the solution outside was more dilute than the cell contents / higher water concentration outside the cells
Across the partially permeable (cell) membrane, so the mass increased
exam.tip: Use the sign of the answer as evidence, then explain with osmosis.

exam.q: A student calculated a percentage change in mass as (2.31 - 2.56) / 2.31 x 100. Identify the error the student made.
model: The student divided by the final mass instead of the initial mass (2.56)
exam.tip: Spot-the-error questions usually test the denominator.

exam.q: A potato cylinder was 50 mm long. After 1 hour in a concentrated salt solution it was 46 mm long. Calculate the percentage change in length.
exam.tip: The same equation works for length: change divided by the starting value, times 100.

exam.q: In sucrose solutions of 0.2 mol dm-3 and 0.4 mol dm-3, potato pieces had percentage changes in mass of +5% and -2%. Explain what these results show about the concentration of the potato cell contents.
model: The potato gained mass at 0.2 and lost mass at 0.4, so the percentage change would be zero / there would be no net movement of water at a concentration between them
So the concentration of the cell contents is between 0.2 and 0.4 mol dm-3
exam.tip: A change of sign between two concentrations tells you the cell concentration lies between them.

worked.q: A potato piece has an initial mass of 6.25 g. After soaking in a sucrose solution its final mass is 5.50 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
steps: Write the equation: percentage change = (final mass - initial mass) / initial mass x 100.
Change in mass = 5.50 - 6.25 = -0.75 g.
Divide by the initial mass: -0.75 / 6.25 = -0.12.
Sense check: the final mass is smaller, so a negative answer is expected.
worked.ans: -12% (a 12% loss in mass, showing a net movement of water out of the potato cells by osmosis).

worked.q: A potato piece has an initial mass of 2.56 g and a final mass of 2.31 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
steps: Change in mass = 2.31 - 2.56 = -0.25 g.
Divide by the initial mass: -0.25 / 2.56 = -0.09765625.
Multiply by 100: -9.765625.
Round to 2 significant figures: the first two significant figures are 9 and 7; the next digit is 6, so round up to -9.8.

worked.q: After 40 minutes in distilled water a potato piece has a final mass of 2.76 g. Its percentage change in mass was +15%. Calculate its initial mass.
steps: A +15% change means the final mass is 115% of the initial mass, so final mass = initial mass x 1.15.
Rearrange: initial mass = final mass / 1.15.
Initial mass = 2.76 / 1.15 = 2.40 g.
worked.ans: Initial mass = 2.40 g

bio_edx.0.4.summary: This core practical is about using a light microscope to observe biological specimens such as onion and cheek cells, working out how much they have been magnified, and recording what you see as a labelled scientific drawing. You need to know how to prepare a slide, how to focus safely starting on low power, and how to use magnification = image size / actual size (with correct unit conversions) to find magnification, real size or image size. Exam questions test the method, the reasons for each step, the calculations and the rules for drawings.

core.h: What the core practical asks you to do
core.p: The Edexcel core practical is to **investigate biological specimens using microscopes, including magnification calculations and labelled scientific drawings from observations**. In practice this means three linked skills: making and viewing a slide, calculating magnification or size, and drawing what you see accurately.
bullets: You prepare a **temporary slide** of a specimen, for example onion epidermis (plant cells) or cheek cells (animal cells).
You view it with a **light microscope**, starting at the lowest magnification and working up.
You produce a **labelled scientific drawing** of a few cells, with a title and the magnification or a scale.
You carry out **magnification calculations** using the lens powers and using image size and actual size.
Questions can be set on any specimen, including ones you have not seen, so learn the principles rather than one recipe.

callouts.p: (1) The method and the reason for each step, (2) calculations with magnification, image size and actual size, (3) the rules for a good biological drawing.

core.h: Parts of the light microscope and what each does
core.p: A light microscope passes light through a thin specimen and uses two lenses to produce a magnified image. You need to be able to name each part and say what it is for.
bullets: Light from the lamp (or mirror) passes up through the specimen on the slide, then through the objective lens, then through the eyepiece lens to your eye.
The specimen must be **thin** so that light can pass through it; a thick specimen looks dark and the cells overlap.
Most school microscopes have three objective lenses on a rotating nosepiece, commonly x4, x10 and x40.

head: Part
Function
rows: The lens you look through; it magnifies the image made by the objective lens (often x10)
Lenses close to the specimen that magnify it; different lenses give different magnifications (for example x4, x10, x40)
The flat platform that holds the slide, usually with clips to keep it still
The glass slide carries the specimen; the thin coverslip holds it flat and keeps it in place
Sends light up through the specimen so that it can be seen
Moves the stage (or lenses) a large distance to bring the image roughly into focus; used with low power
Moves the stage a very small distance to make the image sharp and clear

callouts.p: In a method question write coarse focusing wheel first, then fine focusing wheel. Just writing 'focus it' usually does not gain the mark.

core.h: Preparing a temporary slide of onion cells
core.p: Onion epidermis is ideal because it peels off as a layer that is only **one cell thick**, so light passes through it easily and the cells do not overlap.
bullets: Put a drop of water onto the middle of a clean glass slide.
Use forceps to peel a thin layer of **epidermis** from the inside of an onion scale.
Lay the epidermis flat in the water on the slide, without folding it.
Add a drop of **iodine solution**. This is a **stain**: it makes parts of the cell, such as the nucleus, easier to see because most cell parts are colourless and transparent.
Lower a **coverslip** slowly at an angle, using a mounted needle, so that it comes down gently onto the specimen.
Lowering it slowly at an angle pushes the air out to one side, so there are **no air bubbles** trapped under the coverslip. Air bubbles would hide the cells and can be mistaken for structures.
Use a paper towel to soak up any excess liquid from around the coverslip.

callouts.p: A stain adds colour and contrast so that structures which are normally colourless (for example the nucleus) become visible.
Iodine solution is an irritant and stains skin and clothes, so wear eye protection and avoid contact with skin.

core.h: Preparing a slide of cheek cells
core.p: Animal cells can be observed using cells from the lining of your cheek. The steps are similar but the stain and the safety points are different.
bullets: Gently rub the inside of your cheek with a clean cotton bud to collect cells.
Smear the cotton bud onto the middle of a clean slide.
Add a drop of **methylene blue** stain, which stains the nucleus dark blue so that it stands out.
Lower a coverslip at an angle with a mounted needle to avoid trapping air bubbles.
Place the used cotton bud in **disinfectant** straight away, because it carries cells and microorganisms from your mouth.
Under the microscope you should see the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus. You will **not** see a cell wall, chloroplasts or a large permanent vacuole because animal cells do not have them.

head: Specimen
Stain
What you can expect to see with a light microscope
rows: Cell wall, cytoplasm, nucleus (and vacuole); regular brick-like cells
Cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus; irregular rounded cells

callouts.t: No chloroplasts in onion bulb cells
callouts.p: Onion epidermis from the bulb grows underground in the dark and does not photosynthesise, so do not draw or label chloroplasts in it.

core.h: Using the microscope: the focusing routine
core.p: The order of steps matters. You always start on the **lowest power objective lens** because it gives the widest field of view, which makes the specimen easy to find, and because the lens is furthest from the slide, which makes it safer to focus.
bullets: Clip the slide onto the stage and switch on the lamp (or adjust the mirror).
Turn the nosepiece to select the **lowest power objective lens**.
Looking from the **side** (not through the eyepiece), use the coarse focusing wheel to bring the stage and the objective lens close together, without letting them touch.
Now look through the eyepiece and turn the coarse focusing wheel to move the stage and lens **apart** until the specimen comes roughly into focus.
Turn the **fine focusing wheel** until the image is sharp.
To see more detail, switch to a higher power objective lens and refocus using the **fine focusing wheel only**.
On high power the lens is very close to the slide, so using the coarse wheel could push the lens into the slide and break the coverslip or damage the lens.

callouts.p: Start with the lowest power objective: it has the largest field of view so the specimen is easier to find, and there is less risk of the lens hitting the slide.
If the microscope has a mirror, never point it at the Sun: reflected sunlight could permanently damage your eyes.

core.p: A light microscope magnifies twice: once with the objective lens and again with the eyepiece lens. The two magnifications are **multiplied**, not added.
bullets: **total magnification = eyepiece lens magnification x objective lens magnification**
Example: eyepiece x10 and objective x40 gives 10 x 40 = x400.
With a x10 eyepiece, objectives of x4, x10 and x40 give total magnifications of x40, x100 and x400.
If you know the total and one lens you can rearrange: objective magnification = total magnification / eyepiece magnification.
Magnification has **no units**. Write it with a multiplication sign, for example x400.

callouts.p: Magnification is the number of times larger an image is than the actual object.
A x10 eyepiece with a x40 objective gives x400, not x50.

core.h: The magnification equation: image size and actual size
core.p: For a photograph, drawing or image of a cell you use a second equation that links how big the image is to how big the real object is. You must be able to use it and rearrange it.
bullets: **magnification = image size / actual size**
**actual size = image size / magnification**
**image size = actual size x magnification**
**Image size** is what you measure with a ruler on the picture or drawing. **Actual size** is the real size of the object.
Both sizes must be in the **same units** before you divide. This is where most marks are lost.
1 mm = 1000 micrometres (µm). To change mm into µm multiply by 1000; to change µm into mm divide by 1000.
Cells are usually measured in micrometres, so a sensible routine is: measure the image in mm, multiply by 1000 to get µm, then use the equation.
Check your answer makes sense: a magnified image must be bigger than the real object, so the actual size should be the smaller number.

head: To find
Calculation
Example
rows: image 45 mm, magnification x900: 45 / 900 = 0.05 mm = 50 µm
actual 0.02 mm, magnification x400: 0.02 x 400 = 8 mm

callouts.p: In a 2 or 3 mark calculation one mark is often for the unit conversion or the correct substitution, so write each step down even if you use a calculator.

core.p: Many micrographs have a **scale bar**: a line on the image labelled with the real length it represents. A scale bar lets you work out the magnification, or the real size of a structure, directly from the image.
bullets: To find magnification: measure the length of the scale bar with a ruler (this is the image size), convert it to the units written on the bar, then divide by the length written on the bar (the actual size).
Example: a scale bar labelled 50 µm measures 20 mm. 20 mm = 20 000 µm, so magnification = 20 000 / 50 = x400.
To find the real size of a cell: compare the measured length of the cell with the measured length of the scale bar. If the cell is 3 times as long as a 50 µm bar, the cell is 150 µm long.
A scale bar stays correct if the picture is enlarged or shrunk when printed, because the bar changes size with the picture. A written magnification such as x400 would then be wrong.

callouts.p: Measure the bar, convert to the same units as its label, then magnification = measured length of bar / length the bar represents.

core.h: Field of view and estimating cell size
core.p: The **field of view** is the circle of the specimen you can see when you look down the microscope. If you know its diameter you can estimate the size of the cells in it.
bullets: Place a clear plastic ruler on the stage under low power and count how many millimetre divisions fit across the field of view. This gives the **diameter of the field of view**.
Count the number of cells that fit across the diameter in a straight line.
**estimated length of one cell = diameter of field of view / number of cells across**
Example: field of view 2 mm across, 8 cells fit across: 2 / 8 = 0.25 mm = 250 µm per cell.

When you increase the magnification the field of view gets **smaller** by the same factor. Going from x40 to x400 is 10 times the magnification, so the diameter of the field of view becomes 10 times smaller (2 mm becomes 0.2 mm).
So at higher magnification you see **fewer cells**, but each one looks bigger and shows more detail.
This is an **estimate** because cells are not all the same size and part-cells at the edge are hard to count.

core.h: Rules for a labelled scientific drawing
core.p: A biological drawing is a record of what you actually observed, not a work of art and not a copy of a textbook diagram. Edexcel mark schemes reward the same list of features every time.
bullets: Use a **sharp pencil** so that lines are thin and can be corrected.
Draw **clear, continuous, single lines**: no sketchy, feathery or broken lines, and outlines must join up.
**No shading and no colouring**. Shading hides detail and is not an accurate record.
Make the drawing **large**: it should fill at least half of the space provided.
Draw only what you **can see**, with structures in the correct **proportions** (for example the nucleus the right size compared with the cell).
Draw just a few representative cells (two or three) rather than the whole field of view.
**Label** the structures using straight lines drawn with a **ruler**. Label lines must touch the structure, must not cross each other and should not have arrowheads.
Write labels outside the drawing, horizontally, so they are easy to read.
Add a **title** saying what the specimen is, and give the **magnification** or a **scale bar**.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Shade or colour in the nucleus or cytoplasm
Ruled label lines that touch the structure
Freehand lines, arrowheads or crossing label lines
Draw what is visible in correct proportion
Add parts from memory that you cannot see
Leave the drawing without a title or scale

callouts.p: A very common question shows a poor student drawing and asks for improvements. Go through the list: no shading, continuous lines, ruled label lines with no arrowheads, add a title, add the magnification, make it bigger.

core.p: The magnification of a drawing is **not** the same as the magnification of the microscope, because you choose how big to draw the cell. You calculate it with the same equation.
bullets: Measure the length of the cell in your drawing with a ruler: this is the image size.
Find the actual length of the cell, for example from the field of view estimate.
magnification of drawing = length of cell in drawing / actual length of cell, with both in the same units.
Example: a cell is drawn 60 mm long and its actual length is 0.25 mm. Magnification = 60 / 0.25 = x240.
Write the result beside the drawing, for example 'x240'.

core.p: Examiners often ask why a student could not see a clear image, or how the method could be improved. Link each problem to its cause and its fix.
bullets: **Image is dark or cells overlap**: the specimen is too thick, so light cannot pass through. Use a thinner layer (one cell thick).
**Cells look colourless and nothing can be seen inside**: no stain was used. Add iodine solution or methylene blue.
**Round shapes with thick black edges**: these are air bubbles. Lower the coverslip slowly at an angle.
**Cannot find the specimen**: started on high power. Go back to the lowest power objective and centre the specimen first.
**Image blurred on high power**: adjust the fine focusing wheel; check the lens and slide are clean.

**Risks**: glass slides and coverslips are fragile and can cut (handle with care, report breakages); stains are irritants (eye protection); cheek cell samples are a biohazard (disinfectant); never use direct sunlight with a mirror.
A light microscope can show cells, nuclei and chloroplasts, but very small structures such as ribosomes cannot be seen with it.

callouts.p: For a 2 mark 'explain the problem' question give the cause (for example specimen too thick so light cannot pass through) and the improvement (peel a layer one cell thick).

analogy.t: A photo zoomed on your phone
analogy.p: Think of pinching to zoom on a photo of a friend standing far away. The picture on the screen (the image size) gets bigger, but your friend's real height (the actual size) never changes. The zoom factor is the magnification: screen height divided by real height. Zooming in also means you see less of the scene, just as a higher power objective gives a smaller field of view with fewer cells in it. Where it breaks down: zooming a phone photo eventually just makes it blurry with no new detail, and a phone makes far-away things look smaller than real life, whereas a microscope always produces an image larger than the real object and a better lens really does reveal new detail.

terms.d: The number of times larger an image is than the actual object. It has no units and is written with a multiplication sign, for example x400.
The size of the object as it appears in a drawing, photograph or micrograph, measured with a ruler.
The real size of the object or specimen.
The lens you look through at the top of the microscope; it magnifies the image produced by the objective lens.
A lens close to the specimen that magnifies it. Microscopes usually have several with different magnifications.
Eyepiece lens magnification multiplied by objective lens magnification.
The platform of the microscope on which the slide is placed and held by clips.
The control that moves the stage or lenses by a large amount to bring the image roughly into focus on low power.
The control that moves the stage or lenses by a very small amount to make the image sharp.
A thin square of glass or plastic placed over the specimen to hold it flat and keep it in place on the slide.
A dye, such as iodine solution or methylene blue, added to a specimen so that colourless structures become easier to see.
The sample of biological material being observed.
The circular area of the specimen that can be seen through the microscope at a particular magnification.
A line drawn on an image labelled with the actual length that it represents.
A unit of length equal to one thousandth of a millimetre: 1 mm = 1000 µm.
A photograph taken using a microscope.

mistakes.w: Total magnification = x10 + x40 = x50.
mistakes.r: The lens magnifications are multiplied: 10 x 40 = x400.

mistakes.w: Magnification = actual size / image size.
mistakes.r: Magnification = image size / actual size. The image is the larger value, so it goes on top.

mistakes.w: Dividing 30 mm by 60 µm without converting.
mistakes.r: Convert so both are in the same units first: 30 mm = 30 000 µm, then 30 000 / 60 = x500.

mistakes.w: Start on the highest power lens to see the most detail.
mistakes.r: Start with the lowest power objective lens (largest field of view, easier to find the specimen, less risk of hitting the slide), then move up.

mistakes.w: Use the coarse focusing wheel on high power.
mistakes.r: On high power use only the fine focusing wheel, because the lens is very close to the slide and could break it.

mistakes.w: The stain is added to kill the cells / to feed the cells.
mistakes.r: The stain makes structures such as the nucleus more visible by adding colour and contrast.

mistakes.w: The coverslip is lowered at an angle to stop the cells drying out.
mistakes.r: It is lowered slowly at an angle to prevent air bubbles being trapped under it.

mistakes.w: A good drawing should be shaded to show the nucleus clearly.
mistakes.r: No shading or colouring: use clear, continuous pencil lines, and label the nucleus with a ruled line.

mistakes.w: Giving magnification a unit, for example 400 mm or 400 µm.
mistakes.r: Magnification is a ratio with no units; write x400.

mistakes.w: Labelling chloroplasts in an onion epidermis drawing.
mistakes.r: Draw and label only what is seen; onion bulb epidermal cells do not contain chloroplasts.

exam.q: A microscope has an eyepiece lens with a magnification of x10 and an objective lens with a magnification of x40. Calculate the total magnification.
exam.tip: Multiply the two lens magnifications. Adding them is the standard wrong answer.

exam.q: State why a stain such as iodine solution is added to onion cells before they are viewed with a light microscope.
model: To make cell structures (such as the nucleus) more visible / easier to see
exam.tip: Mention visibility or contrast of structures; 'to colour it' alone is too vague.

exam.q: Explain why a coverslip is lowered slowly at an angle onto the specimen.
model: To prevent air bubbles being trapped under the coverslip
because air bubbles would obscure the cells / make it harder to see the specimen clearly
exam.tip: An 'explain' question needs the reason and its consequence.

exam.q: Explain why a student should begin by using the lowest power objective lens.
model: It gives the largest field of view
so it is easier to find and centre the specimen / less chance of the lens hitting and breaking the slide
exam.tip: Link the property of the lens (wide field of view, further from the slide) to the benefit.

exam.q: The image of a cell in a photograph is 36 mm long. The actual length of the cell is 0.09 mm. Calculate the magnification of the photograph.
model: magnification = image size / actual size = 36 / 0.09
exam.tip: Both values are already in mm so no conversion is needed. Show the substitution for the method mark.

exam.q: A micrograph shows a cell with an image length of 45 mm. The magnification is x1500. Calculate the actual length of the cell in micrometres.
model: actual size = image size / magnification = 45 / 1500
exam.tip: Rearrange first, then convert at the end (or convert 45 mm to 45 000 µm first). Either route gains full marks.

exam.q: A scale bar on a micrograph is labelled 20 µm. The scale bar measures 16 mm. Calculate the magnification of the micrograph.
model: magnification = 16 000 / 20
exam.tip: The measured bar is the image size; the label on the bar is the actual size.

exam.q: A student draws a cheek cell seen with a microscope. The drawing is shaded, has sketchy lines, and the labels are joined to the cell by freehand arrows. Give three improvements the student should make.
model: Do not shade / colour the drawing
Use clear, continuous (single) lines drawn with a sharp pencil
Draw label lines with a ruler / without arrowheads / touching the structure
Add a title / add the magnification or a scale (any three)
exam.tip: Give three different improvements; two versions of the same point only score once.

exam.q: The diameter of the field of view of a microscope is 1.5 mm. A student counts 6 plant cells fitting end to end across the diameter. Estimate the length of one cell in micrometres.
exam.tip: Divide the diameter by the number of cells, then multiply by 1000 to change mm to µm.

exam.q: Describe how a student should use a light microscope to observe a prepared slide of plant cells at high magnification.
model: Place the slide on the stage and select the lowest power objective lens
Use the coarse focusing wheel to bring the lens and stage close together while looking from the side, then look through the eyepiece and move them apart until the cells are in focus
Use the fine focusing wheel to make the image sharp / clear
Change to a higher power objective lens and refocus using the fine focusing wheel (only)
exam.tip: Write the steps in order and name both focusing wheels.

exam.q: Describe how a student could prepare a slide of onion cells and use a light microscope to produce a labelled scientific drawing of the cells.
model: Peel a thin layer of onion epidermis (one cell thick) with forceps and place it flat in a drop of water on a slide
Add a drop of iodine solution to stain the cells so that structures are easier to see
Lower a coverslip slowly at an angle using a mounted needle to avoid air bubbles; remove excess liquid with paper towel
Place the slide on the stage, start with the lowest power objective lens and focus with the coarse focusing wheel, then the fine focusing wheel
Change to a higher power objective and refocus with the fine focusing wheel
Draw a few cells with a sharp pencil using clear continuous lines and no shading, in correct proportion
Label structures (cell wall, nucleus, cytoplasm) with ruled lines, and add a title and the magnification or scale
exam.tip: A 6 mark answer is marked on levels: cover all three parts (slide preparation, using the microscope, the drawing) in a logical order with reasons.

exam.q: When a student changes the objective lens from x4 to x40, the image becomes larger. State what happens to the number of cells that can be seen and give a reason.
model: Fewer cells can be seen
because the field of view is smaller / the diameter of the field of view is 10 times smaller
exam.tip: Higher magnification always means a smaller field of view.

worked.q: A drawing of a red onion cell is 72 mm long. The actual length of the cell is 180 µm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
steps: Write the equation: magnification = image size / actual size.
The units are different, so convert the image size into micrometres: 72 mm x 1000 = 72 000 µm.
Substitute: magnification = 72 000 / 180.
Check: the image is bigger than the real cell, so a magnification greater than 1 makes sense. Magnification has no units.

worked.q: A micrograph of a cell has a magnification of x2500. The nucleus in the micrograph measures 15 mm across. Calculate the actual diameter of the nucleus in micrometres.
steps: Rearrange the equation: actual size = image size / magnification.
Substitute: actual size = 15 / 2500 = 0.006 mm.
Convert to micrometres: 0.006 x 1000 = 6 µm.
Check: 6 µm x 2500 = 15 000 µm = 15 mm, which matches the image size.
worked.ans: 6 µm

worked.q: Using a x10 eyepiece and a x4 objective, a student measures the diameter of the field of view as 4 mm. She then switches to the x40 objective and counts 5 cells across the diameter. Estimate the length of one cell in micrometres.
steps: Total magnification at first = 10 x 4 = x40. After switching = 10 x 40 = x400.
The magnification has increased by a factor of 400 / 40 = 10, so the field of view is 10 times smaller.
New diameter of field of view = 4 / 10 = 0.4 mm.
Convert: 0.4 mm x 1000 = 400 µm.
Length of one cell = 400 / 5 = 80 µm.
worked.ans: About 80 µm
