bio_edx.0.5.summary: Enzymes are biological catalysts: proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being used up. Each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape, and only a substrate with a complementary shape can fit into it (the lock and key model), which is why enzymes are specific. If the shape of the active site changes, for example at high temperature or extreme pH, the substrate can no longer fit and the enzyme is said to be denatured.

core.p: An enzyme is a **biological catalyst**. A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being changed or used up itself. Enzymes are **proteins** made by living cells.
bullets: Thousands of chemical reactions happen in cells. Without enzymes most would be far too slow to keep the organism alive at body temperature.
Enzymes let these reactions happen quickly at the fairly low temperatures found in living things, without the need for the high temperatures that would damage cells.
Because an enzyme is **not used up**, one enzyme molecule can catalyse the same reaction again and again, so only small amounts are needed.
Enzymes are proteins: long chains of amino acids folded into a precise three-dimensional shape. The shape is what makes the enzyme work.
The molecule an enzyme acts on is called the **substrate**. The molecules made are the **products**.

callouts.p: An enzyme is a biological catalyst: a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.
'Biological' (made by living organisms, a protein) and 'catalyst' (speeds up the reaction, not used up or changed). Give both for full marks.

core.p: The **active site** is the small part of the enzyme molecule where the substrate binds and where the reaction takes place. It is a pocket or groove on the surface of the enzyme with a very particular shape.
bullets: The shape of the active site is produced by the way the protein chain is folded.
Only the active site binds the substrate; the rest of the enzyme molecule holds the active site in the correct shape.
The shape of the active site is **complementary** to the shape of its substrate, meaning the two shapes fit together like two jigsaw pieces.
Anything that changes the folding of the protein changes the shape of the active site, and so changes how well the enzyme works.

callouts.p: The active site is the part of an enzyme where the substrate binds (fits) and the reaction is catalysed.
The active site and the substrate do not have the same shape. They have complementary shapes: one fits into the other, like a key into a lock.

core.h: The lock and key model: how enzymes work step by step
core.p: The mechanism of enzyme action is explained by the **lock and key model**. The enzyme is the lock, the substrate is the key, and only the correctly shaped key fits the lock.
bullets: Substrate and enzyme molecules move around randomly in solution and **collide**.
If a substrate molecule collides with the active site in the right way, it **fits into (binds to) the active site** because their shapes are complementary.
This forms an **enzyme-substrate complex**: the enzyme and substrate joined together for a short time.
The reaction takes place while the substrate is held in the active site. The substrate is changed into the **products**.
The products have a different shape from the substrate, so they no longer fit and are **released** from the active site.
The enzyme is **unchanged** and its active site is free to bind another substrate molecule.
Summary: enzyme + substrate -> enzyme-substrate complex -> enzyme + products.

callouts.p: Substrate collides with and fits into the active site; shapes are complementary; enzyme-substrate complex forms; products are released; enzyme is unchanged and can be reused.
If a question says 'explain how an enzyme works' or 'explain the mechanism', the words active site, complementary and enzyme-substrate complex are the ones that earn the marks.

core.p: The lock and key model works in both directions. An enzyme may split one substrate into smaller products, or join two substrates into one larger product.
bullets: **Breakdown**: one large substrate molecule fits into the active site, is split, and two or more smaller product molecules are released.
**Synthesis**: two smaller substrate molecules fit side by side in the active site, are joined together, and one larger product molecule is released.
In both cases the substrate must be complementary to the active site, an enzyme-substrate complex forms, and the enzyme is unchanged at the end.

core.p: Enzymes are **specific**: each type of enzyme catalyses only one type of reaction, because it will only bind one type of substrate. Specificity is a direct result of the shape of the active site.
bullets: Each enzyme has an active site with a unique shape.
Only a substrate with the **complementary shape** can fit into that active site and form an enzyme-substrate complex.
A molecule with a different shape cannot fit, so no enzyme-substrate complex forms and no reaction is catalysed.
This is why the body needs many different enzymes: a different enzyme for each different reaction.
Example: amylase breaks down starch. It cannot break down protein, because a protein molecule is not complementary to the active site of amylase.
To explain specificity in an exam, always link three things: the shape of the active site, the complementary shape of the substrate, and whether they can fit together.

head: Statement
Why it follows from the lock and key model
rows: Each enzyme acts on only one substrate
Only one substrate shape is complementary to the active site
A different molecule is not broken down
It cannot fit into the active site, so no enzyme-substrate complex forms
Each reaction has a differently shaped substrate, so needs its own enzyme
A small amount of enzyme does a lot of work
The enzyme is unchanged after releasing the products and is reused

callouts.p: An enzyme is specific because only one substrate has a shape that is complementary to the shape of its active site.

core.h: Why shape depends on the protein structure
core.p: To understand denaturation you need to see why the active site has its shape in the first place. The reasoning is a chain of cause and effect.
bullets: An enzyme is a chain of amino acids in a particular order.
The chain folds up into a specific three-dimensional shape, which is held in place by **bonds** between different parts of the chain.
This folding creates the active site with its specific shape.
If the bonds holding the protein in shape are broken, the protein unfolds or changes shape, so the **shape of the active site changes**.
Chain of reasoning: bonds broken -> shape of enzyme changes -> shape of active site changes -> substrate no longer fits -> reaction is no longer catalysed.

core.p: An enzyme is **denatured** when the shape of its active site has changed so that the substrate can no longer fit into it. A denatured enzyme can no longer catalyse its reaction.
bullets: When the active site changes shape it is **no longer complementary** to the substrate.
The substrate cannot bind, so **enzyme-substrate complexes cannot form**.
The reaction is no longer catalysed, so the rate of reaction falls. When all the enzyme molecules are denatured the enzyme-catalysed reaction stops.
Denaturation is usually **permanent (irreversible)**: cooling the enzyme down again does not restore the shape of the active site.
The enzyme molecule is still there and is still a protein; it has changed shape, it has not been destroyed or 'killed'.

callouts.p: An enzyme is denatured when the shape of its active site has changed so the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme can no longer catalyse the reaction.
Never write that an enzyme is 'killed' or 'dies'. Enzymes are molecules, not living things. The correct word is denatured.

core.p: The specification links denaturation to **changes in the shape of the active site**. The two causes you must know are high temperature and pH that is too far from the enzyme's optimum.
bullets: **High temperature**: above the enzyme's optimum temperature the enzyme molecule vibrates so much that the bonds holding it in shape break. The active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured.
**Extremes of pH**: a pH much higher or lower than the enzyme's optimum affects the bonds holding the enzyme in shape. Again the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured.

**Low temperature does not denature enzymes**. At low temperature the molecules simply move more slowly, so the reaction is slow; the active site keeps its shape and the enzyme works again when warmed.
Different enzymes are denatured at different temperatures and pH values, because their protein structures are different.
The detailed shapes of the rate graphs for temperature and pH belong to the next spec point; here the key idea is what happens to the active site.

head: Condition
Effect on active site
Denatured?
rows: Bonds break; active site changes shape
pH far above or below optimum
Bonds affected; active site changes shape

callouts.p: 'The enzyme is denatured' on its own is often worth only one mark. Add: the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits / is no longer complementary.

core.h: Explaining denaturation in full: a model chain
core.p: A 3 or 4 mark question on denaturation expects a linked sequence, not a single word. Learn this chain and adapt it to the enzyme named in the question.
bullets: State the cause: for example, the temperature is above the optimum.
Bonds holding the enzyme in its shape are broken.
The **shape of the active site changes**.
The substrate is **no longer complementary** to the active site, so it cannot fit or bind.
No (or fewer) **enzyme-substrate complexes** form.
The enzyme is **denatured** and the rate of reaction decreases, eventually to zero.

callouts.p: If the question is about amylase and starch, write 'starch no longer fits the active site of amylase' rather than the general 'substrate' and 'enzyme'. Applying your answer to the context gains marks.

core.h: Collisions and why binding is needed
core.p: A reaction is only catalysed when a substrate molecule actually reaches and binds to an active site. This links the lock and key model to the movement of particles.
bullets: Enzyme and substrate molecules are in constant random motion in solution.
A reaction can only be catalysed after a **successful collision** between a substrate molecule and an active site.
The more often substrates collide with active sites, the more enzyme-substrate complexes form each second and the faster the reaction.
If the active site has the wrong shape (a denatured enzyme, or the wrong substrate), collisions still happen but they cannot lead to an enzyme-substrate complex.
So an enzyme needs two things to work: collisions with the substrate, and an active site with the correct shape.

core.h: How to use the model in unfamiliar questions
core.p: Edexcel often sets enzyme questions around an enzyme you have never heard of. You do not need to know the enzyme; you apply the same model.
bullets: Identify the enzyme, its substrate and the product(s) from the information given.
If asked why the enzyme only acts on that substrate: active site has a specific shape; only that substrate is complementary; so only it fits.
If asked why a similar molecule is not broken down: its shape is different, so it does not fit the active site.
If asked why the enzyme stops working after heating or in the wrong pH: the active site has changed shape, the substrate no longer fits, the enzyme is denatured.
If asked why only a little enzyme is needed: enzymes are not used up, so each molecule is reused many times.

A substance with a shape similar to the substrate may fit into the active site and block it, so the real substrate cannot bind. You can work this out from the lock and key model if a question describes it.

analogy.t: A lock, a key and a bent lock
analogy.p: An enzyme is like a lock and its substrate is like a key. The keyhole is the active site: only a key cut to the complementary shape will go in and turn, so each lock works with only one key (specificity). The lock is not used up when it is opened, so it can be used thousands of times, just as an enzyme is reused. If the lock is heated until the metal warps, the keyhole changes shape and the right key no longer fits: the lock is 'denatured', and cooling it down does not un-warp it. Where it breaks down: a key comes out of a lock unchanged, but a substrate is changed into different products that leave the active site; and real molecules are not placed carefully into the active site by a hand, they have to collide with it by random movement.

terms.d: A biological catalyst: a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being changed or used up in the reaction.
A catalyst made by living organisms; enzymes are biological catalysts.
A large molecule made of a chain of amino acids folded into a specific shape. All enzymes are proteins.
The molecule that an enzyme acts on; it binds to the active site and is changed in the reaction.
A molecule made in the reaction and released from the active site.
The part of an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction is catalysed; it has a specific shape.
Describes two shapes that fit together exactly, as the substrate fits the active site. It does not mean the same shape.
The temporary structure formed when a substrate is bound in the active site of an enzyme.
The model of enzyme action in which the substrate (key) fits into the complementary active site (lock) of the enzyme.
Each enzyme works on only one substrate, because only that substrate has a shape complementary to the active site.
Describes an enzyme whose active site has changed shape so that the substrate no longer fits and the reaction is no longer catalysed.
The condition (for example the temperature or pH) at which an enzyme works fastest.
To attach; the substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.

mistakes.w: The enzyme was killed by the high temperature.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are not living. The enzyme is denatured: the shape of its active site changes so the substrate no longer fits.

mistakes.w: The substrate has the same shape as the active site.
mistakes.r: The substrate has a shape that is complementary to the active site, so it fits into it.

mistakes.w: The substrate has an active site that the enzyme fits into.
mistakes.r: The active site is part of the enzyme. The substrate fits into the active site of the enzyme.

mistakes.w: The enzyme is denatured (with no further detail) in a 3 mark question.
mistakes.r: Explain it: bonds break, the shape of the active site changes, the substrate is no longer complementary and cannot bind, so no enzyme-substrate complexes form.

mistakes.w: Low temperatures denature enzymes.
mistakes.r: Low temperatures only slow the reaction because molecules move more slowly; the active site is unchanged and the enzyme works again when warmed.

mistakes.w: Enzymes are used up in the reaction, so more must be added.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are catalysts: they are unchanged at the end of the reaction and can be reused.

mistakes.w: The substrate is denatured / the substrate changes shape so it does not fit.
mistakes.r: It is the enzyme that is denatured: the active site of the enzyme changes shape.

mistakes.w: Enzymes are specific because they only work at one temperature.
mistakes.r: Specific means each enzyme acts on only one substrate, because only that substrate is complementary to its active site.

mistakes.w: Enzymes react with the substrate / enzymes are reactants.
mistakes.r: Enzymes catalyse (speed up) the reaction; they are not reactants and are not changed by it.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term enzyme.
model: A biological catalyst / a protein
that speeds up (the rate of) a reaction without being used up / changed
exam.tip: Two marks, two ideas: what it is (biological catalyst, protein) and what it does.

exam.q: Name the part of an enzyme that the substrate binds to.
model: Active site
exam.tip: A one-word recall mark. Do not write 'the lock'.

exam.q: Explain why an enzyme will only catalyse one reaction.
model: The active site has a specific shape
so only one substrate is complementary to it / only one substrate fits into the active site
exam.tip: Link the shape of the active site to the shape of the substrate using the word complementary.

exam.q: Describe how an enzyme breaks down a substrate molecule. Use the lock and key model in your answer.
model: The substrate fits into / binds to the active site of the enzyme
because the substrate and active site have complementary shapes, forming an enzyme-substrate complex
The substrate is broken down and the products are released (leaving the enzyme unchanged / free to be reused)
exam.tip: Write it as a sequence: bind, complex, products released.

exam.q: Lactase is an enzyme that breaks down lactose. Explain why lactase does not break down sucrose.
model: Sucrose has a different shape from lactose / is not complementary to the active site of lactase
so sucrose does not fit into the active site / no enzyme-substrate complex forms
exam.tip: Use the names in the question: lactase, lactose and sucrose.

exam.q: Explain what happens to an enzyme when it is heated to a temperature well above its optimum.
model: The shape of the active site changes (because bonds holding the enzyme in shape are broken)
so the substrate no longer fits / is no longer complementary to the active site
The enzyme is denatured (so it can no longer catalyse the reaction)
exam.tip: Three linked steps. 'Denatured' alone will not gain all three marks.

exam.q: A student writes: 'Boiling kills the enzyme.' Explain why this statement is incorrect and give the correct explanation.
model: Enzymes are not living / are proteins (molecules), so cannot be killed
The enzyme is denatured / the shape of its active site is changed so the substrate cannot fit
exam.tip: State what is wrong, then replace it with the correct scientific idea.

exam.q: Explain why only a small amount of enzyme is needed to break down a large amount of substrate.
model: Enzymes are not used up / are unchanged in the reaction
so each enzyme molecule can be reused / can bind to many substrate molecules one after another
exam.tip: This follows from the word catalyst.

exam.q: An enzyme is placed in a solution with a pH very different from its optimum pH. The enzyme stops working. Explain why.
model: The pH affects the bonds holding the enzyme in shape, so the shape of the active site changes
The substrate can no longer fit into / bind to the active site
so no enzyme-substrate complexes form / the enzyme is denatured
exam.tip: The explanation for extreme pH has the same structure as for high temperature: active site changes shape.

exam.q: An enzyme was cooled to 5 degrees C and then warmed to 35 degrees C. A second sample was heated to 90 degrees C and then cooled to 35 degrees C. Only the first sample catalysed the reaction at 35 degrees C. Explain these results.
model: At 5 degrees C the enzyme is not denatured / the shape of the active site is unchanged
so when warmed the substrate can still fit into the active site and the reaction is catalysed
At 90 degrees C the shape of the active site changes / the enzyme is denatured
This change is permanent (irreversible), so the substrate still cannot fit after cooling
exam.tip: Compare the two samples directly and say what happened to the active site in each.

exam.q: Explain the mechanism of enzyme action and how enzymes can be denatured.
model: Enzymes are biological catalysts (proteins) that speed up reactions without being used up
The enzyme has an active site with a specific shape
The substrate has a complementary shape and fits into / binds to the active site (lock and key model)
An enzyme-substrate complex forms, the reaction takes place and the products are released; the enzyme is unchanged and reused
Enzymes are specific: only one substrate fits the active site
High temperature or extreme pH breaks / affects the bonds holding the enzyme in shape, so the shape of the active site changes
The substrate no longer fits, so no enzyme-substrate complexes form; the enzyme is denatured and the reaction slows or stops
exam.tip: Level-marked: cover both halves of the question (mechanism and denaturation) with correct terms in a logical order.

worked.q: Catalase is an enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Explain, using the lock and key model, how catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide. (3 marks)
steps: Identify the enzyme (catalase), the substrate (hydrogen peroxide) and the products (water and oxygen).
Mark 1: hydrogen peroxide molecules collide with and fit into the active site of catalase.
Mark 2: this happens because the shape of hydrogen peroxide is complementary to the shape of the active site, so an enzyme-substrate complex forms.
Mark 3: the hydrogen peroxide is broken down and the products, water and oxygen, are released from the active site; catalase is unchanged and can be used again.
worked.ans: Hydrogen peroxide fits into the complementary active site of catalase, forming an enzyme-substrate complex; it is broken down into water and oxygen, which are released, leaving catalase unchanged to be reused.

worked.q: A biological washing powder contains a protease enzyme. The instructions say 'do not use above 60 degrees C'. Explain why the powder would not remove protein stains in a 90 degrees C wash. (4 marks)
steps: Recognise that 90 degrees C is far above the temperature at which this enzyme works, so the question is about denaturation.
Mark 1: at 90 degrees C the bonds holding the protease in its shape are broken.
Mark 2: so the shape of the active site of the protease changes.
Mark 3: the protein (substrate) in the stain is no longer complementary to the active site and cannot fit into it, so no enzyme-substrate complexes form.
Mark 4: the protease is denatured, so the protein in the stain is not broken down and the stain is not removed.
worked.ans: The high temperature denatures the protease: its active site changes shape, the protein no longer fits, no enzyme-substrate complexes form, and the protein stain is not broken down.

worked.q: Enzyme X breaks down substance P but has no effect on substance Q, even though P and Q are made of the same elements. Explain this observation. (2 marks)
steps: The question is about specificity, so think about shapes, not about which elements are present.
Mark 1: the active site of enzyme X has a specific shape that is complementary to P.
Mark 2: Q has a different shape, so it does not fit into the active site and no enzyme-substrate complex forms.
worked.ans: Enzyme X is specific: only P has a shape complementary to its active site; Q cannot fit, so Q is not broken down.

bio_edx.0.8.summary: The **rate** of an enzyme-controlled reaction tells you how fast substrate is used up or product is made. You calculate it by dividing the **change** (in mass, volume or number of product or substrate) by the **time taken**, by using **rate = 1 ÷ time** when you only know how long the reaction took, or by finding the **gradient** of a graph of results. Edexcel expects you to choose the right method, do the arithmetic accurately and always give the correct **units**.

core.h: What 'rate' means for an enzyme reaction
core.p: Enzymes are biological catalysts, so the whole point of studying them is to see how **fast** they make a reaction go. Rate is a measure of how much something changes in a given time. For an enzyme reaction, the 'something' is either the amount of **substrate used up** or the amount of **product formed**.
bullets: A **high rate** means a lot of change in a short time: the enzyme is working quickly.
A **low rate** means little change in a long time: the enzyme is working slowly.
A rate of **zero** means no reaction is happening, for example because the enzyme has been denatured or the substrate has run out.
Rate is always a 'per unit time' quantity, so its unit always includes **per second**, **per minute** or **per hour**.
Rate lets you compare enzyme activity fairly at different temperatures, pH values or substrate concentrations.

callouts.p: The amount of substrate used, or the amount of product formed, per unit of time.
rate = change ÷ time taken for that change. Every formula in this topic is a version of this.

core.p: Use this when the experiment measured **how much** substrate was used or product was made, and **how long** it took.
bullets: **rate = amount of product formed ÷ time taken**
or **rate = amount of substrate used ÷ time taken**
The 'amount' could be a **volume** (cm3 of oxygen gas), a **mass** (g of protein digested) or a change in a reading such as pH.
If you are given a start and an end reading, first calculate the **change**: change = final value - starting value.
The unit is the unit of the amount, then 'per', then the unit of time, for example **cm3/s** or **g/min**.
Example: catalase releases 24 cm3 of oxygen in 40 s. Rate = 24 ÷ 40 = **0.6 cm3/s**.

callouts.t: Read the question for the time unit
callouts.p: If the question says 'in cm3 per minute' but the time is given in seconds, convert the time first (divide seconds by 60) or convert the answer at the end (multiply a per-second rate by 60).

core.p: In many enzyme experiments you do not measure an amount at all. You simply time **how long it takes** for a reaction to finish, for example how long amylase takes to digest all the starch in a mixture (the iodine solution stops turning blue-black). The amount of substrate is the same in every tube, so the only thing that changes is the time.
bullets: **rate = 1 ÷ time**
The unit is **per second**, written **s^-1** (or /s). If time is in minutes the unit is min^-1.
A **short time** gives a **large** rate; a **long time** gives a **small** rate. Time and rate are inversely related.
Example: starch is fully digested in 50 s. Rate = 1 ÷ 50 = **0.02 s^-1**.

Because 1 ÷ time often gives awkward small decimals, some questions use **rate = 1000 ÷ time** instead. This just scales every value up by 1000 so the numbers are easier to plot. Use whichever the question tells you to use.
If the reaction never finishes (for example the enzyme is denatured), the time is effectively infinite, so the rate is **0**.

callouts.p: The tube with the SHORTEST time has the FASTEST rate. A very common error is to say the tube that took longest had the highest rate.
Every tube starts with the same amount of substrate. Rate = amount ÷ time, so if the amount is the same each time, rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time.

core.h: Method 3: rate from the gradient of a graph
core.p: If results are plotted with **time on the x-axis** and amount of product (or substrate) on the y-axis, the **gradient** (steepness) of the line is the rate.
bullets: **gradient = change in y ÷ change in x**
For a **straight line**, pick two points far apart on the line, draw a large triangle and divide the vertical change by the horizontal change.
A **steeper** line means a faster rate; a **flat** (horizontal) line means the rate is zero.
The unit is the y-axis unit per x-axis unit, for example cm3/s.
Read values from the **line of best fit**, not from individual plotted points.
Use a **large triangle**: this reduces the percentage error when reading the scales.

core.h: Curved graphs: tangents and initial rate
core.p: Most enzyme graphs of product against time are **curves**. They are steep at the start and then level off, so the rate is changing all the time. To find the rate at one particular moment you draw a **tangent**.
bullets: A **tangent** is a straight line that just touches the curve at one point and has the same steepness as the curve at that point.
Place a ruler on the curve at the time you are asked about, line it up with the slope of the curve there, and draw a long straight line.
Make a large triangle on the tangent and calculate **change in y ÷ change in x**.
The **initial rate** is the gradient of the tangent at **time = 0**. It is the fastest rate of the whole reaction.
Initial rate is used to compare conditions fairly, because at the very start the substrate concentration is the same in every experiment.
Tangent answers vary slightly from person to person, so mark schemes accept a **range** of values.

callouts.p: The rate of reaction at the very start (time = 0), found from the gradient of a tangent to the curve at the origin.

core.p: You may be asked to describe or explain the shape of a product-against-time graph as well as calculate from it.
bullets: **Start (steep):** substrate concentration is highest, so there are many successful collisions between substrate molecules and enzyme **active sites** each second. Rate is fastest.
**Middle (less steep):** substrate is being used up, so its concentration falls. There are fewer collisions per second, so the rate decreases.
**End (flat):** all the substrate has been converted to product. No more product can be made, so the amount stays constant and the rate is zero.
The enzyme itself is **not used up**: the line goes flat because the substrate has run out, not the enzyme.
The **final height** of the plateau shows the total amount of product, which depends on how much substrate you started with.

core.h: Mean rate versus rate at one moment
core.p: There are two different rates you can be asked for from the same set of data.
bullets: **Mean (average) rate** over a period = total change during that period ÷ length of the period.
**Rate at a particular time** = gradient of the tangent at that time.
For a straight-line graph these are the same; for a curve they are different.
Example: 30 cm3 of oxygen is collected in the first 60 s. Mean rate over the first 60 s = 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 cm3/s, even though the initial rate was higher than this and the rate at 60 s was lower.

head: What you are asked for
What to do
rows: Change in amount between those times ÷ time difference
Gradient of tangent drawn at time = 0
Rate at a given time on a curve
Gradient of tangent drawn at that time
Rate when only a time is recorded

core.p: A rate without a unit, or with the wrong unit, loses the mark. Work the unit out from the calculation itself.
bullets: Divide the units in the same way as you divided the numbers: cm3 ÷ s gives **cm3/s** (also written cm3 s^-1).
g ÷ min gives **g/min**.
1 ÷ s gives **s^-1** (per second).
To change a rate **per second into per minute**, multiply by 60. To change **per minute into per second**, divide by 60.
To change per minute into per hour, multiply by 60.

head: Measured
Calculation
Unit of rate
rows: Volume of gas in cm3, time in s
Mass in g, time in min
Only time in s, using 1000 ÷ time
arbitrary units (as given in the question)

core.h: Comparing rates: 'how many times faster?' and percentage change
core.p: Once you have two rates, questions often ask you to compare them.
bullets: **How many times faster** = larger rate ÷ smaller rate. Example: 0.02 s^-1 compared with 0.005 s^-1 is 0.02 ÷ 0.005 = 4 times faster.
**Percentage change** = (change in rate ÷ original rate) × 100.
Example: rate rises from 0.40 cm3/s to 0.50 cm3/s. Change = 0.10. Percentage increase = (0.10 ÷ 0.40) × 100 = 25%.
Always divide by the **original** value, not the new one.
State the direction: 'increase' or 'decrease'.

core.h: Processing repeats before calculating a rate
core.p: Real experiments are repeated, so you often need to process the raw data first.
bullets: Identify any **anomalous result** (one that does not fit the pattern of the other repeats) and leave it out.
Calculate the **mean**: add the remaining values and divide by how many there are.
Then use the mean time or mean volume in the rate calculation.
Give your answer to an appropriate number of **significant figures**, usually the same as the least precise data in the question (often 2 or 3), or whatever the question asks for.
Do not round until the final step; rounding early can change the answer.

core.h: Using rates to find the optimum
core.p: The reason for calculating rates is usually to see the effect of a factor on enzyme activity. You convert each time into a rate and plot rate against the factor.
bullets: Put the factor you changed (the **independent variable**, such as pH) on the x-axis and **rate** on the y-axis.
The **highest point** of the graph is the fastest rate; the pH or temperature at this point is the **optimum**.
If you plotted **time** instead of rate, the optimum would be at the **lowest** point, because the reaction finishes quickest there.
The true optimum may lie between two of the values tested; testing at smaller intervals around the peak gives a more accurate estimate.

core.h: A checklist for any rate calculation
core.p: Follow the same routine every time and you will pick up the method marks even if you make a slip.
bullets: 1. Decide what was measured: an amount and a time, only a time, or a graph.
2. Write the formula: change ÷ time, 1 ÷ time, or change in y ÷ change in x.
3. Convert units if the question asks for a different time unit.
4. Substitute the numbers and **show your working**.
5. Calculate, then round to the required significant figures or decimal places.
6. Write the **unit**.

callouts.p: In a 2 or 3 mark calculation, a correct substitution usually scores a mark even if the final answer is wrong. An answer on its own that is wrong scores nothing.

analogy.t: Rate is the speed of the reaction
analogy.p: Think of a car journey. **Speed = distance ÷ time**, just as **rate = amount of product ÷ time**. If every car drives the same 1 km route, the fastest car is the one with the shortest time, which is why rate = 1 ÷ time works when every tube has the same amount of substrate. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed, just as the gradient of a product-time graph is the rate, and a flat line means the car has stopped. Where it breaks down: a car stops because the driver chooses to, but an enzyme reaction stops because the substrate has run out, and it slows down gradually as the substrate concentration falls rather than at the will of a driver.

terms.d: The amount of substrate used or product formed per unit of time.
How fast an enzyme catalyses its reaction; measured as a rate of reaction.
The molecule that an enzyme acts on; its amount decreases during the reaction.
The molecule made in an enzyme-catalysed reaction; its amount increases during the reaction.
The steepness of a line on a graph, calculated as change in y ÷ change in x.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point and has the same gradient as the curve at that point.
The rate at the very start of the reaction (time = 0), when it is fastest.
The total change in amount over a period divided by the length of that period.
The unit of rate when rate is calculated as 1 ÷ time in seconds.
The value of a factor (such as pH or temperature) at which the rate of the enzyme-controlled reaction is highest.
The factor that is deliberately changed in an investigation; plotted on the x-axis.
The factor that is measured in an investigation (for example time taken or volume of product); plotted on the y-axis.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others; it is left out when calculating a mean.
The sum of the repeat values divided by the number of values.
(change ÷ original value) × 100.
The digits in a number that carry meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit; used to round answers sensibly.

mistakes.w: The reaction took 200 s at pH 5 and 50 s at pH 7, so the rate is higher at pH 5.
mistakes.r: A longer time means a slower rate. Rate = 1 ÷ time, so pH 7 (0.02 s^-1) is faster than pH 5 (0.005 s^-1).

mistakes.w: Rate = time ÷ volume, e.g. 40 ÷ 24.
mistakes.r: Rate = amount ÷ time, so 24 cm3 ÷ 40 s = 0.6 cm3/s. Time always goes on the bottom.

mistakes.w: Giving the answer as 0.6 with no unit, or writing the unit as cm3 or s.
mistakes.r: A rate unit must include both parts: cm3/s (or cm3 per second).

mistakes.w: Writing the unit of 1 ÷ time as seconds.
mistakes.r: 1 ÷ seconds gives per second: s^-1.

mistakes.w: Finding the gradient of a curve by joining the first and last points.
mistakes.r: That gives a mean rate. For the rate at a particular time, draw a tangent at that time and find its gradient.

mistakes.w: Using a tiny triangle on the tangent, or reading values from plotted points that are not on the line.
mistakes.r: Use a large triangle and read both values from the tangent line itself.

mistakes.w: The graph levels off because the enzyme is used up (or denatured).
mistakes.r: Enzymes are not used up. The line levels off because all the substrate has been converted into product.

mistakes.w: Calculating percentage change by dividing by the new value.
mistakes.r: Percentage change = (change ÷ original value) × 100.

mistakes.w: Including an obvious anomalous result when calculating the mean time.
mistakes.r: Leave anomalous results out, then calculate the mean of the remaining repeats.

exam.q: State the equation used to calculate the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction when only the time taken for the reaction to finish is known.
model: rate = 1 ÷ time (accept 1000 ÷ time)
exam.tip: A one-mark 'state' question needs only the equation.

exam.q: An enzyme breaks down hydrogen peroxide and 36 cm3 of oxygen is collected in 90 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of reaction. Give the unit.
model: = 0.4 cm3/s (accept cm3 per second)
exam.tip: One mark for the substitution or evaluation, one for the correct unit with the answer.

exam.q: Amylase digested all the starch in a solution in 80 seconds. Calculate the rate of reaction in s^-1.
exam.tip: Show 1 ÷ 80 before writing the answer.

exam.q: A protease digests 0.60 g of protein in 4 minutes. Calculate the rate of digestion in grams per second.
model: 4 minutes = 240 seconds
exam.tip: Convert the time first when the question asks for a different time unit.

exam.q: At 20 °C a reaction took 120 s. At 40 °C it took 30 s. Calculate how many times faster the reaction is at 40 °C than at 20 °C.
model: = 4 (times faster)
exam.tip: Because the amount of substrate is the same, the ratio of the times gives the same answer as the ratio of the rates.

exam.q: Three repeats at pH 6 gave times of 62 s, 58 s and 95 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction at pH 6, leaving out any anomalous result.
model: 95 identified as anomalous / left out
exam.tip: State which result you ignored so the examiner can follow your working.

exam.q: Describe how a student could use a graph of volume of product against time to find the initial rate of reaction.
model: draw a tangent to the curve at time = 0 / at the start
draw a (large) triangle / read off change in y and change in x from the tangent
divide change in y (volume) by change in x (time) / calculate the gradient
exam.tip: Three steps: tangent, triangle, divide.

exam.q: A graph of mass of product against time is steep at first and then becomes horizontal. Explain the shape of the graph.
model: rate is fastest at the start because substrate concentration is highest
so there are more (frequent) collisions between substrate and active sites
rate decreases as substrate is used up / substrate concentration falls
line is horizontal because all the substrate has been converted to product / reaction has stopped
exam.tip: Link each part of the curve to what is happening to the substrate. Do not say the enzyme is used up.

exam.q: The rate of an enzyme reaction increased from 0.25 cm3/s to 0.40 cm3/s when the temperature was raised. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
exam.tip: Divide the change by the original rate, not the new rate.

exam.q: A student investigates the effect of pH on the activity of amylase by timing how long it takes for starch to be digested at five different pH values. Describe how the student should process and present the results to find the optimum pH for the enzyme.
model: repeat at each pH and identify / discard anomalous results
calculate a mean time for each pH
calculate rate for each pH using rate = 1 ÷ time (or 1000 ÷ time)
plot a graph with pH on the x-axis and rate on the y-axis
draw a line / curve of best fit
the optimum pH is the pH at the highest rate / peak of the graph (shortest time)
test more pH values at smaller intervals around the peak to find the optimum more accurately
exam.tip: A 6-mark answer is marked by levels: give a logical sequence from raw data, to rate, to graph, to conclusion.

worked.q: Catalase is added to hydrogen peroxide. The gas syringe reads 4 cm3 at the start and 46 cm3 after 2 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production in cm3 per second.
steps: Change in volume = 46 - 4 = 42 cm3.
Convert the time: 2 minutes = 2 × 60 = 120 s.
Rate = change ÷ time = 42 ÷ 120.
Add the unit: cm3/s.

worked.q: Amylase digests starch in 40 s at pH 7 and in 160 s at pH 9. Calculate the rate at each pH and state how many times faster the reaction is at pH 7.
steps: Check: the shorter time has the larger rate, as expected.
worked.ans: 0.025 s^-1 at pH 7 and 0.00625 s^-1 at pH 9; the reaction is 4 times faster at pH 7.

worked.q: A tangent drawn at time = 0 on a graph of volume of oxygen (cm3) against time (s) passes through the points (0, 0) and (20, 30). Calculate the initial rate of reaction.
steps: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.
Change in y = 30 - 0 = 30 cm3.
Change in x = 20 - 0 = 20 s.
Gradient = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5.
Unit = y unit per x unit = cm3/s.
worked.ans: Initial rate = 1.5 cm3/s

bio_edx.0.9.summary: Enzymes are **biological catalysts** that speed up both the **breakdown** of large molecules and the **synthesis** (building) of large molecules in living organisms. Carbohydrates are broken down into **sugars**, proteins into **amino acids** and lipids into **fatty acids and glycerol**, and enzymes also join these small molecules back together to make the carbohydrates, proteins and lipids an organism needs. Without enzymes these reactions would be far too slow at body temperature to keep an organism alive.

core.h: The big idea: enzymes build up and break down
core.p: Living things are made mostly of three kinds of large biological molecule: **carbohydrates**, **proteins** and **lipids** (fats and oils). Organisms constantly need to take these molecules apart and put new ones together. Both kinds of reaction are catalysed by **enzymes**.
bullets: **Breakdown** reactions split a large molecule into smaller molecules (this is what happens in digestion).
**Synthesis** reactions join small molecules together to make a larger molecule.
Each reaction needs its **own specific enzyme**, because the shape of an enzyme's active site only fits its own substrate.
The enzyme is **not used up** or changed by the reaction, so one enzyme molecule can catalyse the reaction again and again.
Enzymes are proteins, so they are themselves made by synthesis reactions (from amino acids).

callouts.p: A biological catalyst: a protein that speeds up the rate of a reaction in a living organism without being used up or changed itself.
The building of larger, more complex molecules from smaller subunits.

core.h: The three large molecules and their subunits
core.p: You must be able to match each large molecule to the smaller molecules it is made from. These are exactly the pairs named in the specification.
bullets: **Carbohydrates** (such as starch and glycogen) are made of many **sugar** molecules, such as glucose, joined in long chains.
**Proteins** are made of long chains of **amino acids**.
**Lipids** (fats and oils) are made of **fatty acids and glycerol**. Each lipid molecule is made from one glycerol and three fatty acids.
Carbohydrates and proteins are long chains of repeating units; lipids are not long chains.

head: Large molecule
Broken down into
Type of enzyme that breaks it down
Example
rows: Sugars (simple sugars such as maltose and glucose)
Proteases in the stomach and small intestine

callouts.p: Always write 'fatty acids AND glycerol'. Writing only 'fatty acids' loses the mark.

core.p: Enzymes that break down carbohydrates are called **carbohydrases**. The one you must know by name is **amylase**.
bullets: Starch is a large, insoluble carbohydrate made of many glucose units joined together.
**Amylase** catalyses the breakdown of **starch** into smaller **sugars** (such as maltose).
Other carbohydrases then break these sugars down into simple sugars such as **glucose**.
The small sugar molecules are soluble and small enough to be absorbed.
Glucose is then used in **respiration** to release energy, or built up again into storage carbohydrates.

core.h: Breakdown of proteins into amino acids
core.p: Enzymes that break down proteins are called **proteases**.
bullets: A protein is a long chain of amino acids folded into a particular shape.
**Proteases** catalyse the breakdown of **proteins** into **amino acids**.
Amino acids are small and soluble, so they can be absorbed into the blood and carried to cells.
Cells use the amino acids to synthesise their own new proteins, for example enzymes and the proteins needed for growth and repair.

core.h: Breakdown of lipids into fatty acids and glycerol
core.p: Enzymes that break down lipids are called **lipases**.
bullets: A lipid molecule is made of three fatty acids joined to one glycerol.
**Lipases** catalyse the breakdown of **lipids** into **fatty acids and glycerol**.
The products are small enough to be absorbed.
Because **fatty acids** are acidic, the pH of the mixture **falls** as a lipid is broken down. This is used in experiments to follow the rate of lipid digestion with a pH indicator.
The products can be used in respiration or rebuilt into lipids for energy storage and for cell membranes.

core.h: Why large molecules must be broken down
core.p: The breakdown reactions matter because of **size and solubility**.
bullets: Starch, proteins and lipids in food are **too large** to pass through cell membranes, and many are **insoluble**.
They therefore cannot be **absorbed** from the gut into the blood as they are.
Enzymes break them down into **small, soluble molecules** (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) that **can** be absorbed into the blood and can pass into cells.
The same is true in other organisms: bacteria and fungi release enzymes onto their food to break it down outside their cells and then absorb the small products.

In plants, starch stored in a seed is broken down into sugars by enzymes when the seed germinates. The sugars can be transported to the growing parts and used in respiration to release energy for growth.

callouts.p: Large molecules are broken down into smaller, soluble molecules that can be absorbed and used by cells.

core.p: Organisms also need to **build** large carbohydrates from sugars. Enzymes catalyse these reactions by holding the small molecules in their active site so that they join together.
bullets: Many **glucose** molecules are joined together to make large storage carbohydrates.
In animals, glucose is joined to make **glycogen**, which is stored in liver and muscle cells. The enzyme that does this is **glycogen synthase**.
In plants, glucose made in photosynthesis is joined to make **starch** for storage.

Storing glucose as a large insoluble molecule is useful: it can be kept in the cell without affecting the movement of water by osmosis, and it can be broken down again when glucose is needed for respiration.

core.p: Proteins are synthesised by joining **amino acids** together in a particular order. Enzymes catalyse the reactions that join them.
bullets: The amino acids come from the breakdown of proteins in food.
New proteins are needed for **growth** and the **repair** of tissues.
Many proteins have specific jobs: **enzymes** themselves, and many other molecules that cells need, are proteins.
So protein synthesis depends on enzymes, and making enzymes depends on protein synthesis.

core.p: Lipids are synthesised by enzymes that join **fatty acids** to **glycerol**.
bullets: Lipids are an excellent long-term **energy store**.
Lipids are a major part of **cell membranes**, so new lipids are needed whenever new cells are made.
Stored lipids can be broken down again by lipases when the fatty acids and glycerol are needed.

head: Small molecules
Synthesised into
Why the organism needs it
rows: Carbohydrates (glycogen in animals, starch in plants)

core.h: Why enzymes are so important: speed at body temperature
core.p: This spec point uses the command word **explain**, so you need the reason enzymes matter, not just a list.
bullets: Without a catalyst, breakdown and synthesis reactions in cells would happen **far too slowly** to keep the organism alive.
Reactions could be sped up by raising the temperature, but high temperatures would **damage cells** and would speed up unwanted reactions as well as useful ones.
Enzymes allow reactions to happen **quickly at the relatively low temperature of the body** (about 37 °C in humans).
Because each enzyme is **specific**, the cell can control which reactions happen by controlling which enzymes it makes.
Enzymes are **not used up**, so only small amounts are needed.
All the reactions of an organism, both building up and breaking down, depend on enzymes.

callouts.p: Give two linked ideas: (1) enzymes speed up the reaction, and (2) the consequence, such as 'so food is broken down into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed' or 'so molecules needed for growth can be made fast enough'.

core.h: How one enzyme does its job (brief link to the mechanism)
core.p: You only need the outline here, to explain why different enzymes are needed for different molecules.
bullets: The substrate fits into the enzyme's **active site**, which has a shape that matches that substrate.
In a **breakdown** reaction, one large substrate molecule binds and is split into smaller product molecules, which are released.
In a **synthesis** reaction, two or more small substrate molecules bind and are joined into one larger product molecule, which is released.
A protease cannot break down starch, and amylase cannot break down protein, because the substrate does not fit the active site.
This is why the body needs carbohydrases, proteases **and** lipases.

core.p: Enzyme names usually end in **-ase** and are based on the substrate they act on. This helps you work out what an unfamiliar enzyme does in an exam question.
bullets: **Carbohydrase**: acts on carbohydrates. **Amylase** acts on starch.
**Protease**: acts on proteins.
**Lipase**: acts on lipids.
**Synthase** in a name (as in glycogen synthase) tells you the enzyme catalyses a synthesis reaction.
If a question names an enzyme you have not met, such as 'lactase', work out that it breaks down lactose.

callouts.p: Do not mix up the enzyme with its substrate or product. Amylase is the enzyme; starch is the substrate; sugars are the products.

analogy.t: A construction crew with specialised tools
analogy.p: Imagine a building site where walls are made of bricks. One specialised worker takes old walls apart into single bricks (breakdown), and another lays bricks to build new walls (synthesis). The bricks are the small molecules (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) and the walls are the large molecules (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids). Whole walls are too big to carry through a doorway, just as large molecules are too big to pass through a cell membrane, so they are taken apart, carried through as bricks and rebuilt where they are needed. Each worker has a tool that fits only one type of brick (specificity) and can be used again and again (enzymes are not used up). Where it breaks down: workers choose what to do and get tired, whereas enzymes simply collide with substrate molecules at random, and enzymes can be permanently put out of action by being denatured.

terms.d: A biological catalyst; a protein that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being changed or used up itself.
The molecule an enzyme acts on.
A molecule made in a reaction.
The part of an enzyme into which the substrate fits; its shape matches the shape of the substrate.
Building larger molecules from smaller subunits.
Splitting large molecules into smaller, soluble molecules.
A large molecule such as starch or glycogen, made of sugar molecules joined together.
An enzyme that breaks down carbohydrates into simple sugars.
A carbohydrase that breaks down starch into sugars such as maltose.
A large molecule made of a chain of amino acids.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins into amino acids.
A fat or oil; a molecule made of fatty acids and glycerol.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.
A storage carbohydrate in animals, made of many glucose molecules joined together.
An enzyme that joins glucose molecules together to make glycogen.
Describes an enzyme acting on only one substrate, because only that substrate fits its active site.
Taken into the blood or into cells; only small, soluble molecules can be absorbed.

mistakes.w: Lipids are broken down into fatty acids.
mistakes.r: Lipids are broken down into fatty acids AND glycerol. Both products are needed for the mark.

mistakes.w: Amylase breaks down sugar into starch.
mistakes.r: Amylase breaks down starch into sugars (such as maltose).

mistakes.w: Proteins are broken down into glucose (or into proteases).
mistakes.r: Proteins are broken down by proteases into amino acids.

mistakes.w: Enzymes are only used for digestion (breaking things down).
mistakes.r: Enzymes also catalyse synthesis reactions, building carbohydrates, proteins and lipids from smaller molecules.

mistakes.w: Food is broken down to make it smaller.
mistakes.r: Give the reason: large molecules are broken into small, soluble molecules so they can be absorbed into the blood / pass through cell membranes.

mistakes.w: The enzyme is used up in the reaction, so more must be made each time.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are catalysts: they are not used up and can be used again.

mistakes.w: Enzymes are living things / enzymes are killed by heat.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are protein molecules, not organisms. High temperatures denature them; they are not 'killed'.

mistakes.w: Enzymes provide energy for the reaction.
mistakes.r: Enzymes speed up the rate of reaction; they do not provide energy.

mistakes.w: Any enzyme can break down any food molecule.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are specific: only the correct substrate fits the active site, so carbohydrases, proteases and lipases are all needed.

exam.q: State the products of the breakdown of lipids.
model: fatty acids and glycerol
exam.tip: Both products are needed for the one mark.

exam.q: Name the type of enzyme that breaks down proteins.
model: protease
exam.tip: Spell it clearly: 'protein' is the substrate, 'protease' is the enzyme.

exam.q: Which molecules are produced when starch is broken down by amylase? A amino acids  B fatty acids  C glycerol  D sugars
model: D sugars
exam.tip: Multiple-choice questions on this point test the substrate, enzyme and product pairings.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by the term enzyme.
model: a biological catalyst / a protein that speeds up a reaction
without being used up / changed
exam.tip: Two marks: what it does, and that it is unchanged.

exam.q: Explain why starch in food must be broken down before it can be used by the body.
model: starch molecules are too large / insoluble so cannot be absorbed / cannot pass through cell membranes
broken down into small, soluble sugars that can be absorbed into the blood
exam.tip: Mention both the problem (too large) and the solution (small soluble molecules absorbed).

exam.q: Describe the role of enzymes in the synthesis of large molecules. Give one example.
model: enzymes catalyse / speed up the joining of small molecules
to form larger molecules
example: glucose joined to form glycogen (by glycogen synthase) / amino acids joined to form proteins / fatty acids and glycerol joined to form lipids
exam.tip: The example must name both the small molecules and the large molecule.

exam.q: Lipase is added to milk containing an indicator. Explain why the pH of the mixture decreases.
model: lipase breaks down the lipids / fats in the milk into fatty acids and glycerol
fatty acids are acidic so they lower the pH
exam.tip: Link the product (fatty acids) to the observation (lower pH).

exam.q: Explain why a protease cannot break down lipids.
model: enzymes are specific / the active site of protease has a specific shape
lipid (substrate) does not fit / is not the right shape for the active site of protease
exam.tip: Always refer to the shape of the active site and the substrate fitting.

exam.q: A seed contains stored starch. Explain how enzymes allow the seed to use this starch when it germinates.
model: amylase / carbohydrase breaks down the starch
into sugars / glucose (which are small and soluble)
sugars are used in respiration to release energy for growth / transported to growing parts
exam.tip: Apply what you know about amylase to an unfamiliar context.

exam.q: Explain why enzymes are important for the reactions that take place in living organisms.
model: enzymes are (biological) catalysts that speed up reactions
without enzymes reactions would be too slow to sustain life
they allow reactions to happen quickly at body temperature / without high temperatures that would damage cells
they are not used up so can be reused / they are specific so each reaction is controlled by its own enzyme
exam.tip: For 'explain the importance', say what enzymes do and then what would happen without them.

exam.q: Explain the importance of enzymes in the breakdown and synthesis of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.
model: enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions without being used up
carbohydrases such as amylase break down carbohydrates / starch into sugars
proteases break down proteins into amino acids
lipases break down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol
breakdown produces small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood / pass into cells
enzymes also join sugars to make carbohydrates (e.g. glycogen), amino acids to make proteins, and fatty acids and glycerol to make lipids
synthesised molecules are needed for growth, repair, energy storage and cell membranes
without enzymes these reactions would be too slow at body temperature
exam.tip: A level 3 answer covers BOTH breakdown and synthesis for all three molecules and explains why each matters, in a logical order.

worked.q: Complete the table: for each of carbohydrate, protein and lipid, give the enzyme that breaks it down and the products.
steps: Start with the substrate name and change the ending to -ase to find the enzyme type: carbohydrate gives carbohydrase, protein gives protease, lipid gives lipase.
Recall the subunits of each large molecule: carbohydrates are made of sugars; proteins are made of amino acids; lipids are made of fatty acids and glycerol.
Write each row in full, checking that lipid has two products.
worked.ans: Carbohydrate: carbohydrase (e.g. amylase for starch), sugars. Protein: protease, amino acids. Lipid: lipase, fatty acids and glycerol.

worked.q: Model answer (3 marks): Explain why a person who cannot make enough lipase may lose body mass.
steps: Identify what lipase does: it breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.
Say what happens without it: lipids stay as large molecules, which cannot be absorbed into the blood.
Link to the consequence: fewer fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed, so less is available as an energy source or to synthesise lipids for storage, so body mass falls.
worked.ans: Less lipase means fewer lipids are broken down into fatty acids and glycerol. The undigested lipids are too large to be absorbed, so less is available to be used for energy or to be built into stored lipids, and body mass decreases.

worked.q: Model answer (2 marks): After a meal, glucose is converted into glycogen in liver cells. Explain the role of an enzyme in this process.
steps: Recognise that this is a synthesis reaction: many small glucose molecules are joined into one large glycogen molecule.
State what the enzyme does: it catalyses (speeds up) the joining of the glucose molecules.
Name the enzyme if you can: glycogen synthase.
worked.ans: An enzyme (glycogen synthase) catalyses the joining of many glucose molecules together to synthesise glycogen, so the reaction happens quickly enough at body temperature.

svg.cap: Breakdown reactions. Each large molecule is broken down by its own specific type of enzyme into small, soluble molecules: starch into sugars, proteins into amino acids, and lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

bio_edx.0.10.summary: This triple-only core practical uses **chemical reagents** to find out which biological molecules a food contains. **Iodine solution** tests for **starch**, **Benedict's reagent** (heated) tests for **reducing sugars**, **biuret reagent** tests for **proteins**, and the **ethanol emulsion test** detects **fats (lipids)**. For each test you must know the reagent, the method, the colour before and after, and the safety precautions, because exam questions ask you to describe the tests and interpret results.

core.p: Foods are mixtures of large biological molecules: carbohydrates (sugars and starch), proteins and lipids (fats and oils). Each one reacts with a particular reagent to give a clear change. By testing a food sample with each reagent in turn you can identify which nutrients it contains. These are **qualitative** tests: they show whether a molecule is present, not exactly how much.
bullets: **Starch** is tested with **iodine solution**.
**Reducing sugars** (e.g. glucose, maltose) are tested with **Benedict's reagent** and **heat**.
**Proteins** are tested with **biuret reagent**.
**Fats / lipids** are tested with the **ethanol emulsion test**.
Benedict's test can be **semi-quantitative**: the colour gives a rough idea of how much reducing sugar is present.
This is **triple biology only** (1.13B).

callouts.p: For each test learn: **reagent**, **what you do**, **negative colour**, **positive colour**.

core.p: Most tests need the food in solution. Solid food is broken up so that the molecules can come into contact with the reagent.
bullets: Cut a small piece of food and **grind it with distilled water** using a **mortar and pestle** to make a paste.
Transfer the paste to a beaker, add more distilled water and **stir** to dissolve some of the food.
**Filter** the mixture (filter funnel and paper) to get a clear solution for the colour tests.
Use **distilled water** so no other chemicals interfere with the tests.
Use **clean apparatus** for each test so you do not carry food or reagent between samples.
For the fat test the food is mixed with **ethanol**, not water, because lipids dissolve in ethanol.

callouts.p: Run each test on **distilled water alone** as a negative control. This shows the colour of a negative result so you can compare.

core.p: Iodine solution reacts with starch to form a dark blue-black colour. This is a quick test that can be done on a solid food or a food solution without heating.
bullets: Place a few cm3 of food solution in a test tube, or put the food on a **spotting tile**.
Add a **few drops of iodine solution**.
**Negative:** stays **orange-brown** (the colour of iodine solution).
**Positive:** turns **blue-black**: starch is present.
No heating is needed.
Foods that give a positive result include bread, potato, pasta and rice.

callouts.p: Iodine solution changes from **orange-brown to blue-black** in the presence of **starch**.

core.p: Benedict's reagent is blue because it contains copper(II) ions. When heated with a reducing sugar, the copper ions are reduced and a coloured precipitate forms. The colour depends on how much reducing sugar is present.
bullets: Put about **2 cm3 of food solution** in a test tube.
Add an **equal volume (about 2 cm3) of Benedict's reagent**.
Place the tube in a **hot water bath** (about 80 °C or hotter) for about **5 minutes**.
**Negative:** stays **blue**.
**Positive:** changes to **green, yellow, orange or brick-red** (a precipitate forms).
More reducing sugar gives a colour further along: green (small amount) to **brick-red** (large amount).
Reducing sugars include **glucose**, **fructose** and **maltose**.
**Sucrose** is **not** a reducing sugar, so it gives a negative (blue) Benedict's test.

callouts.p: Benedict's test **only works when heated**. Forgetting the water bath is a very common lost mark.

core.p: Biuret reagent contains sodium hydroxide and copper sulfate, which is why it is pale blue. The copper ions react with the peptide bonds in proteins to give a purple colour.
bullets: Put about **2 cm3 of food solution** in a test tube.
Add an equal volume of **biuret reagent** (or add sodium hydroxide solution, then a few drops of dilute copper sulfate solution) and shake gently.
No heating is needed; leave for a few minutes.
**Negative:** stays **blue**.
**Positive:** turns **purple / lilac / mauve**: protein is present.
Foods that give a positive result include egg white, milk, meat and beans.

callouts.p: Biuret reagent changes from **blue to purple (lilac)** in the presence of **protein**.

core.h: Test for fats: ethanol emulsion test
core.p: Lipids dissolve in ethanol but **do not dissolve in water**. When an ethanol solution containing fat is poured into water, the fat comes out as tiny droplets spread through the water. These droplets scatter light, making a **cloudy white emulsion**.
bullets: Crush the food and **shake it with about 2 cm3 of ethanol** in a test tube to dissolve any lipid.
Allow the solid to settle, then **pour the ethanol (liquid) into a test tube of distilled water**.
**Negative:** the mixture stays **clear**.
**Positive:** a **cloudy white (milky) emulsion** forms: fat is present.
Foods that give a positive result include butter, oil, nuts and cheese.
No heating: **ethanol is highly flammable**.

callouts.p: Tiny droplets of one liquid (here fat) spread through another liquid (water) in which it does not dissolve.

core.h: Summary table of all four tests
core.p: This is the table to memorise. Exam questions often give a table of results and ask which foods contain which nutrients.
bullets: Learn the reagent and both colours for each row.
Only the **Benedict's test needs heating**.
Only the **fat test uses ethanol**.

core.p: Each reagent brings its own hazard. A good risk assessment names the hazard, the risk and a control measure.
bullets: Wear **eye protection** throughout.
**Ethanol** is **highly flammable**: no naked flames nearby, so use an electric water bath for the Benedict's test rather than a Bunsen burner.
**Biuret reagent** contains **sodium hydroxide**, which is **corrosive / irritant**: avoid skin contact and wash off splashes at once.
**Benedict's reagent** is an irritant; the water bath is hot, so use a test tube holder.
**Iodine solution** is an irritant and stains skin and clothes.
**Never eat** food used in the lab, and be aware of food allergies (e.g. nuts).

callouts.p: A water bath heats evenly, avoids the tube boiling over and keeps flames away from the flammable ethanol used in the same practical.

core.p: Because the colour depends on how much reducing sugar there is, you can compare foods. To make this a fair comparison, everything except the food must be the same.
bullets: Use the **same volume** of food solution and of Benedict's reagent each time.
Use the **same mass of food** dissolved in the **same volume of water**.
Heat at the **same temperature** for the **same time**.
Compare colours against a set of **standards** made with known glucose concentrations.
A **colorimeter** can measure the colour objectively instead of judging by eye.
You could also filter and weigh the dried precipitate: more precipitate means more reducing sugar.

callouts.p: Colour by eye only gives an estimate, which is why the test is called **semi-quantitative**.

core.p: A positive test shows a molecule is present, but there are limits to what you can conclude.
bullets: A **negative Benedict's test** does not mean there is no sugar: the food could contain **sucrose** (a non-reducing sugar).
Colour judgements are **subjective**: compare with a control or use a colorimeter.
Strongly coloured foods (e.g. beetroot) can hide colour changes.
Reagents can be **contaminated** if the same pipette is used for different tests.
A food can contain several molecules, e.g. milk tests positive for protein, fat and reducing sugar (lactose).

core.p: These tests are used in other investigations, for example showing that amylase digests starch into sugar.
bullets: Before digestion: starch gives **blue-black** with iodine and Benedict's stays **blue**.
After amylase acts: iodine stays **orange-brown** and Benedict's gives a **brick-red** precipitate, showing maltose (a reducing sugar) has been made.
Proteases break proteins into amino acids; lipases break lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.
Enzymes speed up the breakdown of large molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed.

analogy.p: Each reagent is like a sniffer dog trained to react to just one thing: iodine 'barks' blue-black only at starch, Benedict's glows from blue towards brick-red only at reducing sugars (and only when it is warmed up), biuret turns purple only for proteins, and water turns milky only when fat has been smuggled in with the ethanol. Where it breaks down: a sniffer dog finds an exact location, but these tests only tell you something is in the sample, and apart from Benedict's they say little about how much.

terms.d: A chemical added to a sample to test for a particular substance.
Orange-brown reagent that turns blue-black when starch is present.
Blue reagent that, when heated, forms a green, yellow, orange or brick-red precipitate with reducing sugars.
A sugar such as glucose, fructose or maltose that gives a positive Benedict's test.
A sugar such as sucrose that does not give a positive Benedict's test.
Blue reagent containing sodium hydroxide and copper sulfate that turns purple with protein.
Tiny droplets of one liquid dispersed in another, e.g. fat droplets in water, appearing cloudy white.
Test for lipids: dissolve food in ethanol, pour into water; a cloudy white emulsion shows fat.
Fats and oils, made from fatty acids and glycerol; insoluble in water.
An insoluble solid that forms in a solution during a reaction.
A test that shows whether a substance is present, not how much.
Gives an approximate amount, e.g. Benedict's colour indicating more or less sugar.
A test on distilled water alone to show the colour of a negative result.
An instrument that measures the colour (light absorbed) of a solution objectively.

mistakes.w: Iodine turns blue-black when sugar is present.
mistakes.r: Iodine turns blue-black with **starch**; sugars are tested with **Benedict's**.

mistakes.w: Add Benedict's reagent and look for a colour change.
mistakes.r: Add Benedict's and **heat in a water bath** for about 5 minutes, then look for a brick-red precipitate.

mistakes.w: Benedict's positive result is red.
mistakes.r: Positive is **green, yellow, orange or brick-red** depending on the amount; negative stays **blue**.

mistakes.w: Biuret turns pink / violet goes to blue.
mistakes.r: Biuret changes from **blue to purple (lilac)** when protein is present.

mistakes.w: Heat the ethanol to dissolve the fat.
mistakes.r: **Never heat ethanol**: it is highly flammable. Shake with ethanol, then pour into water.

mistakes.w: Fat test: the mixture turns white and clear.
mistakes.r: A **cloudy white emulsion** forms; a negative result stays **clear**.

mistakes.w: A negative Benedict's test proves there is no sugar.
mistakes.r: It shows no **reducing** sugar; **sucrose** is a non-reducing sugar and gives a negative result.

mistakes.w: Iodine negative result is clear / colourless.
mistakes.r: Negative iodine stays **orange-brown**.

exam.q: Name the reagent used to test for starch.
model: Iodine solution
exam.tip: Say iodine solution, not just 'iodine'.

exam.q: Describe the colour change for a positive biuret test.
model: Blue
to purple / lilac / mauve
exam.tip: Give both the start and end colour.

exam.q: State one food molecule that gives a positive result with Benedict's reagent.
model: Glucose / fructose / maltose / any reducing sugar
exam.tip: Not sucrose and not starch.

exam.q: Describe how to test a food solution for reducing sugars.
model: Add (equal volume of) Benedict's reagent to the food solution
Heat in a (hot) water bath for a few minutes
Positive: colour changes from blue to green / yellow / orange / brick-red (precipitate)
exam.tip: Heating is a mark in itself.

exam.q: Explain why the ethanol emulsion test must not be done near a Bunsen burner flame.
model: Ethanol is (highly) flammable
Could catch fire / so use a water bath / no naked flames
exam.tip: Name the hazard and the consequence.

exam.q: Describe how to test a sample of crushed nuts for fat.
model: Shake / mix the food with ethanol
Pour the ethanol (liquid) into water
Cloudy / milky white emulsion shows fat present
exam.tip: Order matters: ethanol first, then water.

exam.q: Two food samples, A and B, were tested with Benedict's reagent. A turned green and B turned brick-red. Explain what this shows.
model: Both contain reducing sugar
B contains more reducing sugar than A
exam.tip: The colour order is blue, green, yellow, orange, brick-red.

exam.q: A student tested a sugar solution with Benedict's reagent and it stayed blue after heating. Suggest why, even though the solution contained sugar.
model: The sugar was a non-reducing sugar
e.g. sucrose
exam.tip: Know the example: sucrose.

exam.q: Suggest how the Benedict's test could be used to compare the amount of reducing sugar in two fruit juices fairly.
model: Same volume of juice and of Benedict's reagent
Same temperature and time of heating
Compare colour against standards / use a colorimeter
exam.tip: Fair test means naming the control variables.

exam.q: Describe how you would use chemical tests to show which of starch, reducing sugar, protein and fat are present in a sample of milk. Include the expected results.
model: Grind / mix food with distilled water (and filter) to make a solution
Iodine solution: blue-black if starch present (stays orange-brown if not)
Benedict's reagent, heat in water bath: green / yellow / orange / brick-red if reducing sugar present (stays blue if not)
Biuret reagent: purple / lilac if protein present (stays blue if not)
Shake with ethanol then pour into water: cloudy white emulsion if fat present
Safety: eye protection, no flames near ethanol, biuret is corrosive / irritant
Use a negative control with distilled water
exam.tip: For 6 marks cover all four tests with reagent and positive colour, plus a safety point.

worked.q: A food was tested: iodine stayed orange-brown; Benedict's (heated) turned orange; biuret turned purple; ethanol then water gave a clear solution. Which nutrients does the food contain?
steps: Iodine stayed orange-brown: negative, so **no starch**
Benedict's turned orange: positive, so **reducing sugar present** (a moderate amount)
Biuret turned purple: positive, so **protein present**
Emulsion test stayed clear: negative, so **no fat**
worked.ans: The food contains reducing sugar and protein but no starch or fat.

worked.q: A student adds Benedict's reagent to a glucose solution, waits 5 minutes at room temperature and sees no change. She concludes there is no glucose. Evaluate her conclusion and suggest how to improve the method.
steps: Glucose is a reducing sugar, so it should give a positive result
Benedict's test only works when the mixture is **heated**
At room temperature the reaction does not happen, so the result is a **false negative**
Improvement: place the tube in a hot water bath (about 80 °C or more) for about 5 minutes
Include a negative control (water) to compare colours
worked.ans: The conclusion is invalid because the mixture was not heated; heat in a water bath and repeat to see a green to brick-red precipitate.
