bio_edx.0.11.summary: **Calorimetry** measures the energy stored in food by burning it and using the energy released to **heat a known mass of water**. You measure the **temperature rise**, then calculate the energy transferred with **energy (J) = mass of water (g) x 4.2 x temperature change (°C)**, and divide by the mass of food burned to get **energy per gram**. The simple school method always **underestimates** the true value because much of the energy is lost to the surroundings, which is why a **bomb calorimeter** is used to measure the values printed on food labels.

core.p: Food contains chemical energy stored in molecules such as carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. When food burns, this energy is released as heat (thermal energy). In calorimetry the heat from burning food is transferred to water. Because we know how much energy it takes to warm water, the temperature rise of the water tells us how much energy the food released.
bullets: **Calorimetry** = measuring energy by the temperature change it causes in water.
Energy in food is measured in **joules (J)** or **kilojoules (kJ)**; 1 kJ = 1000 J.
Food labels also use **kilocalories (kcal)**, but GCSE calculations use joules.
Burning food in oxygen releases the same total energy as respiration, but all at once as heat.
This is **triple biology only** (1.14B).

callouts.p: A method of measuring the **energy content of food** by burning it and measuring the **temperature rise of a known mass of water**.

core.p: The school method is simple and cheap. Each piece of equipment allows you to measure one of the values in the energy equation.
bullets: **Boiling tube** held in a **clamp stand**, containing water.
**Measuring cylinder** to measure the volume of water (e.g. **20 cm3**).
**Thermometer** to measure the starting and final temperature of the water.
**Balance** (to 0.01 g) to measure the mass of the food sample.
**Mounted needle** to hold the food while it burns.
**Bunsen burner** to light the food.
**Heat-proof mat** under the apparatus.
Small dry foods that burn well, such as crisps, nuts, bread or pasta.

callouts.t: 1 cm3 of water has a mass of 1 g
callouts.p: So 20 cm3 of water = **20 g** of water. This lets you use volume in place of mass.

core.p: Learn the method in order. A common 6 mark question asks you to describe it, including how to make it fair.
bullets: 1. **Measure 20 cm3 of water** with a measuring cylinder and pour it into a boiling tube clamped to a stand.
2. Record the **starting temperature** of the water with a thermometer.
3. **Weigh** a small piece of food on a balance and record its mass.
4. Fix the food on a **mounted needle**.
5. Hold the food in a **Bunsen burner flame** until it **catches fire**.
6. Immediately hold the burning food **under the boiling tube** (about 1 cm below).
7. If it goes out, **relight it** and put it back under the tube, until it will no longer catch fire (fully burnt).
8. Stir the water gently with the thermometer and record the **highest (final) temperature**.
9. Calculate the **temperature rise** = final - starting temperature.
10. Repeat with fresh water for the same food, and then for other foods, to compare.

callouts.p: Keep relighting until the food will not catch light. If some food remains, weigh it and subtract to find the mass actually burned.

core.p: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C is **4.2 J**. This is the specific heat capacity of water. Multiplying by the mass of water and the temperature rise gives the energy transferred to the water.
bullets: **Energy transferred (J) = mass of water (g) x 4.2 x temperature change (°C)**
Temperature change = final temperature - starting temperature.
Mass of water in g = volume in cm3.
To compare foods fairly, find the **energy per gram**:
**Energy per gram of food (J/g) = energy transferred (J) / mass of food burned (g)**
Divide by 1000 to convert J to kJ.

head: Quantity
Unit
How it is found
rows: Volume measured with a measuring cylinder (1 cm3 = 1 g)
Constant: energy to heat 1 g of water by 1 °C
Energy transferred divided by mass of food

callouts.p: **E = m x 4.2 x ΔT**. E in joules, m = mass of water in grams, ΔT in °C.

core.p: To compare the energy in different foods, everything apart from the type of food must be kept the same. Then any difference in energy per gram is due to the food.
bullets: **Independent variable:** type of food.
**Dependent variable:** temperature rise of the water (used to calculate energy per gram).
**Control:** the same **volume of water** each time.
**Control:** the same **distance** between the burning food and the tube.
**Control:** the same **starting temperature** of water (use fresh water each time).
**Control:** use the same type of boiling tube and keep the apparatus out of draughts.
Similar mass of food helps, but calculating **energy per gram** allows for different masses.

callouts.p: Always use **fresh cold water** for each test. Reusing warm water changes the starting temperature.

core.p: The value you calculate is always much **lower** than the value on the food label. This is because not all of the energy from the food ends up in the water.
bullets: **Heat is lost to the surrounding air** because the boiling tube is open and the flame is not enclosed.
Energy **heats the boiling tube, thermometer and needle**, not just the water.
**Incomplete combustion**: some food is left unburnt or turns to soot / ash.
Energy is lost as the food is **moved from the Bunsen flame** to the tube.
Some energy is released as **light**, not heat.
Some water may **evaporate**, carrying energy away.

callouts.p: These losses happen in **every** test, so the results are **all too low** (a systematic error). Repeats do not fix this.

core.p: Improvements aim to make sure more of the energy released ends up in the water, and that the measurements are more precise.
bullets: **Insulate** the boiling tube (e.g. with cotton wool or foil) to reduce heat loss.
Use a **draught shield / screen** around the apparatus.
Keep the food **close to the tube** and at the same distance each time.
**Stir** the water so the temperature is even before reading.
Use a **digital thermometer** (temperature probe) for more precise readings.
Make sure the food is **completely burnt**; weigh any remains.
Use a **calorimeter** (a closed, insulated container) instead of an open tube.

core.p: Food scientists use a **bomb calorimeter** to measure the energy values printed on food labels. It is designed to stop almost all heat escaping, so the result is much more accurate.
bullets: Food is burned in a **sealed chamber** filled with **pure oxygen**, so combustion is **complete**.
The food is lit electrically using **ignition wires**, so no energy is lost moving it from a flame.
The chamber is surrounded by a known mass of **water**.
The whole thing is inside an **insulated container**, so very little heat is lost.
A **stirrer** spreads the heat evenly through the water.
A precise **thermometer** measures the temperature rise.

core.h: Why different foods give different values
core.p: Different nutrients store different amounts of energy per gram, so foods rich in fat release more energy than foods rich in carbohydrate or protein.
bullets: **Lipids (fats)** release roughly **twice as much energy per gram** as carbohydrates or proteins.
Nuts and crisps (high in fat) give high values.
Foods with lots of **water** or **fibre** give lower values per gram.
Comparing energy per gram, rather than total energy, allows for different masses of food.

callouts.p: If asked which food has most energy, compare **energy per gram**, not the temperature rise alone, unless the masses were the same.

core.p: Burning food involves flames and hot apparatus, and some foods can cause allergic reactions.
bullets: Wear **eye protection**: burning food can spit.
Use a **heat-proof mat** and keep the Bunsen on a safety flame when not in use.
Tie back long hair and keep flammable items away.
**Nut allergies**: check before using peanuts or other nuts; some people react to the smoke or touching them.
Do not eat food used in the lab.
Hold the food on a **mounted needle** with the handle away from you to avoid burns.

callouts.p: Peanuts are often used but can trigger serious allergic reactions; a risk assessment must consider this.

core.p: As well as the systematic heat loss, there are random errors from reading instruments and handling the food.
bullets: **Thermometer readings**: read at eye level; a digital probe gives better resolution.
**Small food masses**: a balance reading to 0.01 g reduces percentage error.
**Varying distance** of food from the tube gives different results each time.
Repeat each food **three times** and calculate a **mean** to improve repeatability.
Identify and exclude **anomalous** results before calculating the mean.

analogy.p: Think of the energy in the food as water poured from a jug into a bucket that has holes in it. The bucket is the water in the boiling tube. You only measure what is left in the bucket, but some leaked out on the way (heat to the air, heating the tube, food not fully burnt). A bomb calorimeter is a bucket with almost no holes, so you catch nearly all of it. Where it breaks down: energy is not a substance that drips; it is transferred as heat to many places at once, and some is transferred as light.

terms.d: Measuring the energy in food by burning it and measuring the temperature rise of a known mass of water.
Apparatus in which food is burned to measure the energy released.
A sealed, insulated calorimeter where food is burned in pure oxygen; gives accurate energy values.
The unit of energy; 1 kJ = 1000 J.
The energy needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C: 4.2 J.
Final temperature minus starting temperature, in °C.
Energy transferred divided by the mass of food burned, in J/g or kJ/g.
Burning with enough oxygen so all the food is burnt and all its energy is released.
Burning that leaves unburnt food or soot, so not all the energy is released.
A needle with a handle used to hold food while it burns.
Material that reduces heat transfer to the surroundings.
An error that makes every result too high or too low by a similar amount, e.g. heat loss.
Unpredictable variation between readings, reduced by repeating and taking a mean.
Sum of repeat results divided by the number of results.

mistakes.w: Energy = mass of food x 4.2 x temperature change.
mistakes.r: Use the **mass of water**: energy = mass of water x 4.2 x temperature change.

mistakes.w: The temperature change is the final temperature.
mistakes.r: Temperature change = **final - starting** temperature.

mistakes.w: The result is too low because the thermometer was inaccurate.
mistakes.r: The main reason is **heat lost to the surroundings** (and heating the tube, incomplete burning).

mistakes.w: Repeating the experiment makes the value closer to the label.
mistakes.r: Repeats improve **repeatability**; they do not remove the systematic **heat loss**.

mistakes.w: Food A raised the temperature more so it has more energy.
mistakes.r: Compare **energy per gram**: divide energy by the mass of food burned.

mistakes.w: Answer given in J/g when the question asks for kJ/g, e.g. 4200 kJ/g.
mistakes.r: Divide by **1000** to convert J to kJ: 4200 J/g = 4.2 kJ/g.

mistakes.w: The bomb calorimeter is more accurate because it is bigger.
mistakes.r: It is **insulated** and the food burns **completely in pure oxygen**, so very little energy is lost.

mistakes.w: Reuse the same water for each food to keep it fair.
mistakes.r: Use **fresh water** of the same volume and starting temperature for each test.

exam.q: State the equation used to calculate the energy transferred to the water.
model: Energy (J) = mass of water (g) x 4.2 x temperature change (°C)
exam.tip: The 4.2 is always given in Edexcel questions, but learn it anyway.

exam.q: Explain why 20 cm3 of water can be taken as 20 g in this calculation.
model: 1 cm3 of water has a mass of 1 g
exam.tip: Short and exact.

exam.q: 20 g of water was heated from 20 °C to 35 °C by burning a crisp. Calculate the energy transferred to the water.
model: Temperature change = 35 - 20 = 15 °C
exam.tip: Work out the temperature change first.

exam.q: A crisp of mass 0.60 g transferred 1260 J to the water. Calculate the energy per gram in kJ/g.
exam.tip: Watch the units the question asks for.

exam.q: Give two reasons why the value measured is lower than the value on the food packet.
model: Heat lost to the surroundings / air
Energy used to heat the boiling tube / thermometer / needle
Food not completely burnt / incomplete combustion
exam.tip: Any two different reasons.

exam.q: Suggest two improvements to the method to reduce heat loss.
model: Insulate the boiling tube / use a lid
Use a draught shield
Keep the food close to the tube
exam.tip: Improvements must target the cause of the error.

exam.q: Explain why the student relit the food until it would not burn any more.
model: So all the food is burnt / complete combustion
So all the energy in the food is released / transferred to the water
exam.tip: Link the step to energy released.

exam.q: Give two variables that must be controlled when comparing the energy in different foods.
model: Volume / mass of water
Distance of food from the tube
Starting temperature of the water
exam.tip: Not 'the type of food': that is the independent variable.

exam.q: Explain why a bomb calorimeter gives a more accurate value than the school method.
model: Insulated so less heat lost to surroundings
Food burned in pure oxygen so complete combustion
Ignited electrically inside so no energy lost moving food / sealed chamber
exam.tip: Each feature should be linked to less energy lost.

exam.q: Describe how to use calorimetry to compare the energy content of two different foods.
model: Measure a fixed volume of water (e.g. 20 cm3) into a boiling tube in a clamp
Record starting temperature with a thermometer
Weigh the food sample
Set food alight using a Bunsen and hold under the tube on a mounted needle
Relight until fully burnt; record the highest temperature
Calculate energy = mass of water x 4.2 x temperature change
Divide by mass of food to get energy per gram
Repeat with fresh water and the other food, same distance and volume; repeat and take means
exam.tip: Include the calculation and fair test points to reach 6 marks.

worked.q: A 0.50 g piece of peanut was burned under 20 cm3 of water. The water rose from 21 °C to 46 °C. Calculate the energy released per gram in kJ/g.
steps: Mass of water = 20 cm3 = 20 g
Temperature change = 46 - 21 = 25 °C
Energy = 20 x 4.2 x 25 = 2100 J
Energy per gram = 2100 / 0.50 = 4200 J/g
Convert to kJ: 4200 / 1000 = 4.2 kJ/g
worked.ans: 4.2 kJ/g (much lower than the label value of about 25 kJ/g because of heat loss and incomplete burning)

worked.q: Food X: 0.80 g, 25 g water, rise of 18 °C. Food Y: 0.40 g, 25 g water, rise of 12 °C. Which food contains more energy per gram?
steps: Food X energy = 25 x 4.2 x 18 = 1890 J
Food X per gram = 1890 / 0.80 = 2362.5 J/g, about 2400 J/g
Food Y energy = 25 x 4.2 x 12 = 1260 J
Food Y per gram = 1260 / 0.40 = 3150 J/g
Y has the smaller temperature rise but more energy per gram, because less of it was burned
worked.ans: Food Y contains more energy per gram (3150 J/g compared with about 2360 J/g for X).

bio_edx.0.2.summary: Microscopes have improved from simple hand lenses to modern electron microscopes. Each big jump in **magnification** and especially **resolution** let scientists see cells with more clarity and detail than before. Light microscopes revealed that living things are made of cells with a nucleus, but only the **electron microscope** (from the 1930s) revealed sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes, the folded inner membrane of mitochondria and the double membrane of the nucleus. Seeing these structures in detail increased our understanding of what each sub-cellular structure does.

core.h: What the spec wants you to explain
core.p: Edexcel asks you to explain how changes in microscope technology, including electron microscopy, have let us see cell structures with **more clarity and detail** than in the past, and how this has **increased our understanding of the role of sub-cellular structures**. Every answer should link a technology change to a better image and then to new biological knowledge.
bullets: Better technology gives **higher magnification** (makes the image bigger) and **higher resolution** (shows more detail).
Higher resolution means structures that were once blurred together can be seen as **separate**.
Seeing a structure clearly lets scientists work out its **function** (for example the folded inner membrane of a mitochondrion links to respiration).
Use the chain: **new technology -> higher resolution -> new structures seen -> better understanding of function**.

callouts.p: Technology improves -> resolution increases -> more detail is seen -> scientists understand the structure and role of sub-cellular structures better.

core.p: These two words are not the same, and mixing them up is the most common way to lose marks. Magnification is how many times bigger the image is than the real object. Resolution is the ability to tell apart two points that are very close together. You can magnify a blurry image as much as you like, but if the resolution is poor you just get a bigger blur.
bullets: **Magnification = size of image / size of real object** (you use this in calculations in 1.6).
**Resolution** is the **smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as two separate points**.
A **higher resolution** (smaller resolving distance) means **more detail** can be seen.
Light microscope resolution is limited to about **200 nm (0.2 µm)** because of the wavelength of light.
Electron microscope resolution is about **0.2 nm** or better, about **1000 times better** than a light microscope.
Increasing magnification without increasing resolution gives **empty magnification**: bigger but no clearer.

callouts.p: How many times bigger the image is compared with the real object.
The ability to distinguish between two points that are close together; the smallest distance between two points that can be seen as separate.
Electron microscopes are better mainly because of their higher RESOLUTION, not just their higher magnification.

core.h: Early light microscopes and the discovery of cells
core.p: The first microscopes were made in the late 1500s and 1600s by grinding glass lenses. Even with blurry lenses and low magnification they changed biology, because for the first time people could see that living things are built from tiny units.
bullets: **Late 1500s**: early **compound microscopes** (more than one lens) were built by spectacle makers in the Netherlands.
**1665 - Robert Hooke** looked at thin slices of **cork** and saw tiny box-like spaces. He called them **cells**. He was actually seeing the empty cell walls of dead plant cells.

**1670s - Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** made very good **single-lens** microscopes (about x200 to x270). He was the first to see and describe **bacteria**, single-celled organisms, **sperm cells** and **red blood cells**.
These early microscopes had **low magnification and poor resolution**, so they showed only the outline of cells, not what was inside them.

callouts.t: Name the scientist and what was seen
callouts.p: Hooke = cork, named 'cells'. Van Leeuwenhoek = first to see bacteria and sperm cells.

core.p: Over the next 200 years lenses, light sources and stains improved. Better glass and lens design reduced blurring and coloured fringes, which increased the resolution until it reached the physical limit set by the wavelength of light.
bullets: Better quality **lenses** (including lenses that stop coloured fringes) gave clearer images.
**Stains** (dyes) such as **methylene blue** or **iodine** made colourless structures visible by colouring them.
In **1831 Robert Brown** described the **nucleus** in plant cells.
By the late 1830s scientists (Schleiden and Schwann) proposed **cell theory**: all plants and animals are made of cells.
Modern light microscopes magnify up to about **x1500 to x2000** with a resolution of about **200 nm**.
With a light microscope you can see the **cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, cell wall, chloroplasts and vacuole**, and just about make out **mitochondria** as tiny dots.

callouts.p: No matter how good the lenses are, a light microscope cannot resolve objects closer together than about 200 nm, because the wavelength of visible light is too long.

core.p: You need to know the main parts because questions on microscopy often start with a labelled diagram. Light passes up through the specimen and two sets of lenses magnify it.
bullets: **Eyepiece lens**: the lens you look through; usually x10.
**Objective lenses**: usually x4, x10 and x40; rotate to change magnification.
**Stage**: flat platform where the slide is placed, held by clips.
**Light source or mirror**: shines light up through the thin specimen.
**Coarse focus knob**: moves the stage a large distance for rough focusing.
**Fine focus knob**: small movements to make the image sharp.
**Total magnification = eyepiece magnification x objective magnification** (for example x10 x x40 = x400).

core.p: The first electron microscope was built in **1931** (by Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll in Germany). Instead of light it uses a **beam of electrons**. Electrons have a **much shorter wavelength than light**, so the microscope can resolve points that are much closer together. This is the key reason electron microscopes show far more detail.
bullets: Uses a **beam of electrons** instead of light.
The beam is focused by **electromagnets** (magnetic lenses) instead of glass lenses.
Electrons have a **shorter wavelength** than visible light -> **higher resolution** (about 0.2 nm) -> much more **detail**.
Magnifies over **x1 000 000** (up to about x2 000 000 for the best TEMs).
The image is formed on a screen or computer, not seen directly through an eyepiece.
Images are **black and white**; colours in textbook pictures are added later by computer (**false colour**).

callouts.p: Electrons have a shorter wavelength than light, so the electron microscope has a much higher resolution and can show much smaller structures in detail.

core.p: There are two main types. Both use electron beams, but they make different kinds of image and answer different questions.
bullets: **TEM (transmission electron microscope)**: electrons pass **through** a very thin slice of specimen that has been stained with heavy metals.
TEM gives a **2D** image of the **inside** of cells, with the **highest resolution** (shows ribosomes, membranes and organelle structure).
**SEM (scanning electron microscope)**: electrons are scanned across and bounce off the **surface** of a specimen coated in a thin layer of metal (such as gold).
SEM gives a **3D** image of the **surface** (for example the surface of a pollen grain or an insect's eye) but has a **lower resolution than TEM**.
The first commercial SEM went on sale in the **1960s**.

core.p: Each type has advantages. Electron microscopes show far more detail, but light microscopes are still used every day in schools and hospitals because they are cheap, easy and can look at living cells.
bullets: Electron microscopes need a **vacuum** inside, because air molecules would scatter the electrons. So specimens must be **dead**.
Preparing electron microscope specimens is **complex** (fixing, thin slicing, staining with metals) and can create **artefacts**: features that were not in the living cell.
Electron microscopes are **very expensive**, very **large**, need **trained operators** and must be kept in special rooms.
Light microscopes are **cheap, portable, simple to use** and can show **living** cells moving and dividing, **in colour**.

callouts.p: If asked to compare, give a point FOR the electron microscope (resolution, detail) AND a point AGAINST it (dead specimens, cost, size, complex preparation).

core.p: Electron microscopes did not just make known structures bigger. They revealed **completely new sub-cellular structures** and the **internal structure** of organelles, which let scientists explain how those organelles do their jobs.
bullets: **Ribosomes** (about 20 to 30 nm) were discovered; they are too small to see with a light microscope. Their link to **protein synthesis** followed.
**Mitochondria** were shown to have a **double membrane** with a highly **folded inner membrane**. The folds give a **large surface area** for the enzymes of **aerobic respiration**.
**Chloroplasts** were shown to contain stacks of membranes where the **chlorophyll** is found, linking structure to **photosynthesis**.
The **nucleus** was shown to have a **double membrane** (nuclear envelope) with **pores** that let substances such as mRNA leave.
Networks of internal membranes, such as **endoplasmic reticulum**, with ribosomes attached, were seen for the first time.
The **cell membrane** structure and the fine structure of **bacteria** (including flagella) could be studied in detail.
**Viruses** (about 20 to 300 nm) were seen for the first time; most are too small for a light microscope.

callouts.p: Seeing the folded inner membrane of mitochondria explained why they are so good at respiration: more surface area for respiration enzymes.

core.h: How this increased our understanding of sub-cellular structures
core.p: Before electron microscopes, scientists knew cells had a nucleus, cytoplasm and membrane, but the cytoplasm looked almost empty and grainy. Electron microscopes showed it is packed with membranes and organelles. Linking each structure to a job became possible because scientists could see shape, size, number and position.
bullets: Seeing **many mitochondria** in cells that use lots of energy (such as muscle and sperm cells) supported their role in **respiration**.
Seeing **ribosomes** on membranes and free in the cytoplasm helped explain where **proteins are made**.
Seeing **nuclear pores** helped explain how the genetic code is carried out of the nucleus.
Comparing **prokaryotic** cells (no nucleus, no mitochondria, smaller ribosomes) with **eukaryotic** cells was based on electron microscope evidence.
Electron microscopes are combined with other techniques (for example breaking cells up and separating organelles) to test what each organelle does.

callouts.p: For each development: name the technology, say what it improved (magnification or resolution), state what new structure was seen, then say what this told us about its function.

core.p: A timeline is a useful way to remember the order of developments and what each one revealed.
bullets: **Late 1500s**: early compound light microscopes.
**1665**: Robert Hooke sees and names cells in cork.
**1670s**: van Leeuwenhoek sees bacteria, sperm and blood cells.
**1800s**: better lenses and stains; nucleus described (1831); cell theory.
**1931**: first electron microscope (TEM).
**1950s onwards**: detailed images of ribosomes, mitochondria and membranes.
**1960s**: first commercial scanning electron microscope (SEM).

core.h: Why the limits of light microscopes matter
core.p: A light microscope cannot separate two points closer than about 200 nm. Anything smaller than this, or any detail finer than this, blurs into one. That is why ribosomes, viruses and the inner folds of mitochondria were invisible before the electron microscope.
bullets: Ribosome (about 25 nm) is about **8 times smaller** than the light microscope's resolution limit, so it cannot be seen.
A mitochondrion (about 1 to 2 µm long) is just bigger than the limit, so it appears as a **dot or rod with no detail**.
Making a light microscope image bigger does **not** reveal these details, because resolution, not magnification, is the problem.
Only a microscope using radiation with a **shorter wavelength** (electrons) could overcome this limit.

callouts.p: Do not write that ribosomes cannot be seen because 'the magnification is too low'. They cannot be seen because the RESOLUTION of a light microscope is too low.

core.p: Microscopy questions often give you a photo or a table of data and ask you to explain, compare or evaluate. Use precise vocabulary and always link back to detail and function.
bullets: Use the words **resolution**, **magnification**, **detail** and **wavelength** precisely.
For 'explain why electron microscopes show more detail' always mention **shorter wavelength of electrons -> higher resolution**.
For 'suggest why light microscopes are still used' mention **living specimens, colour, cheap, portable, simple preparation**.
For 'what did electron microscopes reveal', name a **specific structure** (ribosomes, folded inner membrane of mitochondria, nuclear pores) and its **function**.
If given numbers, compare resolutions as a ratio, for example 200 nm / 0.2 nm = **1000 times better**.

analogy.t: Seeing a city at night from a plane
analogy.p: Looking at a cell with a light microscope is like looking at a city at night from a high plane: you can see the city (the cell) and the bright centre (the nucleus), but nearby streetlights merge into one glow. Zooming in with a camera on the same plane (more magnification) only gives a bigger glow. The electron microscope is like landing and walking the streets: now every single lamp (ribosome) and every building's layout (mitochondrion folds) is clear, because you have more resolution, not just a bigger picture. Where it breaks down: walking the streets lets you watch the city living, but an electron microscope needs a vacuum, so the cells it shows are dead and specially prepared, and the image is black and white.

terms.d: An instrument that produces a magnified image of an object too small to see clearly with the naked eye.
How many times bigger the image is than the real object; image size divided by actual size.
The ability to distinguish between two points close together; the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate.
Another name for resolution; a microscope with high resolving power can separate points that are very close together.
A microscope that uses visible light and glass lenses; magnifies up to about x1500 to x2000 with a resolution of about 200 nm.
A light microscope with two sets of lenses, the eyepiece and the objective lens.
A microscope that uses a beam of electrons focused by electromagnets; it has a much higher resolution and magnification than a light microscope.
Electron microscope in which electrons pass through a very thin stained specimen, giving a 2D image of internal structures at the highest resolution.
Electron microscope in which electrons bounce off a metal-coated specimen surface, giving a 3D image of the surface.
The distance between repeating points on a wave; shorter wavelength radiation gives higher resolution.
A space with no air; needed inside an electron microscope so air molecules do not scatter the electrons.
A dye used to colour parts of a specimen (for example methylene blue or iodine) so they can be seen more clearly.
A feature in a microscope image that was caused by the preparation process and was not present in the living cell.
Colour added to black and white electron micrographs by computer to make structures easier to tell apart.
A photograph or image taken using an electron microscope.
A structure inside a cell, such as a nucleus, mitochondrion, ribosome or chloroplast, that carries out a particular function.

mistakes.w: Electron microscopes are better because they magnify more.
mistakes.r: Electron microscopes have a higher resolution (because electrons have a shorter wavelength than light), so they show more detail.

mistakes.w: Resolution is how big the image is.
mistakes.r: Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two points close together; magnification is how many times bigger the image is.

mistakes.w: Electron microscopes use electrons instead of light so they are brighter.
mistakes.r: Electrons have a shorter wavelength than light, which gives a higher resolution.

mistakes.w: You can look at living cells under an electron microscope.
mistakes.r: Specimens must be dead, because the inside of an electron microscope is a vacuum and preparation involves fixing and staining.

mistakes.w: Electron micrographs show the real colours of cells.
mistakes.r: Electron micrographs are black and white; any colour is false colour added by a computer.

mistakes.w: Robert Hooke saw living cells with a nucleus in cork.
mistakes.r: Hooke saw the empty cell walls of dead cork cells and named them cells.

mistakes.w: An SEM gives a more detailed image of organelles than a TEM.
mistakes.r: A TEM has the higher resolution and shows internal structures; an SEM shows 3D surface detail at lower resolution.

mistakes.w: Light microscopes are no longer useful.
mistakes.r: Light microscopes are cheap, portable, simple to use and can show living cells in colour, so they are still widely used.

mistakes.w: Ribosomes are not seen with a light microscope because they are inside the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Ribosomes are smaller than the resolution limit of a light microscope (about 200 nm), so they cannot be seen.

exam.q: State what is meant by the resolution of a microscope.
model: The ability to distinguish between two points that are close together / the smallest distance between two points that can be seen as separate.
exam.tip: Do not say 'how clear the image is' on its own; mention two separate points.

exam.q: Name the scientist who first described cells in cork in 1665.
model: Robert Hooke.
exam.tip: Hooke = cork; van Leeuwenhoek = bacteria and sperm.

exam.q: Give one reason why a light microscope cannot be used to see ribosomes.
model: Ribosomes are smaller than the resolution (limit) of a light microscope / the resolution of a light microscope is too low.
exam.tip: The keyword is resolution, not magnification.

exam.q: Explain why an electron microscope can show more detail than a light microscope.
model: Electrons have a shorter wavelength than light.
So the electron microscope has a higher resolution / can distinguish points closer together.
exam.tip: Two linked steps: wavelength then resolution.

exam.q: Give two disadvantages of using an electron microscope compared with a light microscope.
model: Specimens must be dead / cannot view living cells (vacuum).
Very expensive / large / not portable / needs specialist training / complex preparation / images black and white / artefacts may form.
exam.tip: Any two different points; do not give two cost points.

exam.q: A light microscope has a resolution of 200 nm. A transmission electron microscope has a resolution of 0.2 nm. Calculate how many times greater the resolution of the electron microscope is.
model: = 1000 (times)
exam.tip: Check both values are in the same units before dividing.

exam.q: Describe the differences between the images produced by a transmission electron microscope and a scanning electron microscope.
model: TEM produces a 2D image of internal structures / electrons pass through the specimen.
SEM produces a 3D image of the surface / electrons bounce off the surface; TEM has a higher resolution.
exam.tip: Compare directly using 'whereas'.

exam.q: Suggest why a biology teacher uses light microscopes rather than electron microscopes in a school lesson.
model: Light microscopes are cheap / portable / easy to use / quick to prepare slides.
Can view living cells / see colour / electron microscopes too expensive or large for a school.
exam.tip: Give practical reasons linked to the school setting.

exam.q: The electron microscope revealed that the inner membrane of a mitochondrion is highly folded. Explain how this discovery helped scientists understand the function of mitochondria.
model: Folded inner membrane gives a large surface area.
Enzymes for (aerobic) respiration are found on the membrane.
More enzymes / more reactions can take place at once.
So more energy can be released (by aerobic respiration) / explains why active cells such as muscle contain many mitochondria.
exam.tip: Link structure (folds) to surface area to enzymes to respiration.

exam.q: Explain how developments in microscopy have increased our understanding of cells and sub-cellular structures.
model: Early light microscopes (Hooke, 1665) showed that living things / cork are made of cells.
Van Leeuwenhoek's microscopes revealed single-celled organisms / bacteria / sperm cells.
Improved lenses and stains increased resolution and showed the nucleus / chloroplasts / cell theory developed.
Light microscopes are limited to a resolution of about 200 nm due to the wavelength of light.
Electron microscopes (1930s) use electrons with a shorter wavelength, giving much higher resolution and magnification.
Revealed new structures such as ribosomes / internal structure of mitochondria and chloroplasts / nuclear membrane and pores.
Seeing these structures in detail allowed scientists to link structure to function, e.g. folded inner membrane for respiration / ribosomes for protein synthesis.
TEM shows internal detail and SEM shows 3D surfaces.
exam.tip: Work in time order and give a technology, an improvement and a discovery for each stage.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of electron microscopes compared with light microscopes for studying cells.
model: Electron microscopes have a much higher resolution (about 0.2 nm vs 200 nm).
And higher magnification (over x1 000 000 vs about x1500).
So they show sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and the detail of mitochondria.
But specimens must be dead because of the vacuum, so living processes cannot be observed.
Preparation is complex and may produce artefacts; images are black and white.
Electron microscopes are expensive, large and need trained operators.
Light microscopes are cheap, portable, show colour and living cells.
Conclusion: electron microscopes are best for fine detail, light microscopes for living cells and routine work.
exam.tip: Evaluate means advantages, disadvantages and a justified conclusion.

worked.q: A virus is 100 nm in diameter. Explain whether it could be seen as a separate object with a light microscope (resolution 200 nm) and with a TEM (resolution 0.2 nm).
steps: Compare the virus size with each resolution.
Light microscope: 100 nm is smaller than 200 nm, so the virus cannot be resolved; at best it blurs into a speck with no detail.
TEM: 100 nm is 500 times larger than 0.2 nm (100 / 0.2 = 500), so the virus and its structure can be seen clearly.
worked.ans: Only the electron microscope can show the virus clearly, because the virus is smaller than the light microscope's resolution limit but much larger than the TEM's.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain how the development of the electron microscope increased our understanding of sub-cellular structures. (4 marks)
steps: Point 1: The electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, which have a shorter wavelength than light.
Point 2: This gives a much higher resolution (and magnification), so much smaller structures can be seen in detail.
Point 3: It revealed new structures such as ribosomes and the folded inner membrane of mitochondria and the pores in the nuclear membrane.

Point 4: Seeing their structure helped scientists work out their function, for example ribosomes as the site of protein synthesis and folded inner membranes giving a large surface area for respiration enzymes.
worked.ans: Shorter wavelength -> higher resolution -> new structures seen -> structure linked to function.

worked.q: A light microscope magnifies x1500 and an electron microscope magnifies x1 500 000. How many times greater is the electron microscope's magnification? Write the electron microscope's magnification in standard form.
steps: Standard form: 1 500 000 = 1.5 x 10^6.
worked.ans: 1000 times greater; x1.5 x 10^6.

bio_edx.0.3.summary: Cells and the structures inside them are tiny, so biologists measure them in **millimetres (mm), micrometres (µm), nanometres (nm) and picometres (pm)**, each 1000 times smaller than the one before. Very large and very small numbers are written in **standard form** (A x 10^n) so they are easy to compare and calculate with. You must be able to convert between units, calculate with standard form, compare sizes using orders of magnitude, and use sensible **estimations** to check answers or when exact measurement is not possible.

core.p: A typical animal cell is about 0.00002 m across, and a ribosome is about 0.000000025 m. Numbers like these are hard to read, easy to copy wrongly and almost impossible to compare at a glance. Using smaller units and standard form makes them manageable.
bullets: Biology covers a huge range of sizes: from atoms (about **0.1 nm**) to whole organisms (metres).
Choosing the **right unit** keeps numbers sensible: an animal cell is **20 µm**, not 0.00002 m.
**Standard form** lets you write any very large or very small number in a short, clear way.
Being able to **compare sizes** tells you what you can see with the naked eye, a light microscope or only an electron microscope.

callouts.p: Each unit (m, mm, µm, nm, pm) is 1000 times smaller than the one before it.

core.h: The prefixes: milli, micro, nano and pico
core.p: A prefix in front of a unit tells you what to multiply it by. Edexcel expects you to know four prefixes for small sizes, and their values as powers of ten.
bullets: **milli (m)** = one thousandth = **10^-3**. 1 mm = 10^-3 m = 0.001 m.
**nano (n)** = one billionth = **10^-9**. 1 nm = 10^-9 m.
**pico (p)** = one trillionth = **10^-12**. 1 pm = 10^-12 m.
The same prefixes are used for other units, for example mg (milligram), µl (microlitre) and ms (millisecond).
The symbol for micro is the Greek letter **µ** (mu); 'um' is sometimes used when µ cannot be typed.

head: Prefix
Symbol
Power of ten
As a decimal of a metre
Number in 1 m

core.p: Because each unit is 1000 times smaller than the one before, converting is always multiplying or dividing by 1000 for each step. The trick is to decide which way to go.
bullets: Going to a **smaller unit** (for example mm -> µm): the number gets **bigger**, so **multiply by 1000** for each step.
Going to a **bigger unit** (for example nm -> µm): the number gets **smaller**, so **divide by 1000** for each step.
Two steps = x or ÷ by **1 000 000** (10^6); three steps = x or ÷ by **10^9**.
Sense check: a smaller unit should always give a **larger number** for the same length.

callouts.p: Ask: am I going to a smaller unit? Then I need MORE of them, so the number must get bigger.

core.p: Standard form writes a number as **A x 10^n**, where **A is at least 1 but less than 10** (1 ≤ A < 10) and **n is a whole number**. Positive n means a big number; negative n means a small number (less than 1).
bullets: Small numbers: count how many places the decimal point moves **right** to make A between 1 and 10; n is that number but **negative**.
Example: 0.000 008 m -> point moves 6 places right -> **8 x 10^-6 m** (= 8 µm).
Big numbers: count how many places the point moves **left**; n is **positive**. Example: 37 000 000 000 000 cells = **3.7 x 10^13**.
To convert back, move the point the other way: 4.2 x 10^-5 = 0.000 042.
**Not** standard form: 25 x 10^-9 (A is more than 10) or 0.5 x 10^-3 (A is less than 1).
On a calculator use the **x10^x** or **EXP** button rather than typing x 10 ^ by hand, to avoid bracket errors.

callouts.p: A number written as A x 10^n where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer.
If the number in front is 10 or more, or less than 1, it is not in standard form yet: adjust the power.

fig.cap: Writing 0.000008 m in standard form. The decimal point jumps 6 places to the right to sit after the 8, so the power of ten is -6. The answer is 8 x 10^-6 m, which is 8 µm (about the size of a red blood cell).

core.p: You need to multiply, divide and compare numbers in standard form, usually with a calculator. Knowing the rules helps you check the calculator answer is sensible.
bullets: **Multiplying**: multiply the A numbers and **add** the powers. (2 x 10^-6) x (3 x 10^2) = 6 x 10^-4.
**Dividing**: divide the A numbers and **subtract** the powers. (8 x 10^-6) ÷ (2 x 10^-9) = 4 x 10^3.
If the answer's A is not between 1 and 10, adjust: 12 x 10^-5 = **1.2 x 10^-4**.
Before comparing or calculating, put both numbers in the **same unit** (for example both in m, or both in µm).
To find **how many times bigger** one thing is than another: bigger size ÷ smaller size (same units).
Round final answers to a sensible number of **significant figures**, usually the same as the data given.

callouts.p: Most lost marks in size calculations come from dividing a µm value by an nm value. Convert first, then divide.

core.h: Typical sizes of cells and sub-cellular structures
core.p: Knowing rough sizes helps you check answers, choose units and decide which microscope is needed. Values vary, so learn the order of magnitude rather than an exact number.
bullets: Light microscopes can resolve down to about **200 nm**, so anything smaller needs an **electron microscope**.
Most cells are measured in **µm**; most sub-cellular structures smaller than mitochondria are measured in **nm**.
Atoms and the distances between them are measured in **pm** or tenths of a nm.
Larger things such as egg cells or small organisms may be given in **mm**.

core.h: Number, size and scale: orders of magnitude
core.p: An **order of magnitude** is a factor of 10. Saying two things differ by three orders of magnitude means one is about 10^3 = 1000 times bigger. This is a quick way to compare sizes without exact numbers.
bullets: Order of magnitude difference = difference in the **powers of ten** when both sizes are in standard form in the same unit.
Example: animal cell 2 x 10^-5 m and ribosome 2.5 x 10^-8 m: powers -5 and -8, so about **3 orders of magnitude** (about 1000 times) different.
Each step on the unit ladder (m -> mm -> µm -> nm -> pm) is **3 orders of magnitude**.
Scale matters in biology: smaller cells have a larger **surface area to volume ratio**, and size decides which microscope you need.
Scale bars on micrographs show a real length (for example a bar labelled 10 µm) so you can work out actual sizes.

callouts.p: A factor of ten; two numbers differ by one order of magnitude if one is about ten times the other.

core.h: Estimations and when to use them
core.p: An **estimate** is an approximate value worked out quickly using rounded numbers. Edexcel wants you to be able to make estimations and to **explain when they should be used**.
bullets: Use estimates to **check** that a calculated answer is the right order of magnitude (for example, a cell calculated as 3 m long must be wrong).
Use estimates when an **exact measurement is not possible or not needed**, such as counting very large numbers of cells.
Use estimates to **quickly compare** sizes, for example 'about 1000 times bigger'.
Estimate the **size of a cell** by seeing how many fit across a field of view of known diameter: size ≈ field diameter ÷ number of cells.
Estimate **large numbers** by counting a small sample and scaling up, for example counting cells in one small square and multiplying by the number of squares.
Round to **1 significant figure** for quick estimates: 18.6 µm ≈ 20 µm.
Do **not** use estimates when a precise final answer is asked for, or when small differences matter.

callouts.p: To check a calculation is sensible, when exact counting or measuring is impossible or too slow, and to compare sizes quickly.

core.h: Linking size to the right microscope
core.p: Size and scale link directly to microscopy. Whether a structure can be seen depends on how it compares with the resolution of the microscope.
bullets: Naked eye: can see objects down to about **0.1 mm (100 µm)**, such as a human egg cell as a tiny dot.
Light microscope: resolves down to about **200 nm (0.2 µm)**: cells, nuclei, chloroplasts.
Electron microscope: resolves down to about **0.2 nm**: ribosomes, membranes, viruses.
Compare like with like: to decide if a 25 nm ribosome can be seen with a light microscope, convert 200 nm and 25 nm into the same unit, then compare.

core.p: Size questions often hide one of these traps: mixed units, wrong rounding or a wrong direction of conversion. A short checklist avoids them.
bullets: 1. Write down the values with their **units**.
2. Convert into **one unit** (pick the one the question wants the answer in).
3. Do the calculation (x, ÷) with a calculator.
4. Give the answer in the unit asked and in **standard form** if asked.
5. **Estimate** to check the order of magnitude is sensible.
6. Use a sensible number of **significant figures**.

callouts.p: Write each conversion step. Even if the final answer is wrong, method marks are often given for correct conversion.

analogy.t: Units as a set of nested boxes
analogy.p: Think of the units like a giant warehouse (metre) full of 1000 shelves (millimetres), each shelf holding 1000 boxes (micrometres), each box holding 1000 envelopes (nanometres), each envelope holding 1000 grains of sand (picometres). To count something in a smaller container you need far more of them (multiply by 1000), and to describe it using a bigger container you need fewer (divide by 1000). Standard form is like a label saying how many layers of containers deep you are. Where it breaks down: real lengths are continuous, not counted in whole boxes, and the factor of 1000 between the four units is fixed by definition, not a choice of packing.

terms.d: One thousandth of a metre; 1 mm = 10^-3 m.
One millionth of a metre; 1 µm = 10^-6 m = 1/1000 mm.
One billionth of a metre; 1 nm = 10^-9 m = 1/1000 µm.
One trillionth of a metre; 1 pm = 10^-12 m = 1/1000 nm.
Prefix meaning x 10^-3 (one thousandth).
Prefix meaning x 10^-6 (one millionth); symbol µ.
Prefix meaning x 10^-9 (one billionth).
Prefix meaning x 10^-12 (one trillionth).
A way of writing numbers as A x 10^n, where A is at least 1 and less than 10 and n is a whole number.
The number n in 10^n; it tells you how many places the decimal point moves.
A factor of 10; used to compare sizes roughly.
An approximate value found using rounded numbers, used to check answers or when exact values are not possible.
The digits in a number that carry meaning about its precision, starting from the first non-zero digit.
A line on an image labelled with the real length it represents, used to work out actual sizes.
The smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate; decides the smallest size a microscope can show.

mistakes.w: 1 mm = 100 µm.
mistakes.r: 1 mm = 1000 µm; every step between mm, µm, nm and pm is a factor of 1000.

mistakes.w: To change 5 µm into nm, divide by 1000 to get 0.005 nm.
mistakes.r: nm is a smaller unit, so multiply by 1000: 5 µm = 5000 nm.

mistakes.w: Writes 25 x 10^-9 m as the standard form answer.
mistakes.r: A must be between 1 and 10: 2.5 x 10^-8 m.

mistakes.w: Writes 0.000 03 m as 3 x 10^5 m.
mistakes.r: Numbers smaller than 1 have a negative power: 3 x 10^-5 m.

mistakes.w: micro = 10^-3 and milli = 10^-6.
Divides a size in µm by a size in nm without converting.
mistakes.r: Convert both sizes into the same unit before dividing.

mistakes.w: When multiplying standard form numbers, multiplies the powers.
mistakes.r: Multiply the A numbers and ADD the powers; when dividing, SUBTRACT the powers.

mistakes.w: An estimate is just a guess.
mistakes.r: An estimate is an approximate value calculated from rounded data, used to check answers or when exact measurement is not possible.

exam.q: State the number of micrometres in one millimetre.
exam.tip: Every step down the unit ladder is x 1000.

exam.q: Which prefix means x 10^-9? A milli B micro C nano D pico
model: C nano
exam.tip: Learn the four in order: 10^-3, 10^-6, 10^-9, 10^-12.

exam.q: Write 0.000 045 m in standard form.
exam.tip: Count the jumps to make A between 1 and 10.

exam.q: A red blood cell has a diameter of 7.5 µm. Convert this to metres and give your answer in standard form.
model: m (correct unit / standard form)
exam.tip: µm to m is ÷ 1 000 000, which is the same as x 10^-6.

exam.q: A ribosome is 25 nm wide. A bacterium is 2 µm long. Calculate how many times longer the bacterium is than the ribosome.
model: Convert to same units: 2 µm = 2000 nm
exam.tip: Convert first, then divide bigger by smaller.

exam.q: Explain why biologists usually measure cells in micrometres rather than metres.
model: Cells are very small / about 10^-5 m.
Measuring in µm gives numbers that are easier to read / write / compare (no long decimals).
exam.tip: Give the size and the benefit.

exam.q: A virus has a diameter of 1.2 x 10^-7 m. A light microscope can resolve objects down to 2 x 10^-7 m. Explain whether the virus can be seen clearly with a light microscope.
model: The virus (1.2 x 10^-7 m) is smaller than the resolution limit (2 x 10^-7 m).
So it cannot be seen clearly / would need an electron microscope.
exam.tip: Compare the powers first, then the A numbers.

exam.q: Calculate (6 x 10^-6) ÷ (3 x 10^-9). Give your answer in standard form.
exam.tip: Subtract the powers when dividing; watch the double negative.

exam.q: A student sees 8 cells side by side across a field of view of diameter 0.4 mm. Estimate the length of one cell in µm and explain why this is an estimate.
model: It is an estimate because cells are not all the same size / cells may not exactly fill the diameter.
Cells may not be lying in a straight line / gaps between cells.
exam.tip: Convert to µm first; then give a reason linked to the method.

exam.q: Explain when scientists should use estimations when studying cells. Use examples in your answer.
model: To check a calculated answer is the right order of magnitude / sensible.
Example: a cell calculated to be 2 m wide must be a mistake.
When exact measurement or counting is not possible / too time consuming.
Example: counting cells in a sample area and scaling up / estimating cell size from number of cells across a field of view.
exam.tip: Give a 'when' and an example for each.

exam.q: The table shows sizes: nucleus 6 µm, mitochondrion 1500 nm, ribosome 0.025 µm, cell membrane thickness 7.5 nm. Put them in order from largest to smallest and calculate how many times wider the nucleus is than the cell membrane is thick.
model: Convert all to nm: nucleus 6000 nm, mitochondrion 1500 nm, ribosome 25 nm, membrane 7.5 nm.
Order: nucleus, mitochondrion, ribosome, cell membrane.
= 800 (times)
exam.tip: Put everything in the smallest unit so every value is a number bigger than 1.

worked.q: A mitochondrion is 0.0015 mm long. Give its length in µm, in nm and in metres in standard form.
steps: mm to µm: smaller unit, so x 1000: 0.0015 x 1000 = 1.5 µm.
Standard form: point moves 6 places right to give 1.5, so 1.5 x 10^-6 m.
Estimate check: mitochondria are about 1 to 2 µm, so 1.5 µm is sensible.

worked.q: An animal cell has a diameter of 2 x 10^-5 m. A ribosome has a diameter of 2.5 x 10^-8 m. How many ribosomes could fit in a line across the cell?
steps: Both values are in metres, so they can be divided directly.
Divide the A numbers: 2 ÷ 2.5 = 0.8.
Subtract the powers: 10^(-5 - (-8)) = 10^3.
0.8 x 10^3 = 800. In standard form 8 x 10^2.
Order of magnitude check: powers differ by 3, so about 1000: 800 is sensible.
worked.ans: 800 ribosomes (8 x 10^2)

worked.q: A drop of blood of volume 1 mm^3 is spread on a grid. A student counts 50 red blood cells in one small square. The drop covers 100 000 squares. Estimate the number of red blood cells in 1 mm^3 and explain why it is an estimate.
steps: Number of cells = cells per square x number of squares.
Standard form: 5 x 10^6 cells per mm^3.
It is an estimate because only one square was counted; cells are not spread evenly, so other squares may hold more or fewer cells.
Counting several squares and taking a mean would give a better estimate.
worked.ans: About 5 x 10^6 red blood cells per mm^3

bio_edx.0.6.summary: Enzyme activity depends on how often enzyme and substrate molecules collide and on whether the **active site** keeps its exact shape. Raising **temperature** speeds up collisions until the **optimum**, but above it the active site changes shape and the enzyme is **denatured**. Every enzyme also has an **optimum pH**; too acidic or too alkaline alters the active site. Increasing **substrate concentration** increases the rate until all active sites are occupied, then the rate levels off because the amount of enzyme becomes the limiting factor.

core.h: What controls the rate of an enzyme reaction
core.p: An enzyme works when a substrate molecule collides with, and fits into, its **active site** to form an **enzyme-substrate complex**. So the rate depends on two things: how many successful collisions happen each second, and whether the active site is the right shape for the substrate to fit. Temperature, pH and substrate concentration each affect one or both of these.
bullets: **Rate of reaction** = how much substrate is used up, or product made, per unit time.
More **collisions** between enzyme and substrate -> more **enzyme-substrate complexes** -> faster rate.
The active site has a **specific shape** that is **complementary** to the substrate.
Anything that changes the shape of the active site stops the substrate fitting, so the rate falls.
Temperature affects **both** collisions and shape; pH mainly affects **shape**; substrate concentration affects **collisions**.

callouts.t: Two ideas to use in every answer
callouts.p: 1. Collisions (kinetic energy, number of enzyme-substrate complexes). 2. Shape of the active site (denaturation).

core.h: Effect of temperature: below the optimum
core.p: As temperature rises, enzyme and substrate molecules gain **kinetic energy** and move faster. They collide more often and with more energy, so more enzyme-substrate complexes form per second and the rate increases.
bullets: Higher temperature -> molecules have **more kinetic energy** -> move faster.
-> **More frequent collisions** between substrate and active site.
-> **More enzyme-substrate complexes** formed per second -> **faster rate**.
At low temperatures (for example 5 °C) the enzyme is **not denatured**; it is just working slowly because collisions are less frequent.
If a cold enzyme is warmed up, it works faster again: the effect of low temperature is **reversible**.
A rough rule: below the optimum, a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate for many enzymes.

callouts.p: Never say low temperatures denature or kill enzymes. The molecules simply have less kinetic energy so there are fewer collisions.

core.h: Effect of temperature: the optimum and above
core.p: The **optimum temperature** is the temperature at which the enzyme works fastest. For most human enzymes this is about **37 °C** (body temperature). Above the optimum the rate falls rapidly because the enzyme is denatured.
bullets: Above the optimum, the extra energy makes the enzyme molecule **vibrate** more.
This **breaks the bonds** that hold the enzyme's 3D shape together.
The **active site changes shape**, so the substrate **no longer fits** (no longer complementary).
Fewer enzyme-substrate complexes can form -> rate decreases; when all enzyme molecules are denatured the rate is **zero**.
**Denaturation is permanent (irreversible)**: cooling a denatured enzyme does not restore its activity.
Enzymes from organisms living in hot places (such as bacteria in hot springs) have **higher optimum temperatures**, for example about 70 °C or more.

callouts.p: When the shape of an enzyme's active site is changed (by high temperature or extreme pH) so that the substrate can no longer fit; the change is permanent.
The temperature (or pH) at which an enzyme works at its fastest rate.

fig.cap: Effect of temperature on the rate of a human enzyme reaction. The rate rises as kinetic energy and collisions increase, peaks at the optimum of about 37 °C, then falls steeply as the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured.

core.h: Why the active site changes shape when denatured
core.p: An enzyme is a **protein**: a long chain of amino acids folded into a precise 3D shape. The shape, including the active site, is held in place by bonds between different parts of the chain. High temperatures and extreme pH break these bonds, so the chain unfolds or folds differently.
bullets: The order of amino acids decides how the chain folds and so the shape of the **active site**.
Weak bonds hold the folded shape; they are easily broken by **heat** or **changes in pH**.
Once the bonds break, the active site is a **different shape**, so it is **no longer complementary** to the substrate.
The substrate cannot bind, so **no enzyme-substrate complex** forms and the reaction is no longer catalysed.
The enzyme molecule still exists; it has not been 'killed' (enzymes are not alive), it has just lost its working shape.

callouts.p: Do not write that enzymes die or are killed. Write that they are denatured and the active site has changed shape.

fig.cap: Left: a working enzyme. The substrate is complementary to the active site, so an enzyme-substrate complex can form. Right: after high temperature or extreme pH the bonds holding the enzyme's shape have broken, the active site has changed shape and the substrate no longer fits.

core.p: Each enzyme has an **optimum pH** at which it works fastest. If the pH is higher or lower than the optimum, the bonds holding the enzyme's shape are affected, the active site changes shape and the substrate fits less well, so the rate falls. Far from the optimum the enzyme is denatured.
bullets: pH is a measure of how acidic or alkaline a solution is (concentration of hydrogen ions).
Changing pH alters the **charges** on the amino acids, which affects the **bonds** holding the 3D shape.
Small changes from the optimum: active site shape slightly altered, **fewer** substrates fit, rate falls.
Large changes (very acidic or very alkaline): active site shape changes permanently -> enzyme **denatured** -> rate falls to zero.
The optimum pH of an enzyme matches **where it works in the body**.
pH graphs are usually a **symmetrical peak** around the optimum, unlike the lopsided temperature graph.

callouts.p: Pepsin works best at about pH 2 because the stomach contains hydrochloric acid. When food moves into the small intestine (higher pH) pepsin stops working.

fig.cap: Each enzyme has its own optimum pH. Pepsin from the stomach works best at about pH 2, salivary amylase at about pH 7 and trypsin from the small intestine at about pH 8. Either side of the optimum the active site changes shape and the rate falls.

core.p: When there is plenty of enzyme, adding more substrate means more substrate molecules collide with active sites each second, so the rate increases. Eventually every active site is occupied all the time: the enzyme is working as fast as it can. Adding more substrate then makes no difference and the graph levels off (plateaus).
bullets: Low substrate concentration: many active sites are **empty**; substrate is the **limiting factor**.
Increasing substrate concentration -> **more frequent collisions** -> **more enzyme-substrate complexes** -> faster rate.
At first the rate rises roughly in **proportion** to substrate concentration (straight part of the graph).
At high substrate concentration **all active sites are occupied** (the enzyme is **saturated**).
The rate **plateaus**: now the **enzyme concentration** (number of active sites) is the **limiting factor**.
Adding **more enzyme** at this point would increase the rate again (a higher plateau).
Substrate concentration does **not** denature the enzyme; the active site shape is unchanged.

callouts.p: All the active sites are occupied, so the enzyme cannot work any faster; the concentration of enzyme is now limiting the rate.

fig.cap: Effect of substrate concentration on rate. At first more substrate gives more collisions and more enzyme-substrate complexes, so the rate rises. Then all the active sites are occupied, the curve levels off and enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor.
