core.p: Although the spec focuses on temperature, pH and substrate concentration, exam questions often ask what happens if more enzyme is added. With excess substrate, doubling the enzyme concentration doubles the number of active sites, so the rate roughly doubles.
bullets: More enzyme -> **more active sites** available -> more enzyme-substrate complexes per second.
If substrate runs low, adding more enzyme has **little effect** because substrate becomes limiting.
This explains why, on the substrate graph, a higher enzyme concentration gives a **higher plateau**.

core.p: Many marks come from describing a graph accurately before explaining it. Describe first (with data), then explain using collisions or active site shape.
bullets: **Describe**: say what happens to the rate as the variable increases, name the **optimum** with its value and **quote data** with units.
**Explain**: use kinetic energy, collisions and enzyme-substrate complexes for rising parts; use active site shape and denaturation for falling parts; use 'all active sites occupied' for plateaus.
The temperature graph is **not symmetrical**: a gradual rise then a **steep fall** after the optimum.
The optimum is the **peak** of the curve, read straight down to the x-axis.
If data are only taken at 10 °C intervals, the true optimum may lie **between** readings; more readings close to the peak would find it more precisely.

callouts.p: Describe: 'The rate increases from 10 °C to a maximum at 40 °C, then decreases to zero at 60 °C.' Explain: give a reason for each part.

core.p: A summary table helps you pick the right explanation for each factor.
bullets: Temperature below optimum and substrate concentration: **collision** explanations.
Temperature above optimum and pH away from optimum: **shape/denaturation** explanations.
Only high substrate concentration causes a **plateau**; temperature and pH cause **peaks**.

head: Factor
Rising rate because
Falling or level rate because
Graph shape
rows: More kinetic energy, more collisions, more E-S complexes
Above optimum bonds break, active site changes shape, denatured
Moving towards optimum shape of active site
Away from optimum active site shape changes, denatured if extreme
All active sites occupied, enzyme limiting

core.h: Applying the ideas to living organisms
core.p: These factors explain why the body keeps conditions so stable, and why enzymes from different places have different optima.
bullets: Human body temperature is kept at about **37 °C** so enzymes work close to their optimum.
A high **fever** (above about 40 °C) is dangerous partly because enzymes may start to denature.

Different parts of the gut have different pH, so different enzymes work there: **pepsin** in the acidic stomach, **amylase** and **trypsin** in the less acidic or slightly alkaline small intestine (bile helps neutralise stomach acid).
Enzymes from **thermophilic bacteria** in hot springs have high optimum temperatures, which is useful in industry and in biological washing powders that work at higher temperatures.
Food is kept in a **fridge** to slow down enzyme reactions in microorganisms (not denature them), and **cooking** at high temperatures denatures enzymes.

core.h: Investigating these factors (link to practical work)
core.p: Enzyme activity can be measured by timing how quickly substrate disappears or product appears. The core practical for pH is covered in 1.10, but you should know how to design a fair test for any of these factors.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the factor being changed (temperature, pH or substrate concentration).
**Dependent variable**: the rate, for example the time for starch to disappear (iodine no longer turns blue-black) with amylase.
**Control variables**: keep the other factors the same, for example enzyme concentration and volume, substrate concentration, temperature (water bath) and pH (**buffer solution**).
Use a **water bath** to keep temperature constant and **buffers** to keep pH constant.
Repeat readings and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability; take extra readings near the optimum.

callouts.p: Rate = 1000 / time (or 1 / time) gives a value that gets bigger as the reaction gets faster.

analogy.p: Think of enzymes as locks on doors and substrates as people with keys trying to get through. On a cold day people wander slowly, so few reach the doors each minute (low rate). On a warm day they move faster and more get through (higher rate). If you add more people (substrate), the doors get busier until every door has a queue: now adding more people does not help, only more doors (enzyme) would. But if the building gets too hot or is sprayed with acid, the locks warp and the keys no longer fit (denatured), and the locks do not unwarp when things cool down. Where it breaks down: enzymes are not fixed rigid locks, the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds, and the enzyme is not used up, it is released to catalyse again.

terms.d: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up a reaction without being used up.
The molecule that an enzyme acts on, which binds to the active site.
The region of an enzyme with a specific shape that the substrate binds to.
Having a shape that fits another shape exactly, like the active site and its substrate.
The structure formed when a substrate is bound to an enzyme's active site.
The amount of substrate used up or product formed per unit time.
The temperature at which an enzyme works fastest; about 37 °C for most human enzymes.
The pH at which an enzyme works fastest, for example about pH 2 for pepsin.
Describes an enzyme whose active site has permanently changed shape, so the substrate can no longer fit.
The energy of movement; higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy, so they collide more often.
When substrate and enzyme molecules meet; successful collisions form enzyme-substrate complexes.
The factor in short supply that stops the rate increasing further.
When all active sites of the enzyme molecules are occupied by substrate, so the rate cannot increase further.
A scale measuring how acidic or alkaline a solution is; below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.
A solution that keeps the pH of a reaction mixture constant.
The flat part of a graph where the rate stays the same even when the variable increases.

mistakes.w: At high temperatures the enzyme is killed.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are not alive; they are denatured: the bonds holding the shape break and the active site changes shape.

mistakes.w: At low temperatures the enzyme is denatured.
mistakes.r: At low temperatures the enzyme is not denatured; molecules have less kinetic energy so there are fewer collisions.

mistakes.w: The substrate changes shape and no longer fits.
mistakes.r: It is the enzyme's active site that changes shape, so it is no longer complementary to the substrate.

mistakes.w: The rate levels off because the substrate runs out.
mistakes.r: On a substrate concentration graph the rate levels off because all the active sites are occupied; enzyme concentration is limiting.

mistakes.w: Denatured enzymes work again when they are cooled.
mistakes.r: Denaturation is permanent; the active site does not return to its original shape.

mistakes.w: All enzymes have an optimum pH of 7.
mistakes.r: Different enzymes have different optimum pH values, for example pepsin about 2 and trypsin about 8.

mistakes.w: Higher temperature makes the enzyme work harder.
mistakes.r: Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and more enzyme-substrate complexes form.

mistakes.w: The optimum is where the enzyme is denatured.
mistakes.r: The optimum is the temperature or pH where the rate is highest; denaturation happens above (or away from) the optimum.

mistakes.w: Adding more substrate denatures the enzyme so the graph flattens.
mistakes.r: Substrate concentration does not change the active site shape; the plateau is because all active sites are occupied.

exam.q: State what is meant by the optimum temperature of an enzyme.
model: The temperature at which the enzyme works fastest / the rate of reaction is highest.
exam.tip: Do not just say 'the best temperature'; say fastest rate.

exam.q: Give the optimum pH of pepsin, an enzyme found in the stomach.
model: About pH 2 (accept 1.5 to 2.5 / acidic).
exam.tip: Link the value to the stomach acid.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increases as temperature increases from 10 °C to 30 °C.
model: Molecules have more kinetic energy / move faster.
More collisions between enzyme and substrate / more enzyme-substrate complexes formed.
exam.tip: Kinetic energy then collisions.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction decreases above 45 °C.
model: Enzyme is denatured / bonds holding the enzyme's shape break.
Active site changes shape.
Substrate no longer fits / is not complementary, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.
exam.tip: Always mention the active site changing shape.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of reaction stops increasing at high substrate concentrations.
model: All active sites are occupied / enzyme is saturated.
Enzyme concentration is the limiting factor.
exam.tip: Avoid saying the substrate has run out.

exam.q: A student kept an enzyme at 5 °C and then at 80 °C. Both samples were then put at 37 °C. Predict and explain what happens to the activity of each sample.
model: The 5 °C sample will work (at the normal rate) at 37 °C.
Because it was not denatured at low temperature / only had low kinetic energy.
The 80 °C sample will not work / very little activity at 37 °C.
Because it was denatured / active site permanently changed shape.
exam.tip: Contrast reversible (cold) with permanent (hot).

exam.q: Trypsin works in the small intestine. Suggest why trypsin does not work in the stomach.
model: Stomach is acidic / low pH / pH about 2; trypsin optimum is about pH 8.
So the active site changes shape / trypsin is denatured, substrate cannot fit.
exam.tip: Compare the stomach pH with the optimum pH.

exam.q: Describe how you could keep the pH and temperature constant when investigating the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity.
model: Use a buffer solution (of the same pH) in each tube.
Use a (thermostatically controlled) water bath at the same temperature.
exam.tip: Name the equipment, not just 'keep it the same'.

exam.q: Explain the shape of a graph of rate against substrate concentration.
model: At low substrate concentration the rate increases as substrate concentration increases.
Because there are more collisions / more enzyme-substrate complexes formed.
At high concentration the rate levels off / plateaus.
Because all active sites are occupied / enzyme concentration is limiting.
exam.tip: Two parts of the graph, each described and explained.

exam.q: Explain how temperature, pH and substrate concentration affect the activity of an enzyme such as amylase.
model: As temperature increases to the optimum, molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more often.
So more enzyme-substrate complexes form and the rate increases.
Above the optimum (about 37 °C for amylase in humans) bonds holding the enzyme's shape break and the active site changes shape.
Substrate (starch) no longer fits, enzyme is denatured and rate falls; this is permanent.
Amylase has an optimum pH (about 7); pH above or below changes the active site shape, so rate decreases; extreme pH denatures it.
Increasing starch concentration increases rate because of more collisions.
Until all active sites are occupied, then rate stays constant because enzyme concentration is limiting.
exam.tip: Cover all three factors; collisions for rises, shape for falls, saturation for plateau.

exam.q: Enzymes from bacteria that live in hot springs at 80 °C are used in some industrial processes. Suggest why.
model: They have a high optimum temperature / are not denatured at high temperatures.
So reactions can be carried out quickly at high temperatures / faster rate.
exam.tip: Link high optimum to faster reactions.

worked.q: The time taken for amylase to digest starch was measured at different temperatures: 20 °C 300 s, 30 °C 150 s, 40 °C 100 s, 50 °C 250 s, 60 °C no reaction. Calculate the rate at 30 °C using rate = 1000 / time, and identify the optimum.
steps: Rate at 30 °C = 1000 / 150 = 6.7 s^-1 (to 2 significant figures).
The shortest time is at 40 °C (100 s), so the rate is highest there: 1000 / 100 = 10 s^-1.
The optimum is about 40 °C, but it could lie between 30 °C and 50 °C because readings were only every 10 °C.
At 60 °C there is no reaction because the amylase has been denatured; the active site has changed shape.
worked.ans: Rate at 30 °C = 6.7 s^-1; optimum about 40 °C.

worked.q: Model answer: Describe and explain the effect of pH on the activity of pepsin, which has an optimum pH of 2.
steps: Describe: the rate of pepsin activity is highest at about pH 2 and decreases as the pH increases or decreases from pH 2.
Explain the peak: at pH 2 the active site has the correct shape, so it is complementary to the protein substrate and the most enzyme-substrate complexes form.
Explain the fall: away from pH 2 the charges on the amino acids change, bonds holding the shape break and the active site changes shape.
So the substrate fits less well and the rate falls; at very high pH (such as pH 8 in the small intestine) pepsin is denatured.
worked.ans: Rate is highest at pH 2 and falls on either side because the active site changes shape and pepsin is denatured at extreme pH.

worked.q: An enzyme reaction at a fixed enzyme concentration gives rates of 2, 4, 6, 7, 7 and 7 units at substrate concentrations of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 units. Explain the results and predict the effect of doubling the enzyme concentration at substrate concentration 6.
steps: From 1 to 3 units, the rate doubles and triples as substrate doubles and triples: substrate is limiting, more substrate means more collisions with free active sites.
From 4 to 6 units the rate stays at 7: all active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration is limiting.
Doubling the enzyme doubles the number of active sites.
At substrate concentration 6 there is excess substrate, so the rate would increase, up to about 14 units if substrate is still in excess.
worked.ans: Rate rises then plateaus at 7 because active sites become saturated; doubling enzyme would increase the rate (up to about 14).

bio_edx.0.7.summary: In this core practical you measure how pH affects the activity of the enzyme **amylase**, which breaks down **starch** into **maltose**. A mixture of starch, amylase and a **buffer solution** is kept in a water bath, and drops are tested with **iodine** every 30 seconds until the iodine stays **orange-brown**, showing all the starch has gone. The shorter the time, the faster the reaction, so you can calculate **rate = 1 / time** and plot rate against pH to find the **optimum pH**, then explain the drop on either side using **denaturation** and the shape of the **active site**.

core.p: The aim is to find out how the pH of the solution changes how fast amylase digests starch. Amylase is a carbohydrase made in the salivary glands and pancreas. It catalyses the breakdown (hydrolysis) of starch into the disaccharide maltose. Because iodine solution turns blue-black only when starch is present, you can tell when the starch has been used up.
bullets: **Enzyme:** amylase (a protein, so its shape can be changed by pH).
**Substrate:** starch. **Product:** maltose (a sugar).
**Indicator:** iodine solution, orange-brown, turns **blue-black** with starch.
**Independent variable:** pH (set using buffer solutions, e.g. pH 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9).
**Dependent variable:** the time taken for the starch to be completely broken down (end point).
**Control variables:** temperature, volume and concentration of amylase, volume and concentration of starch, volume of buffer, time between samples.

callouts.p: The end point is the first sample where the iodine **stays orange-brown** (does not turn blue-black). This means **no starch is left**.

core.p: Every item has a job: the buffer fixes the pH, the water bath fixes the temperature, and the spotting tile lets you test lots of small samples quickly.
bullets: **Spotting tile** with a drop of iodine solution in each well.
**Boiling tube** or test tube to hold the reaction mixture.
**Water bath** (or beaker of water) at a set temperature, e.g. **35 °C**, close to body temperature.
**Thermometer** to check the water bath temperature stays constant.
**Buffer solutions** of different pH values.
**Syringes or measuring cylinders** to measure equal volumes (e.g. 2 cm3 amylase, 1 cm3 buffer, 2 cm3 starch).
**Dropping pipette** (plastic) to transfer drops of mixture to the iodine.
**Stopwatch** to time the reaction and the 30 second sampling interval.
**Eye protection** (iodine is an irritant and stains).

core.p: This is the standard Edexcel method. Learn it in order, as 6 mark questions often ask you to describe it.
bullets: 1. Put **one drop of iodine solution** into each well of a spotting tile.
2. Use a syringe to put **2 cm3 of amylase** solution into a boiling tube.
3. Add **1 cm3 of buffer solution** of one pH (e.g. pH 5) to the tube.
4. Place the tube, and a separate tube of **starch solution**, in the **water bath at 35 °C** and leave for about **5 minutes** so both reach the right temperature (equilibrate).
5. Add **2 cm3 of starch solution** to the amylase and buffer, mix, and **start the stopwatch** at once.
6. Every **30 seconds**, use a pipette to take one drop of the mixture and add it to a new well of iodine.
7. Keep going until the iodine **stays orange-brown**; record the time taken (the end point).
8. Repeat the whole method with buffers of different pH values (e.g. pH 4, 6, 7, 8, 9).
9. Repeat each pH **three times** and calculate a **mean** time, ignoring anomalies.

callouts.p: Mix amylase with the buffer **before** adding starch, so the enzyme is already at the correct pH when the reaction starts. Start the clock the moment the starch goes in.

core.h: Why each control step is needed
core.p: Examiners reward reasons, not just steps. Every control variable is kept the same so that **pH is the only factor** affecting the rate, making the test **fair** and the results **valid**.
bullets: **Water bath:** temperature also changes enzyme activity, so it must be kept constant.
**Leaving solutions to equilibrate:** if cold starch is added, the mixture starts below 35 °C and the first part of the reaction is slower.
**Same volumes and concentrations:** more enzyme or more substrate would change the rate on their own.
**Same sampling interval:** sampling every 30 s for every pH makes the times comparable.
**Clean pipette / rinse between tests:** stops starch or iodine contaminating other wells.
**Buffer:** keeps the pH constant even as the reaction happens.

head: Variable
Type
How it is controlled or measured
rows: Water bath at 35 °C, checked with thermometer
Same stock solution, 2 cm3 by syringe
Same stock solution, 2 cm3 by syringe

callouts.p: A solution that **keeps the pH constant** at a known value.

core.p: Iodine solution is orange-brown. While starch is still present, a drop of the mixture turns the iodine **blue-black**. As amylase breaks the starch down the colour becomes less dark, and once no starch is left the iodine **stays orange-brown**.
bullets: Blue-black = **starch still present**, reaction not finished.
Orange-brown = **no starch left**, all starch converted to maltose.
The **time of the first orange-brown well** is the time taken for the reaction.
If the very first sample stays orange-brown the reaction was too fast; use less enzyme or sample more often (e.g. every 10 s).
If the iodine never stays orange-brown (e.g. after 10 minutes), the enzyme may be denatured at that pH: record this as no reaction / rate of zero.

callouts.p: Write **blue-black** for a positive starch test and **orange-brown** for negative. Do not write 'clear' or 'goes yellow'.

core.p: A short time means a fast reaction, so the rate is the **inverse** of the time. This turns your times into a number that goes up when the enzyme works faster.
bullets: **rate = 1 / time** (units s-1, or per second).
Some questions use **rate = 1000 / time** to give larger, easier numbers; the units are then 'arbitrary units'.
Alternatively, if you know the amount of starch: rate = amount of starch used / time (e.g. g/s).
Calculate the **mean** time for each pH first, then the rate.
Plot **pH on the x-axis** and **rate on the y-axis**; join points with a smooth curve or straight lines.
The **highest point** of the graph shows the **optimum pH**.

callouts.p: Give rates to 2 or 3 significant figures and always include units, e.g. 0.017 s-1.

core.p: At the **optimum pH** the enzyme's **active site** has exactly the right shape, so the most starch molecules fit into active sites and form **enzyme-substrate complexes** each second. This gives the highest rate and the shortest time.
bullets: Salivary amylase has an optimum pH of about **pH 7** (neutral), matching the mouth.
Pancreatic amylase works in the small intestine, which is slightly alkaline.
Different enzymes have different optimum pH values, e.g. **pepsin** in the stomach works best around **pH 2**.
Your measured optimum is only as precise as your pH intervals: if you tested pH 6, 7 and 8, the true optimum could be anywhere between about 6 and 8.

callouts.p: Only a substrate with a **complementary shape** fits the active site. Anything that changes the shape of the active site lowers the rate.

core.p: If the pH is **too far above or below the optimum**, the bonds holding the enzyme's 3D shape are disrupted. The **active site changes shape**, so starch **no longer fits** and cannot form enzyme-substrate complexes. The enzyme is **denatured**.
bullets: Rate falls on **both sides** of the optimum, giving a peaked curve.
Near the optimum, small pH changes slightly alter the active site and reduce the rate.
At extreme pH, the active site is so changed that the enzyme is **denatured** and the rate drops to **zero**.
Denaturation by extreme pH is usually **permanent**.
Always link: pH change, active site **changes shape**, substrate **no longer fits / not complementary**, fewer enzyme-substrate complexes, **lower rate**.

callouts.p: Enzymes are proteins, not living things. Say **denatured**, never 'killed' or 'dead'.

core.p: The method has some built-in limitations. Knowing them lets you answer 'evaluate' and 'suggest an improvement' questions.
bullets: **Sampling every 30 s** means the true end point could be up to 30 s earlier than recorded; sample every **10 s** to improve resolution.
**Judging the colour** is subjective; compare against a reference well of iodine alone, or use a **colorimeter** to measure the colour objectively.
**Temperature drift** in a beaker of water; use an electric **thermostatic water bath**.
**Reaction starts before timing** if there is a delay; start the stopwatch the instant starch is added.
**Carry-over** of starch on the pipette; rinse it with water between samples.
**Repeats and means** improve the reliability (repeatability) and help identify anomalies.
Test **more pH values** near the peak (e.g. 6.5, 7.0, 7.5) to find the optimum more precisely.

core.p: The hazards in this practical are low, but you should still be able to state them with a control measure.
bullets: **Iodine solution** is an irritant to eyes and skin and stains: wear **eye protection** and wipe up spills.
**Amylase** can cause allergic reactions if inhaled as a powder or splashed: avoid skin contact, wash hands.
**Hot water bath:** water at 35 °C is not a scald risk, but keep electrical water baths away from spills.
**Glassware** can break: report breakages and do not pick up broken glass with fingers.

core.h: Linking to the rest of Topic 1
core.p: This practical draws on the enzyme ideas from 1.7 to 1.9 and the rate calculations in 1.11. Expect exam questions that combine them, for example describing the method and then calculating rate from a table.
bullets: Same method can be adapted for **temperature** (change the water bath temperature, keep pH constant).
Can be adapted for **substrate concentration** (vary starch concentration, keep pH and temperature constant).
Rate graphs for temperature and pH have a similar peaked shape for the same reason: active site shape changes.
Enzymes are **biological catalysts**: they speed up reactions without being used up.

callouts.p: A **biological catalyst**: a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.

analogy.t: A key cut for one lock
analogy.p: The active site is like a lock and starch is the key. At the optimum pH the lock has its perfect shape and keys slot in and turn quickly. Change the pH and it is like the lock being bent: at first the key fits badly and works slowly, and at extreme pH the lock is so warped that the key no longer fits at all. Where it breaks down: a real enzyme is not rigid; its active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, and unlike a key, the substrate is changed (broken into maltose) by the reaction.

terms.d: A carbohydrase enzyme that catalyses the breakdown of starch into maltose.
A carbohydrate (polysaccharide) that is the substrate in this practical.
The sugar (disaccharide) produced when amylase breaks down starch.
Orange-brown reagent that turns blue-black when starch is present.
A solution that keeps the pH constant at a set value.
The pH at which an enzyme works fastest (highest rate of reaction).
The region of an enzyme where the substrate binds; its shape is complementary to the substrate.
Formed when the substrate binds to the active site of the enzyme.
When the shape of the active site has changed so the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme cannot work.
The first sample where iodine stays orange-brown, showing all the starch has been broken down.
How quickly the reaction happens; here calculated as 1 / time taken.
The variable you change on purpose; in this practical, pH.
The variable you measure; here the time for starch to be broken down.
A variable kept the same so that only the independent variable affects the results.
An instrument that measures how much light passes through a solution, giving an objective colour reading.

mistakes.w: The enzyme is killed at high or low pH.
mistakes.r: The enzyme is **denatured**: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.

mistakes.w: The iodine turns clear / yellow when the starch has gone.
mistakes.r: Iodine **stays orange-brown** when no starch is present; it turns **blue-black** if starch is present.

mistakes.w: A longer time means a faster rate.
mistakes.r: A longer time means a **slower** rate; rate = 1 / time.

mistakes.w: The buffer is used to keep the temperature the same.
mistakes.r: The buffer keeps the **pH** constant; the **water bath** keeps the temperature constant.

mistakes.w: The active site is destroyed / the enzyme dissolves.
mistakes.r: The bonds holding the shape are disrupted, so the **active site changes shape**.

mistakes.w: Control variable: use the same equipment.
mistakes.r: Name a measurable variable: same **temperature**, same **volume and concentration** of amylase and of starch.

mistakes.w: Add the starch then wait 5 minutes before timing.
mistakes.r: Equilibrate the solutions **separately** in the water bath, then mix and **start timing immediately**.

mistakes.w: Repeating makes the results more accurate.
mistakes.r: Repeating and taking a mean makes results more **repeatable / reliable** and helps spot anomalies; accuracy improves by reducing errors e.g. sampling more often.

exam.q: Name the enzyme used in the pH core practical and the product it forms from starch.
model: Amylase
Maltose (sugar)
exam.tip: Name the specific product, maltose, not just 'glucose' or 'sugar'.

exam.q: State the colour of iodine solution when starch is present.
model: Blue-black
exam.tip: Write both words: blue-black.

exam.q: Explain why a buffer solution is added to the reaction mixture.
model: To keep the pH constant / at a set value
So that the effect of each pH can be measured (fair test)
exam.tip: Buffer is about pH, never temperature.

exam.q: Explain why the solutions are placed in the water bath for 5 minutes before they are mixed.
model: So they reach the required temperature (e.g. 35 °C)
Temperature affects enzyme activity / rate, so it must be the same in every test
exam.tip: Link the step to a variable being controlled.

exam.q: At pH 7 the iodine first stayed orange-brown after 50 s. Calculate the rate of reaction. Give the unit.
model: s-1 (per second)
exam.tip: Show the formula rate = 1 / time first.

exam.q: Give two variables, other than temperature, that should be controlled in this investigation.
model: Volume / concentration of amylase
Volume / concentration of starch
(also: volume of buffer, time between samples)
exam.tip: Be specific: 'same amount of amylase' is weaker than 'same volume and concentration'.

exam.q: Suggest one improvement to the method that would give a more accurate end point.
model: Take samples more frequently, e.g. every 10 s
Because the end point could be anywhere between two samples / reduces the interval
exam.tip: Always say why the improvement helps.

exam.q: At pH 3 the iodine was still blue-black after 10 minutes. Explain this result.
model: pH 3 is far from the optimum / too acidic
Active site changes shape / enzyme denatured
Starch no longer fits active site / no enzyme-substrate complexes so starch not broken down
exam.tip: Use the chain: pH, shape, fit, complex, rate.

exam.q: Explain why the rate of reaction is highest at pH 7.
model: pH 7 is the optimum pH for amylase
Active site has the correct shape / is complementary to starch
Most enzyme-substrate complexes formed per second
exam.tip: Mention the active site, not just 'enzyme works best'.

exam.q: Describe a method to investigate the effect of pH on the activity of amylase.
model: Drop of iodine in each well of a spotting tile
Measure fixed volumes of amylase and buffer solution of known pH into a tube
Place amylase/buffer and starch in a water bath at a constant temperature (e.g. 35 °C) to equilibrate
Add starch, mix and start stopwatch
Every 30 s add a drop of mixture to iodine
Record time when iodine stays orange-brown / no longer turns blue-black
Repeat with buffers of different pH, keeping volumes and temperature the same
Repeat at each pH and calculate a mean / calculate rate = 1/time
exam.tip: For 6 marks give a logical sequence, include the measurement, the control of temperature and the range of pH values.

worked.q: A student recorded these times for starch to disappear: pH 5: 150 s, 170 s, 160 s. Calculate the mean time and the rate in s-1.
steps: Add the three times: 150 + 170 + 160 = 480 s
Divide by 3: 480 / 3 = 160 s mean time
Rate = 1 / time = 1 / 160
= 0.00625 s-1, which is 0.0063 s-1 to 2 significant figures
worked.ans: Mean = 160 s; rate = 0.0063 s-1

worked.q: Results: pH 4 no end point after 600 s; pH 6 = 80 s; pH 7 = 40 s; pH 8 = 100 s. State the optimum pH and calculate how many times faster the reaction is at pH 7 than at pH 8.
steps: The shortest time is 40 s at pH 7, so the optimum (from these results) is pH 7
pH 4 had no end point: the enzyme was denatured, rate taken as zero
worked.ans: Optimum about pH 7; the reaction is 2.5 times faster at pH 7 than at pH 8.
